sens: To make a deep and prolonged cry (referring to a bovine animal)
To express a violent feeling through a cry (figuratively)
H1600.detail:
1. To bellow is to make the characteristic cry of cows and oxen — a deep, resonant sound. In 1 Samuel 6:12, the cows that are bringing the ark of God back to Israel bellow along the way: they can be heard from afar, which shows both their presence and their distress at being separated from their calves.
2. Figuratively, to bellow describes a cry that expresses suffering or intense emotion. In Job 6:5, it is asked: "Does the ox bellow over his fodder?" — the idea is that an animal only cries out if it is lacking something or suffering. This cry becomes the image of a raw and authentic complaint.
H1600.origine: The verb גָּעָה comes from a Hebrew root that imitates the deep sound of the beast. In Hebrew, many verbs of cry or sound are formed on the same principle: the word reproduces or suggests the image of the noise itself. This onomatopoeia captures the visceral cry of cattle.
H1600.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Old Testament, in two very different contexts. In 1 Samuel 6:12, the cows bellow while performing a miracle — they travel without a driver to bring the ark back to the land of Israel, and their bellowing accompanies this wonder. In Job 6:5, the verb serves as a comparison: Job asks if a beast cries out for no reason, to say that his own complaint, like the cry of the ox, has a real cause. In both cases, the bellowing evokes the raw reality of suffering or a condition that cannot be ignored.
H1600.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is as real and audible as the cry of a beast. For Job, it is a defense: he does not complain without cause, just as an animal has no reason to cry if it has something to eat. For us, the bellowing of the cows in 1 Samuel shows how God even uses mute creatures to accomplish His purposes and proclaim His action.

sens: Place near Jerusalem
H1601.detail: Goath is a location situated near Jerusalem, mentioned in the description of the boundaries of the restored city. The prophet Jeremiah describes the line that the measuring cord will follow during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile: the line will extend to the hill of Gareb, then make a circuit near Goath (Jeremiah 31:39). This place thus marks a boundary of the holy city in its restored form.
H1601.origine: The Hebrew name גֹּעָה (goah) literally means "roaring" or "crying" (from the root expressing noise, particularly that of cattle). Although the name originally evokes a powerful sound, it designates a specific geographical location here. The etymology may suggest a place characterized by animals or rugged terrain.
H1601.emploi: Goath appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 31:39. It is mentioned in the context of the promise of restoration of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. The prophet lists the points that mark the new boundary of the holy city, from north to south. Goath is one of these landmarks, associated with the hill of Gareb, two points that likely delineated an area known to the contemporary inhabitants of Jeremiah.

sens: To feel intense repugnance or disgust towards something or someone
To reject with aversion, to push away as abominable
To be defiled, profaned (passive sense)
H1602.detail:
1. To abhor is to feel a deep, almost physical repugnance towards someone or something. It is to say "I cannot stand that" — not merely out of disapproval, but from visceral disgust. When the Lord says to Israel, "My soul will not abhor you" (Leviticus 26:11), He means that He will not reject you with disgust, that He will not find you repugnant.
2. The verb can also mean to reject or push away something as abominable and intolerable. When the people abhor the divine laws (Leviticus 26:15), they actively reject them, pushing them away because they find them intolerable.
3. In the passive form, the word evokes defilement, profanation — being cast out or rejected as impure. This is what happens to the shields of warriors "cast away" on Mount Gilboa (2 Samuel 1:21), abandoned like dirty objects that no one wants.
H1602.origine: The verb גָּעַל comes from a root that expresses physical disgust, bodily repugnance. It evokes the idea of something that provokes an instinctive reaction of rejection — like in the presence of filth or refuse. The family of the word includes other terms related to defilement and ritual impurity. It is a strong word, speaking of the body as well as the soul.
H1602.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in curses or judgment speeches. It is particularly concentrated in Leviticus 26, where the Lord states the consequences of Israel's unfaithfulness: if the people despise the divine laws and abhor them, then the Lord will abhor the people (Leviticus 26:43-44). The usage fluctuates between divine disgust towards the unfaithful and human rejection of the covenant. It is also found in prophetic laments (Jeremiah 14:19; Ezekiel 16:45), where it expresses the mutual rejection between the people and their God. It is a word of rupture, of radical separation.
H1602.portee: This word confronts us with the reality of divine judgment and the separation that sin brings. It is not an abstract punishment, but a personal rupture — God turns His face away in disgust. Conversely, God assures that He will not abhor us (Leviticus 26:44): it is a promise that even in exile, His relationship with His people does not turn into repugnance. This reminds the believer that forgiveness is not merely an erasure, but a restoration of relationship.

sens: Son of Ebed, a man who led a revolt against Abimelech at Shechem
H1603.detail: Gaal is a man who appears in the story of Shechem during the time of the Judges. He arrives in Shechem with his brothers and gains the trust of the inhabitants (Judges 9:26). He incites the Shechemites to revolt against Abimelech by persuading them that they should not serve a man like him (Judges 9:28). However, his revolt fails: Abimelech drives him out of the city and forbids him from returning (Judges 9:35-41).
H1603.origine: The name Gaal means "disgust" or "abomination" in Hebrew, an image that perhaps reflects the role of this character: someone who inspires rejection or provokes trouble. It comes from the root געל which expresses the idea of repulsion.
H1603.emploi: Gaal appears only in chapter 9 of the book of Judges (nine mentions in total). He is a secondary but important protagonist in the story of the revolt of Shechem against Abimelech, the son of Gideon who had proclaimed himself king. Gaal provokes the indignation of Zebul, the governor of the city, who denounces him to Abimelech. The confrontation between Gaal and Abimelech illustrates the political instability and conflicts that mark the time of the Judges, before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy.
H1603.portee: The story of Gaal shows how a promise of liberation based solely on words, without real force to support it, quickly collapses. It invites the reader to reflect on the difference between carnal rebellion and the true fight for justice, and reminds us that only God can offer lasting deliverance.

sens: A feeling of deep disgust and rejection towards something or someone
An intense aversion that drives one to push away or avoid
H1604.detail:
1. This word expresses a visceral disgust, a feeling of revulsion towards what is rejected. In Ezekiel 16:5, the newborn girl inspires this horror: no one wants to look at her, so despised and abandoned is she. It is the opposite of tenderness and compassion.
2. Horror is also this aversion that distances, that causes one to turn away. It conveys the deepest contempt, a rejection that goes beyond mere disagreement.
H1604.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally expresses the idea of rejecting or pushing away. It is related to the physical image of turning away one's gaze or stepping aside from what is displeasing. The same family of words in Hebrew can denote vomiting or violent rejection, which clearly shows the intensity of the feeling: it is a natural and instinctive repugnance.
H1604.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in this poignant passage from Ezekiel where the prophet describes the total abandonment of a newborn child. This context shows that horror is the supreme feeling of cruel indifference: no one casts a pitying glance at this rejected child. The word emphasizes the extreme humiliation and contempt.
H1604.portee: This image of a child inspiring horror reveals the depth of human abandonment and rejection — a reality that the heart of God cannot bear. It prepares the reader to grasp how God, on the contrary, looks at this little girl with love and mercy, saves her, and makes her His beloved. This word helps to measure the immense gap between human contempt and the grace of God.

sens: to address a severe reprimand to someone, to blame them with authority
to firmly forbid, to order to cease
to exert a force that stops or repels something
to exercise divine authority by chastising or reprimanding
H1605.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to reprimand someone severely, as Jacob reprimands Joseph after his dream (Genesis 37:10) — he blames him for what he dared to say, belittling him. It is a word of authority that exposes wrongdoing and expresses disagreement.
2. The word can also mean "forbid" or "order to stop": Boaz threatens the young men who were harassing Ruth (Ruth 2:16), firmly commanding them to leave the young girl alone. It is an authoritative and often threatening order.
3. In texts where nature or opposing forces are at play, the word describes a force that repels: God threatened the Red Sea and it dried up, or He threatens the clouds and they flee (Psalms 106:9; Isaiah 17:13). The image is that of a word or power that stops, that drives away.
4. Applied to God and His justice, to threaten means to chastise or reprimand: God chastises wicked nations, or reprimands Satan himself (Psalms 9:6; Zechariah 3:2). It is the sovereign exercise of divine authority to correct or punish.
H1605.origine: The root גער (ga'ar) evokes the idea of a strong word, a noise that stops or repels. The word belongs to the vocabulary of authority and command in the Old Testament. It expresses the power of the word — that of a father, a leader, or God — capable of correcting, repelling, imposing order. It is a verb that does not describe a silent brutal force, but an authoritative word.
H1605.emploi: The verb appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms, Isaiah, and the prophets. It is first used for human reprimand (Jacob reprimands Joseph), then for a severe order (Boaz threatens the harvesters not to harass Ruth). Very often, it describes the action of God: He threatens nature (the sea, the clouds, the wind) and it obeys; He chastises the wicked nations and demons (Satan in Zechariah 3:2). The meaning varies slightly: reprimanding a close one, ordering another to cease, or exercising divine authority that corrects or repels. In all cases, it is a word of authority that imposes itself.
H1605.portee: This word reminds the reader that God speaks with authority — not by brute force, but by His word that commands and is fulfilled. When the text says that God threatens the sea and it dries up, it is an image of His sovereignty: His word is enough. For the believer, this means that God corrects those He loves (as a father reprimands his child) to set them right. It is also a call to respect the authority that comes from God, whether parental or divine.

sens: A severe reproach addressed to someone to correct or punish them
The act of blaming with authority
A word or action that expresses discontent and seeks to intimidate
In God, the terrible sound of His anger that shakes creation
H1606.detail:
1. The threat is primarily an energetic reproach, a reprimand intended to correct someone who is acting wrongly. In Proverbs 13:1 and 17:10, we see that the threat of the wise or that of a discerning person carries more weight than physical punishment: it touches the mind and heart. It is the voice of one who holds authority and wants to bring someone back to better dispositions.
2. The threat can also be the very expression of discontent, the outburst of anger. This is what the passages describe where it accompanies terrifying phenomena: in Psalms 18:16 and 2 Samuel 22:16, God's threat causes tremors, shaking the earth itself, as if His reprimand had physical power.
3. In prophetic passages like Isaiah 30:17, the threat almost designates a cry, a vocal expression that is enough to make the enemy flee — a single man who growls can put a thousand to flight. It is the intimidating power of reproach.
4. Applied to God in apocalyptic or descriptive texts of His power, the threat becomes a cosmic force, the formidable sound of His anger that disrupts the universe — His nostrils that breathe, His words that shake the heavens.
H1606.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to growl," "to make noise," in the sense of a voice that rises with force. This root first evokes the growl of an animal or thunder, then extends to the reproach that growls, to the blame pronounced with authority. The threat carries within it the image of terrible noise, of a voice that imposes silence or flight.
H1606.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms and wisdom literature, but also in the prophets. In Proverbs (13:1, 13:8, 17:10, Ecclesiastes 7:5), the threat is that of the instructor or the wise — a word that is meant to educate. In the Psalms (18:16, 76:7, 80:17, 104:7), it is the threat of God that resounds over the world, that makes the waters and mountains tremble, that inspires fear even in angels. In the prophets (Isaiah 30:17, 50:2, 51:20, 66:15), the threat is directed at the enemy or the rebellious people, expressing divine resistance and the coming judgment. The context changes but the word always retains its weight: it is a powerful word that holds authority.
H1606.portee: For the believer, God's threat in the Bible is not merely the expression of His wrath; it reveals His holiness and rightful authority over the world. It reminds us that God does not turn a blind eye to evil and that a simple reprimand from Him is enough to shake the powers of the world. This should inspire reverential fear and submission to His word. Conversely, the threats of the wise to the foolish in Proverbs show that a strong word, spoken with authority and love, remains more effective than blind violence.

sens: To tremble, physically oscillate
To be agitated, shaken forcefully
To lose balance, stagger
To be troubled morally or spiritually
H1607.detail:
1. To tremble, physically oscillate: the word describes the movement of something shaking back and forth. The earth itself can be shaken by the anger of God: "The earth shook and trembled, the foundations of the heavens quaked, and they were shaken" (2 Samuel 22:8). It is a violent and involuntary movement.
2. To be agitated, shaken forcefully: the image extends to anything that moves turbulently. The waves of the sea "are agitated" without being able to cross the boundary that God has set for them (Jeremiah 5:22); the waters of the Nile "are agitated like torrents" (Jeremiah 46:7). The word paints a picture of tumult and agitation.
3. To lose balance, stagger: in a more abstract sense, it means to stumble, to topple. A whole people "stumbles" and perishes in one night, "without the hand of any man" (Job 34:20). Death causes them to collapse suddenly.
4. To be troubled morally or spiritually: the word also expresses inner shaking, the loss of emotional control. Those who drink the wine of divine wrath "will stagger and be like madmen" (Jeremiah 25:16), deprived of their reason and stability.
H1607.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּעַשׁ (ga'ash) expresses oscillatory movement, that of something shaking. It is related to other words in the family that describe chaos and disturbance. The root image is that of something agitated, tossed from side to side, like a leaf in the wind or a person shaken by an irresistible force. The word appears only a few times in the Bible, but each usage retains this power of agitation and disturbance.
H1607.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms, in Job, and in the prophets. It is first used literally to describe the tremors of creation before the manifestation of divine power (2 Samuel 22:8 and its parallel in Psalms 18:8). It then applies to the forces of nature—the waves and waters—that move uncontrollably (Jeremiah 5:22 and 46:7). Finally, it describes the fate of men in the face of God's anger: they stagger, lose their footing, and sink into madness or death (Job 34:20 and Jeremiah 25:16). Each time, it highlights the absence of stability, the submission to a greater force.
H1607.portee: This word reminds the believer that God alone is stable and unchanging, while everything that strays from Him—nature, peoples, individuals—finds itself in the grip of instability and trouble. It invites one to seek their foundation not in oneself or in creatures, but in the One who "trembles" before His own justice. It is a warning against pride and a call to reverential respect.

sens: Mountain in the region of Ephraim in Israel
Torrents or valley near this mountain
H1608.detail:
1. Gaasch is a mountain located in the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. Its name means "trembling" or "shaking," possibly evoking earthquakes in this terrain. It is where Joshua, the great leader of Israel after Moses, was buried after his death (Joshua 24:30 and Judges 2:9).
2. The name "Nachalé-Gaasch" ("torrents of Gaasch") refers to the valley or waterways that form on the slopes of this mountain. It is from here that Hiddaï, one of the warriors of King David's personal guard, originated (2 Samuel 23:30 and 1 Chronicles 11:32).
H1608.origine: The Hebrew name גַּעַשׁ comes from a root that expresses the idea of vibration or shaking. This image evokes the movements of the ground or natural tremors in this mountainous region of Ephraim. The word Nachalé ("torrents") complements this geographical name to designate the valleys or periodic waterways characteristic of mountainous slopes.
H1608.emploi: Gaasch appears four times in the Hebrew Bible: twice in the account of Joshua's death and burial (Joshua 24:30 and Judges 2:9, which report the same event), and twice in the lists of David's warriors (2 Samuel 23:30 and 1 Chronicles 11:32, which are also parallels). The mountain of Gaasch, north of another mountain bearing the same name, marks the precise location of Joshua's tomb at Timnath-Serah. Nachalé-Gaasch is mentioned to indicate the geographical origin of a soldier: it is an identifiable region, important for situating families.
H1608.portee: Joshua's tomb at Gaasch reminds believers that this great liberator and conqueror of Israel, despite his victories and unwavering faith, remains a mortal man, buried in the ground like all others. It is a mark of humility: even the most glorious leader enters into death, and his success belonged to the Lord far more than to his own strength.

sens: Son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau
Edomite chief during the Patriarchs' time
H1609.detail:
1. Gaetham is one of the sons of Eliphaz, who was himself the son of Esau (Genesis 36:11). He thus belonged to the lineage of the Edomites, descendants of Esau, the older brother of Jacob. His brothers were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz, Amalek, and Korah.
2. Gaetham became a chief among the Edomites (Genesis 36:16), like his brothers. He represents one of the leading families of the Edomite people during the patriarchal era, before the establishment of Israel in Canaan.
H1609.origine: The name Gaetham literally means "burnt valley," composed of Hebrew elements evoking a desert or arid area. This name reflects the nature of the Edomite territory, a mountainous and rocky region located southeast of the Dead Sea, often inhospitable. The genealogical context shows that the Edomites bore names tied to their local geography.
H1609.emploi: Gaetham is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in connection with the genealogy of Esau: twice in chapter 36 of Genesis (verses 11 and 16) and once in Chronicles (1:36). These passages follow the same pattern: listing the sons of Eliphaz and the Edomite chiefs descended from him. No particular event is reported concerning him; his mention is purely genealogical, attesting to his existence as an ancestor of the Edomite clans.

sens: Without company, by oneself
The highest point, summit of an elevation
H1610.detail:
1. This word denotes solitude, the state of one who is alone, without accompaniment. In Exodus 21:3-4, it describes the slave who leaves alone from his servitude: "If he came in alone, he shall go out alone"—the emphasis on this solitude contrasts with the case where the slave had a wife or children at the time of his release, who would then remain with the master. It is a concrete word to say "by himself, without anyone with him."
2. The word can also denote the upper part of something, its summit or height. In Proverbs 9:3, wisdom "cries out on the heights of the city"—it refers to the elevated point, the peak from which its voice carries far and is heard.
H1610.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of standing up, of rising. Its primary meaning is related to solitude or separation (one who stands "by himself"), and by extension to physical elevation, to the summit or height. The root evokes the image of one who is isolated, unique, or of that which dominates by its height.
H1610.emploi: The word appears only three times in biblical Hebrew. Two usages are found in Exodus 21:3-4, in the code regarding the release of slaves: the word "alone" (gaph) qualifies the slave who enters servitude without family and who exits in the same manner, unlike one who married during his servitude. A third usage appears in Proverbs 9:3, where "summit" denotes the high point from which wisdom proclaims its invitation. In all cases, the word remains rare and specialized, used for strong images: social isolation or spatial elevation.
H1610.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize two aspects of life before God: the trial of solitude (one who finds themselves alone, without support) and the position of strength (one who occupies the summit, from which they speak with authority). In the legal context of Exodus, the solitude of the freed slave reminds of God's justice that does not leave anyone abandoned. In the context of Proverbs, the image of the summit evokes the power and clarity of divine wisdom, audible and visible from afar.

sens: Wing of a bird or a flying creature
Extension, lateral or protruding part of the body or a structure
H1611.detail:
1. The wing is the part of a bird's body that allows it to fly. In Daniel's vision, the lion has "eagle's wings" (Dan 7:4), an image of power and speed — the eagle is the most majestic bird. These wings can be plucked, which signifies that the power of the kingdom is neutralized.
2. By extension, the word refers to any part that extends or protrudes to the side, like the wings of a creature or a structure. The leopard in the vision has "four wings like a bird" on its back (Dan 7:6): here too, the wing represents the ability to act quickly, to impose itself, even though the leopard itself is not a bird. The image is one of mobility and dominance.
H1611.origine: The Hebrew word gaph comes from a root that evokes the idea of something that extends or protrudes. In Hebrew, the wing is always associated with movement, lightness, and power. The word is close to other Hebrew terms describing what is extended or floating. In the Greek Old Testament, it is rendered by the Greek ptéryx (πτέρυξ), the common word for "wing."
H1611.emploi: The word gaph appears only twice in biblical Hebrew, both in the prophetic vision of Daniel 7. In these two instances, it describes the wings of mysterious creatures emerging from the sea. These wings are not ordinary wings: they represent superhuman power and the ability to dominate. The plucking of the lion's wings marks the end of its dominance; the four wings of the leopard symbolize its formidable speed and agility. The prophetic context makes the wing a symbol of political and military power.
H1611.portee: For the Bible reader, the image of the wing in these visions reminds us that earthly kingdoms, no matter how powerful, are ultimately creatures subject to the will of God. The removal of the lion's wings shows that God can take away power as quickly as He can grant it. It is an invitation not to marvel at the power of the world, but to recognize that only God controls history.

sens: Climbing plant that produces clusters of grapes
The grape cluster itself, or the fruit of the grape
Image of prosperity, fertility, and divine blessing
Symbol of the people of Israel, of their covenant with God
Metaphor for fragility or God's judgment
H1612.detail:
1. The vine is the cultivated plant that produces grapes: it is a climbing shrub, rooted near waters like in Egypt (Ezekiel 19:10), from which clusters are harvested at the time of the vintage. The word sometimes refers to the grape itself (Numbers 6:4 speaks of not eating dried or fresh grapes).
2. It symbolizes wealth and well-being: to possess one's vine, to sit under one's vine without fear, is to enjoy peace and abundance (Micah 4:4, Zechariah 3:10). The harvesters bring in the fruits, a sign of prosperity and stable life.
3. Israel is compared to the vine planted by God: "Your mother was like you, a vine planted near the waters" (Ezekiel 19:10). Similarly, Psalm 80:9 speaks of God who rooted a vine in the land of Israel and established it.
4. When Israel turns away, the vine becomes barren, stripped, judged: Jeremiah 6:9 speaks of gleaning the remnants of Israel like a vine, and Joel 1:7 describes how the enemy has ravaged it. This is the image of divine punishment for unfaithfulness.
H1612.origine: The Hebrew word גֶּפֶן (gephen) refers to both wild and cultivated vines. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of growth and spreading: the vine winds, climbs, and extends. This plant was central to life in the ancient Near East: wine was a common drink, grapes a precious food, and vineyards a major economic asset. Hence its constant role in the Bible as a symbol of wealth and blessing.
H1612.emploi: The word appears 53 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the poetic and prophetic books. In historical narratives (Kings, Chronicles), it evokes the possession of vineyards as a sign of prosperity and stable social order. In the psalms, the vine of Israel becomes the central image of the covenant: God planted it, protected it, but also threatens it if it is unfaithful. In the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel), this symbolism intensifies: the vine ravaged by enemies represents Israel judged. The Song of Songs uses it to evoke natural beauty and fertility. Ezekiel even compares Israel to a vine tree, barren and good for burning (15:2-6).
H1612.portee: The vine teaches believers that God's blessing creates a fruitful work, but one that requires protection and faithfulness. It reminds us that unfaithfulness to God exposes one to barrenness and judgment. Finally, it invites the reader to recognize themselves in this vine planted by God, called to produce good fruit in the covenant.

sens: The wood used to build Noah's ark
An ancient wood whose exact nature remains uncertain
H1613.detail:
1. Gopher wood is the material that God prescribes to Noah for the construction of the ark: "Make yourself an ark of gopher wood" (Genesis 6:14). This is the only place in the Bible where this word appears. God requires this specific wood, suggesting that it possessed particular qualities — sturdiness, durability, or resistance to moisture — essential for a vessel capable of navigating during the flood.
2. The exact botanical identity of gopher wood remains a mystery. Ancient translators and scholars have proposed various hypotheses: some think of cypress (known for its durability in wet environments), others of acacia or another wood from the ancient Near East. The Hebrew word itself does not reappear anywhere, and no known root explains it clearly, making any certainty impossible.
H1613.origine: The exact etymology of the Hebrew term remains obscure. No identified Hebrew or Aramaic root clarifies it with certainty. The word could come from an ancient Near Eastern language or be a very old term that has disappeared from the common vocabulary of biblical Hebrew. Its uniqueness in the Bible suggests that it is a technical or regional term, perhaps borrowed, whose meaning has been lost over the centuries.
H1613.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 6:14, where God commands Noah to build the ark of gopher wood. This unique and precise usage underscores the divine importance of this material choice: it is not an ordinary construction, but a project specially commanded by God Himself, carried out according to His exact specifications. The context of the flood, where the ark must float for forty days and forty nights, shows that this wood was reputed to be capable of withstanding such an ordeal.
H1613.portee: This enigmatic detail teaches us that God leaves nothing to chance: He chooses the materials and prescribes the means. Even if we do not know what gopher wood really is, this mention reminds us that God precisely provides for the survival of His people (Noah and his family), and that obedience to the divine plan — even when it asks us for unusual or misunderstood things — is the key to salvation and life.

sens: Flammable yellow substance that burns with a suffocating odor
Divine destruction of evil by fire
Sign of God's anger and judgment
Punishment of the wicked and the evil
H1614.detail:
1. Sulfur is a natural yellow substance that ignites easily and produces acrid smoke: it is the concrete material of destruction (Genesis 19:24, where the Lord rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah).
2. The Bible uses sulfur as an image of God's destructive judgment: it is His way of purifying the earth from injustice and sin, not just a weapon, but a divine signature (Psalms 11:6: "He rains coals, fire, and sulfur on the wicked").
3. Sulfur concretely expresses divine anger: it is not an abstraction, but a terrifying physical reality, the weapon that God uses against His enemies (Isaiah 34:9, where the torrents of Edom become sulfur).
4. It is a punishment reserved specifically for the wicked and the evil: those who reject God will see sulfur fall upon them, as a deserved and inevitable judgment (Job 18:15, where sulfur is poured upon the dwelling of the criminal).
H1614.origine: The Hebrew word goph-rit literally refers to sulfur, this natural substance extracted from the earth. Its basic image is that of a substance that burns, consumes, and destroys everything it touches — hence its constant use in passages of judgment and destruction. This root evokes final devastation, the complete annihilation of evil or a wicked presence.
H1614.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in passages of divine judgment. It is especially found among the prophets (Isaiah 2 times, with Ezekiel) and at key moments when God destroys guilty peoples: Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis), the judgment of the wicked (Psalms), the destruction of Edom (Isaiah 34). Each occurrence shows it as the material instrument of divine fury, accompanied or not by fire. In Deuteronomy 29:23, it describes the ravaged state of a land judged by the Lord. It is always an image of judgment, never a mere landscape element.
H1614.portee: Sulfur in the Bible reminds us that God judges evil with a concrete reality: it is not an abstract threat, but a formidable power. For the Christian, it is a call to take divine anger against sin seriously and not to despise His justice. It also warns us against hardening our hearts: God does not leave injustice unanswered. Finally, it is a sign of the urgency of conversion, for those who reject God will face a judgment as real and destructive as the sulfur that fell on Sodom.

sens: White powder obtained by burning limestone, used for whitening or binding stones
H1615.detail: 1. Lime is a powder obtained by intensely heating limestone; it is used for construction, for whitewashing walls, or for whitening them. In Isaiah 27:9, the prophet says that the Lord will reduce the stones of the idolatrous altars "like lime stones turned to dust" — a powerful image of complete and irreversible destruction, as if these monuments of sin were collapsing and disintegrating into sterile powder.
H1615.origine: The Hebrew word גִּר comes from a root meaning to burn or to cook; it is a concrete term for this well-known building material in the ancient Near East. Its Aramaic equivalent, גִּיר, means "plaster" and refers to the same type of white powder used for coating and sealing. This family of words reflects a universal construction technique in antiquity.
H1615.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 27:9. The prophet uses it in a context of judgment and destruction of idolatrous sanctuaries: the Lord will break the stones dedicated to sin and reduce them to powdered lime, symbolizing their total and irreversible annihilation. It is a raw and familiar image — lime turned to dust evokes complete nothingness.
H1615.portee: This image of lime turned to dust reminds the reader that God radically destroys everything that opposes Him and His holiness. It calls to recognize the fragility of all human rebellion in the face of divine power and invites trust in the Lord rather than in human constructions.

sens: Person who temporarily lives in a country that is not their own, without hereditary rights
One who does not belong to the established community and does not own land
Resident protected by law, but subject to special rules
Figuratively: one who feels isolated or without a true home
H1616.detail:
1. A foreigner is primarily one who resides in a country other than their homeland. It is a newcomer, someone who lives there temporarily, without owning the land or having inherited rights. When Abram learns that his descendants will be foreigners in Egypt (Genesis 15:13), it means they will live there without belonging to that country, as temporary and vulnerable residents.
2. The foreigner in Israelite law is a well-defined legal category: they enjoy certain protections (they must rest on the Sabbath like the Israelites, according to Deuteronomy 5:14), but they are subject to obligations and restrictions (in Leviticus 17:10, foreigners who eat blood are punished just like the Israelites). They are "inhabitants" without full property rights.
3. The Law of Moses offers foreigners a gradual and protected integration: they participate in the feasts and harvests (Deuteronomy 26:11), receive a share of the gleanings (Leviticus 19:10), and enjoy equality before justice (Leviticus 24:22). They are not slaves, but residents of lower status.
4. Figuratively, the word also expresses a feeling of isolation or non-belonging: David confesses, "I am a foreigner and a traveler here" (Psalms 39:13), expressing human fragility and the feeling of being far from one's true home with God.
H1616.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of "to stay" or "to reside temporarily." It contrasts with one who owns the land by right and with one who is born of the country. The term describes a concrete social status in the ancient Near East: one who lives among others without being a property owner or a full member of the group. Its frequent use in the Law reflects the importance of this intermediate status in the civil life of Israel.
H1616.emploi: The word appears 83 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and in the historical books. It concretely designates foreign residents in Israel (2 Chronicles 2:17 counts them in thousands), and also the Israelites themselves when they live in exile (Genesis 15:13, Psalms 39:13). The Law mentions the foreigner dozens of times to specify their rights and obligations: they share the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10), must respect certain prohibitions (Leviticus 17:10-15), and benefit from social protections (Deuteronomy 10:18-19). The word can also simply mean "to dwell" as a foreigner (Exodus 2:22, where Moses names his son Gershom, meaning "foreigner there"). The meaning varies according to context: legal status, condition of vulnerability, or metaphorically, condition of spiritual exile.
H1616.portee: This word reminds the believer that God cares for those who do not have a secure place: foreigners benefit from the care of the Law, and God Himself presents Himself as their protector (Deuteronomy 10:18). For the Christian, it also evokes the condition of God's people in this world: we are foreigners and travelers (1 Peter 2:11), awaiting a city whose architect is God. This biblical perspective broadens compassion towards migrants and the uprooted, and places all human existence under the sign of an ultimate belonging to God rather than to a terrestrial territory.

sens: Son of Benjamin, ancestor of the Geraites tribe
Father of Ehud, the judge who delivered Israel
Member of the Geraite family in the tribe of Benjamin
H1617G.detail:
1. Gera is a son of Benjamin mentioned among the ten sons of this patriarch, founder of the tribe of Benjamin. His name appears in the genealogical list of Genesis 46:21 during Jacob's descent into Egypt, alongside his brothers Bela, Beker, Ashbel, and others.
2. Gera is best known as the father of Ehud, who became a judge and deliverer of Israel. Ehud became famous for delivering Israel from the oppression of the Moabite king Eglon (Judges 3:15), making Gera the ancestor of an important line of Israelite leaders.
3. The name Gera also designates the family or clan of the Geraites, members of the tribe of Benjamin, whose trace can be found in later genealogies (1 Chronicles 8:5).
H1617G.origine: The name Gera literally means "a grain" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of seed or a small fruitful thing. Although it is a personal name, its etymology suggests an image of fertility and multiplication, appropriate for a founding ancestor of a lineage and a tribal family.
H1617G.emploi: Gera appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. First in Genesis 46:21, he is listed among the sons of Benjamin at the time Jacob descends into Egypt. He reappears in Judges 3:15 as the father of Ehud, the judge who saves Israel from Moabite oppression, highlighting the importance of his descendants. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 8:5, he appears again in the genealogy of the Benjamites, confirming his role as a patriarch of a recognized branch of the tribe.
H1617G.portee: Gera reminds us that the spiritual greatness of Israel rests on faithful ancestors and generations of believers. His grandson Ehud became a powerful deliverer, showing how God blesses the descendants of those who walk in His will. It is an invitation to see our own heritage in a perspective of spiritual fertility: what we root in faith can bear fruit in our children and grandchildren.

sens: Ancestor of the Benjamite lineage during the time of the united monarchy
Father of Shimei who cursed King David
H1617H.detail: Gera is the name of a Benjamite family whose members are mentioned during the time of King David. The most famous is his son Shimei, who becomes notorious during David's flight from Absalom: Shimei comes out from Bahurim and violently curses King David while shouting against him (2 Samuel 16:5). Later, after Absalom's death, this same Shimei, son of Gera, hurries down to meet David to seek his favor, and the king spares his life in exchange for an oath (1 Kings 2:8). Gera thus represents a Benjamite house loyal to the old dynasty of Saul, which must reconcile with the new order established by David.
H1617H.origine: The name Gera literally means "a grain" in Hebrew, perhaps recalling a simple and humble image to designate a descendant or family. This name marks the identity of a lineage from the tribe of Benjamin, which also included several other people bearing the same name across different generations. The name appears four times in Scripture, always associated with the tumultuous events of David's reign.
H1617H.emploi: Gera is mentioned four times in the Bible, exclusively in 2 Samuel and 1 Kings, always as the father of Shimei. The first two occurrences (2 Samuel 16:5 and 19:16) recount how Shimei, son of Gera, curses David during his flight, then rushes to meet him when David is reconciled with Israel. The third (2 Samuel 19:18) mentions him again in the context of crossing the Jordan. The fourth (1 Kings 2:8) reminds the aging king of this cursing episode and the promise made to the Benjamite. Thus, Gera is never the main subject of the narratives, but his name remains attached to the story of the dynastic transition and reconciliation between the tribes.
H1617H.portee: The story of Gera's family, through his son Shimei, illustrates the grace and forgiveness offered even to those who have cursed God's anointed king. It also shows how ancient tribal rivalries (Benjamin against Judah) find resolution in submission and humility before the power established by God.

sens: Son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin
Member of the Gera family in the tribe of Benjamin
H1617I.detail:
1. Gera is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin himself. He appears in the genealogy of the sons of Benjamin listed in 1 Chronicles 8:3, where he is named among the sons of Bela alongside Addar and Abihud. He is an ancestor of the Gera family that will mark the tribe of Benjamin in its history.

2. The name Gera also designates, by extension, the members of the family or clan of Gera descended from this ancestor. This family bears his name and descends from him, which is common in biblical genealogies where an entire lineage takes the name of its founder.
H1617I.origine: The name Gera literally means "grain" or "seed," evoking the image of a seed or a small element that multiplies. This meaning reflects the biblical genealogies where a founding ancestor gives rise to an entire descent and a family bearing his name. The meaning of the name thus emphasizes the idea of foundation and family multiplication.
H1617I.emploi: Gera appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:3, in the context of the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is listed as one of the sons of Bela, alongside several brothers. This genealogical mention makes him an important link in the family chain that connects Benjamin to the following generations and to the families of Benjamites who will see other biblical figures bearing the same name emerge.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
Son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin
Member of the Gera family among the Benjamites
H1617J.detail:
1. Gera is a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived before the Israelite monarchy. He is an ancestor among the genealogies of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 8:7, where he appears as a link in a long genealogical chain.
2. According to the genealogical context, Gera is the son of Bela and the grandson of Benjamin himself, making him an important figure in the origins of the tribe, although very little information is transmitted to us about him.
3. His name gave rise to a family, the Geraites or members of the family of Gera, which constituted a family group within the tribe of Benjamin.
H1617J.origine: The name Gera literally means "a grain" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking an idea of smallness or multiplication. It is a simple and concrete name, like many ancient Hebrew names that drew their meaning from the realities of daily life — food, land, plants. The text of 1 Chronicles 8:7 also designates him by the name "Heglam," which refers to the idea of transport or deportation.
H1617J.emploi: Gera appears only once in the biblical text: in 1 Chronicles 8:7, in the genealogy of Benjamin. He is presented there as the father of Uzza and Ahichud, and as an active character since it is said that he "transported them." His role in the passage is not one of significant action, but of genealogical link: he allows the transmission between an earlier generation of Benjamin and a later generation. This passage simply enumerates the ancestors of Benjamin and their descendants, with Gera appearing as an important genealogical link of this tribe.

sens: Contagious skin disease causing intense itching
Pustular skin sore or lesion
In a broader sense, any repugnant or disqualifying dermatological condition
H1618.detail:
1. Scab is a skin disease characterized by intense itching and often oozing. It renders the afflicted person unclean and excludes them from worship: a priest afflicted with scab cannot serve in the sanctuary (Leviticus 21:20), and a sick animal cannot be offered as a sacrifice (Leviticus 22:22).
2. In a context of curse, scab is among the terrible plagues that strike an unfaithful people: God threatens to send the ulcer of Egypt, hemorrhoids, scab, and itch, from which one cannot be healed (Deuteronomy 28:27). It expresses humiliation and physical suffering as divine punishment.
3. More broadly, this word designates any repugnant or dishonorable skin condition: it stands in opposition to the purity and health required to approach God or to be a worthy instrument of His worship.
H1618.origine: The Hebrew word garav comes from the root meaning "to scratch" or "itching," evoking the action of constant scratching. It belongs to the family of names for skin diseases in the Bible, where cultic purity also involves physical integrity. The term first denotes a concrete reality — a visible and contagious lesion — before taking on a symbolic meaning of defilement or a mark of divine judgment.
H1618.emploi: The word garav appears three times in the Bible, always in a context of cultic purity or punishment. Two uses concern the conditions for access to worship: the Law excludes from the priesthood any man with scab (Leviticus 21:20) and forbids offering a sacrifice of an animal afflicted with this disease (Leviticus 22:22), as it symbolizes impurity. A third, more dramatic use mentions it as one of the plagues sent by God upon a rebellious people (Deuteronomy 28:27), where it is added to other incurable diseases. Each time, scab marks a rupture, an exclusion, or inevitable suffering.
H1618.portee: Scab in the Bible reminds us that access to communion with God requires integrity of the whole person — not out of pride, but because God is holy and sin wounds the human being entirely, body and soul. It invites us to see in diseases and infirmities not defects of worth, but calls to mercy and compassion. It also reminds us that God does not spare punishment for those who persistently reject Him.

sens: One of David's elite warriors
A man from the tribe of Judah
H1619G.detail: Gareb is a warrior who is listed among the thirty mighty men of King David. He is mentioned in the list of David's military heroes (2 Samuel 23:38 and 1 Chronicles 11:40), always associated with Ira the Jetherite, suggesting that they may have formed a pair of fighters or came from the same clan. His name literally means "scabby" (afflicted with scab or leprosy), but this nickname likely does not describe his physical condition in the biblical context: he was a man recognized for his courage in service to the king.
H1619G.origine: The name Gareb comes from a Hebrew root referring to a skin condition. Although the literal meaning of the name is not flattering, it was borne by this renowned warrior, showing that the ancient Hebrews were not afraid to use direct nicknames as proper names. The original meaning of the name does not imply anything about the worth or status of the one who bore it.
H1619G.emploi: Gareb appears twice in the Bible, exclusively in the lists of David's elite warriors: in 2 Samuel 23:38 and 1 Chronicles 11:40. These two references are nearly identical and present him as one of the thirty mighty men who served King David during the period of the united monarchy. He is always mentioned immediately after Ira the Jetherite, suggesting a close association between these two fighters or belonging to the same group.

sens: Hill near Jerusalem
H1619H.detail: Gareb is a hill located near Jerusalem, apparently to the southwest of the city. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 31:39, in a prophetic vision where the prophet describes the future boundaries of rebuilt Jerusalem: "The measuring line shall go out further straight ahead, to the hill Gareb, and it shall turn toward Goath."
H1619H.origine: The name Gareb literally means "scabby" or "one who has scab," probably referring to the rocky or rough appearance of this hill. It is a common descriptive name in biblical topography, where places are named after their visible natural characteristics.
H1619H.emploi: Gareb appears only once in Scripture, in Jeremiah 31:39. It is mentioned in the context of a prophetic promise concerning the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile. The prophet lists the geographical points that will mark the boundaries of the restored city, suggesting that even the marginal or damaged areas of Jerusalem will participate in this future reconstruction. This passage shows that the divine promise of restoration covers the entire geography of the city.
H1619H.portee: This discreet mention of Gareb in a prophecy of restoration reminds us that divine grace extends even to the most humble and least remarkable places. No location, however modest, is excluded from God's renewal plan.

sens: Fruit of the olive tree, small and hard, containing a pit and rich in oil
The olive itself, as a berry remaining attached to the tree after harvest
H1620.detail: 1. The word concretely refers to the fruit of the olive tree: a small, hard, oval berry, green and then darkening to black at maturity, which contains a pit and very oily flesh. It is one of the oldest and most important crops in the Middle East: olives are eaten, but especially the oil is pressed from them, valuable for cooking, lighting, and religious rituals. In Isaiah 17:6, the prophet speaks of the shaken olive: when harvesting, most of the fruit falls, but a few olives remain attached to the top and branches, two or three here, four or five there — these "gleanings" of forgotten olives symbolize the survivors who will remain in Israel after divine judgment.
H1620.origine: The Hebrew word גַּרְגַּר (garghar) is an onomatopoeic formation that perhaps imitates the sound of shaking — this repetition of syllables is found in other Hebrew words for fruits or seeds. The word reflects the image of a small, round, hard berry that can be rolled, hence the idea of something small and dense. The cultivation of the olive tree was so central in Israel that the same root gave the name of the tree itself (זַיִת, zaïth): the word "olive" and "olive tree" share the same word family.
H1620.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 17:6. The prophet describes a judgment on Israel: the once-productive olive will be shaken by the Lord, and only a few isolated olives will remain — the image is that of gleaning, this meager and scattered harvest that recalls famine and desolation. The unique use of the term emphasizes its very precise usage: not the olive tree in general or its wood, but the fruit in this concrete situation of remnant and scarcity, which reinforces the idea of divine judgment as impoverishment.
H1620.portee: This image of the forgotten olive on the tree teaches the believer that even in divine judgment, God leaves a remnant — a few survive. It is a message of hope hidden within a word of threat: there will be a continuation, a seed for the future. This tension between destruction and preservation invites the reader to meditate on the divine mercy that remains even in the heart of punishment.

sens: Part of the body connecting the head to the trunk
What one wears around the neck, such as an ornament or clothing
Symbol of what one keeps close, that which is precious and inseparable
H1621.detail:
1. The neck is the part of the body that connects the head to the trunk. It is a visible and exposed area, hence its use to speak of what is suspended or attached to it.
2. When speaking of adorning the neck, it evokes jewelry, crowns, or ornaments placed there (Proverbs 1:9: "a crown of grace for your head, and a necklace for your neck"). These visible elements show what is valued in the eyes of others.
3. To tie something around one's neck means to carry it with oneself, to keep it constantly close to one's heart and mind (Proverbs 3:3: "Bind them around your neck," referring to kindness and faithfulness). It is a strong image: these virtues must be inseparable from the one who possesses them, visible and constant, like a necklace that is never taken off.
H1621.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of throat or narrow passage. In Hebrew, the neck ("garog") is the link between the upper and lower parts of the body. This word appears mainly in Proverbs, where it is used figuratively to evoke what one carries, retains, or shows.
H1621.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, all in the book of Proverbs. It is always used figuratively: never to describe the neck in purely anatomical terms, but always to speak of what is attached or suspended from it. Sometimes it refers to adornments and crowns of grace that adorn the one who possesses wisdom (Proverbs 1:9), and sometimes to moral values that one ties to oneself like inseparable jewels (Proverbs 3:3, 3:22, 6:21). The neck thus becomes the image of the intimate and visible link between what one cherishes and who one is.
H1621.portee: For the believer, this image of the neck invites reflection on what one constantly carries with oneself: one's convictions, values, faith. To bind kindness and faithfulness around one's neck is to ask whether these virtues are truly visible in one's life, inseparable from who one is. The neck, an exposed area, also reminds us that our faith and choices are not hidden: they are carried openly for others to see.

sens: Canaanite people of antiquity, descendants of Canaan
Inhabitants of the promised land before the arrival of Israel
H1622.detail:
1. The Girgashites are a Canaanite people, meaning one of the nations descended from Canaan, son of Ham. Their name could mean "inhabitants of a clayey land," which evokes a people established in a specific region of the ancient Levant.

2. At the time of Israel's entry into the promised land, the Girgashites were among the indigenous peoples that the Israelites had to fight and drive out. They are regularly listed alongside other Canaanite nations: Jebusites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Hivites. This list shows that the promised land was occupied by several distinct peoples that Israel had to conquer.
H1622.origine: The name likely comes from a Semitic root designating a type of soil or habitat. Girgas would be an eponymous ancestor of this people. The name appears in the genealogies of Genesis as one of the sons of Canaan, alongside Sidon, Heth, and other founding peoples. The Girgashites represent one of the Canaanite nations whose existence the Bible documents before the Israelite conquest.
H1622.emploi: The Girgashites appear seven times in the Bible, exclusively in enumerative lists of Canaanite peoples. They are first mentioned in the genealogy of Genesis 10:16 as descendants of Canaan. God later reminds Abraham of their presence (Genesis 15:21) among the nations from which his descendants would inherit the land. Later, Moses lists the Girgashites among the seven nations that the Israelites would confront upon entering Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:1). Joshua mentions their presence during the entry into the promised land (Joshua 3:10 and 24:11), and a historical note in 1 Chronicles 1:14 reproduces the genealogy. In each occurrence, they are listed alongside the same peoples, illustrating their role as a Canaanite nation to be driven out before Israel.
H1622.portee: The Girgashites remind the reader that the promise of the promised land to Abraham was not an empty land: it was inhabited by established peoples that God had decided to drive out before Israel. This mention maintains the historical and realistic dimension of the biblical narrative, showing that the conquest of Canaan involved real and distinct peoples. It also invites reflection on God's faithfulness to fulfill His promises, even against apparent obstacles.

sens: to scrape the skin with a hard object
to remove something by scraping
to scratch oneself
H1623.detail:
1. To scratch means to scrape the skin with a hard object, usually to relieve an itch or irritation. Job, afflicted with a painful disease, scratches himself with a shard (a piece of broken pottery) while sitting in ashes, an act that expresses both physical suffering and humiliation (Job 2:8).
2. More broadly, to scratch means to remove a layer of material by scraping with something sharp or rough, as one would remove dirt or dust from a surface.
3. The verb can also refer to the action of scratching oneself, scraping the skin repetitively, often a natural gesture in response to discomfort.
H1623.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּרַד (garad) literally means "to scratch" or "to scrape." It evokes the image of a hard object scraping a surface, creating a characteristic noise and sensation. The word belongs to an ancient Semitic family related to gestures of friction and cleaning. It expresses a rudimentary and often uncomfortable action.
H1623.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 2:8. It describes the gesture of Job who, covered in painful sores and sitting in ashes as a sign of mourning and humiliation, scratches himself with a shard. This context of extreme illness and suffering gives the word its full weight: scratching is not a trivial gesture here, but the physical expression of agony and despair. The verb emphasizes the intensity of Job's torments and the absence of true relief.
H1623.portee: This gesture of Job scratching himself speaks to the raw reality of suffering. It reminds us that illness and pain are never abstract: they are experienced in the body, they overwhelm, they despair. In reading of Job scratching himself with a shard, we face a man laid bare before God, without artifice or pretense. It is a lesson in humility and compassion: those who suffer deserve our tenderness, not our hasty judgment.

sens: Provoke a quarrel or dispute
Engage in a confrontation or combat
Resist, oppose
Act in a way that creates trouble or agitation
H1624.detail:
1. To provoke a quarrel means to be the cause of a dispute or fight between people. It is to intentionally instigate a conflict: the violent man provokes quarrels (Proverbs 15:18), and the proud also stirs up strife (Proverbs 28:25). The image is that of one who throws oil on the fire.
2. To engage in a confrontation or combat means to initiate an armed struggle or enter into open conflict. God commands Israel not to attack certain peoples (Deuteronomy 2:5, 2:19), as this would be to engage in an endeavor that He does not approve. In 2 Kings 14:10, the king is warned not to embark on a disastrous venture.
3. To resist or oppose head-on is a nuance of the word: Babylon fought against the Lord (Jeremiah 50:24), meaning it stood against Him in active opposition.
4. To create trouble and agitation in order, either through words or actions — this is the general image of the verb, which applies to all contexts where someone provokes a disturbance.
H1624.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of lifting, stirring, or setting in motion. The Piel form (which we see here) intensifies the action: it makes it intentional, repeated, or causative. In Hebrew, the same root can express physical movement or moral disturbance — which shows that the ancients saw dispute as a 'trouble' of social order, a disorder that one 'raises' intentionally.
H1624.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the wisdom books (Proverbs) and in historical narratives (Kings, Chronicles) where it concerns military conflicts. In Deuteronomy, it refers to the prohibition of attacking certain neighboring peoples (2:5, 2:9, 2:19, 2:24): God denies Israel the right to engage in these wars. In Proverbs, the word describes the character of the violent or proud man who provokes disputes by his very nature. In Jeremiah and Daniel, it takes on the meaning of resistance or opposition to divine power. The meaning thus oscillates between two poles: intentionally creating a dispute and engaging in a risky combat.
H1624.portee: This word reminds us that conflicts do not arise from nothing: someone 'stirs' them up. Biblical wisdom invites the believer to examine their heart so as not to be the one who throws the spark of discord. It also emphasizes that opposing God is to fight against the order of the world — a futile and ruinous struggle. The word calls us to caution in our words and actions, and to submission to divine will rather than rebellion.

sens: Bring food from the stomach back to the mouth to chew it again
Characteristic behavior of certain hoofed animals that allows them to be classified as clean or unclean according to Mosaic law
H1625.detail:
1. Rumination is the biological process by which certain animals (ruminants) bring their partially digested food from the stomach back to the mouth to chew it again, which allows them to better assimilate it. This is the literal and concrete meaning of the word: 'You may eat any animal that has a split hoof, is cloven-footed, and chews the cud' (Leviticus 11:3).
2. In the law of Moses, rumination is one of the two criteria — along with having a split hoof — that determines whether an animal is clean or unclean and therefore whether it can be eaten. An animal that ruminates alone, without having a split hoof (like the camel) or that has a split hoof but does not ruminate (like the pig), is declared unclean. This criterion structured the daily life of the people of Israel and expressed the order established by God.
H1625.origine: The Hebrew word גֵּרָה (gera) likely comes from a root expressing the idea of 'rejecting' or 'spitting,' as rumination involves bringing back to the mouth what had been swallowed. It denotes a natural and observable process, accessible to the ordinary Israelite who lived in contact with herds. In Greek, the corresponding word is χύλος (chylos) in some translations, but more often the process itself was described.
H1625.emploi: The word 'ruminate' appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the dietary laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy (chapters 11 and 14). It is repeated to state the criteria for purity: a clean animal must both have a split hoof AND ruminate. The usages list the animals that ruminate but are not clean because they do not have all the required signs (camel, rock badger, hare, Leviticus 11:4-6), and those that have a split hoof but do not ruminate (pig, Leviticus 11:7). This repetition shows that Israel needed to memorize these distinctions to live in accordance with the covenant.
H1625.portee: These laws remind believers that the relationship with God is based on obedience to clear and concrete commandments, sometimes without rational explanation. Today's believer also sees that God observes and ordains the details of our daily lives. For early Christians, these rules took on new meaning: Peter learns through a vision that what was unclean becomes clean in Christ (Acts 10), suggesting that the law of purity pointed towards a spiritual cleansing accomplished in Him.

sens: unit of weight used in commercial transactions and value estimations
subdivision of the shekel, representing one-twentieth of this unit
H1626.detail:
1. The guéra is a small unit of weight used to measure and weigh precious metals, particularly silver, during transactions. It is the basic standard of the Israelite monetary system, used to set prices and mandatory contributions. When counting the people, each must give a half-shekel as an offering to the Lord, which is ten guéras (Exodus 30:13).
2. The guéra functions as the main subdivision unit of the shekel: one shekel is always worth twenty guéras, without variation. This fixed equivalence is repeated in all contexts where the law mentions monetary values, whether for the redemption of firstborns, property estimations, or the payment of contributions to the sanctuary (Leviticus 27:25; Numbers 3:47; Numbers 18:16; Ezekiel 45:12). Adhering to this proportion ensures fairness and certainty in all religious and civil transactions.
H1626.origine: The word guéra comes from Hebrew and literally means a grain (like a grain of grape or seed). This image of the grain reflects the idea of a very small portion, a minimal but precise unit. Its actual weight was equivalent to that of about 16 grains of barley or 4 to 5 carob seeds, according to ancient estimates. This origin in the vocabulary of small things shows how the ancient Israelites measured in a concrete and practical way: by comparing to everyday objects that could be weighed and verified.
H1626.emploi: The word 'guéras' appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in regulatory and legislative texts. It appears in Exodus 30:13 for the counting and offering to the sanctuary, in Leviticus 27:25 and Numbers 3:47, 18:16 for the estimations and redemptions prescribed by the law, and in Ezekiel 45:12 in the vision of the restored temple. Everywhere, it serves to precisely establish the value of contributions and payments due to God. The context is always one of moral and religious purity: what is given to the sanctuary must be measured accurately, without fraud or shortcuts.
H1626.portee: The guéra reminds us that in the relationship with God, nothing is too small to count, and that faithfulness is also measured in the details. The precise weight of each piece of silver symbolizes the righteousness and honesty required of God's people: one cannot cheat God, not even by a grain. This meticulousness in measurement taught Israel that God sees everything and expects complete integrity, even in the most routine acts.

sens: The throat or neck, part of the body through which voice passes
The voice itself, what comes from the throat
The mouth, the seat of words
Metaphorically, an abyss or a threatening depth
H1627.detail:
1. The throat primarily refers to the neck or throat, the part of the body that connects the head to the trunk. It is a concrete word for the physical passage of breathing and voice (Isaiah 3:16 speaks of the haughty neck of the daughters of Zion).
2. By extension, the throat represents the voice that comes from it — this power to speak, to shout, to cry "at full throat" (Isaiah 58:1) means to shout with all one's voice.
3. The throat can also simply refer to the mouth or the seat of words, as in Psalms 149:6 where the praises of God are in the throat (rendered as "mouth"), meaning on the lips that utter them.
4. Figuratively, the Bible uses "throat" to evoke the emptiness or depth of a well: in Psalms 5:10, the throat of the wicked is "an open grave," an image of death that swallows and a gaping throat ready to devour.
H1627.origine: The Hebrew word גָּרוֹן (garone) comes from a simple root meaning that which opens or hollows out — the idea of a cavity through which one breathes, speaks, and swallows. It is related to other Hebrew words describing openings or depths. It is a physical and direct term, without sophistication, to name this vital part of the body through which a person makes their voice heard.
H1627.emploi: The word appears about 8 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the Psalms and the prophets. It is used in three ways: (1) in the physical and literal sense, for the neck or throat as a part of the body (Isaiah 3:16 on the haughty bearing); (2) for the voice and cry, as it is from the throat that sound comes (Isaiah 58:1 "cry with a full throat"); (3) in a figurative and dark sense, associated with death or evil. In Psalms 5:10, the throat of the wicked is compared to an open grave, a terrifying image of the mouth that never ceases to swallow and devour. These uses show that the word oscillates between the anatomical concrete and the threatening symbolic.
H1627.portee: The throat reminds the reader that voice and speech spring from the heart and body — it is through the throat that a person expresses their faith, their cry to God, or their lies and curses. In Psalms 5:10, the image of the open grave warns that the flattering and malicious words of the wicked arise from a spiritually dead soul. In Isaiah 58:1, the prophet must cry "with a full throat" for the word of God to be heard — a lesson on the strength and courage required to proclaim divine truth.

sens: place of stop or lodging
H1628.detail: Gueruth is the name of a place mentioned only once in the Bible. It is a location serving as a refuge or stop, where one can rest. The name literally means "place of stay" or "lodging."
H1628.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root gur (גור) which means "to stay" or "to dwell temporarily." This same term is used in the Bible to refer to a stranger or an immigrant, one who resides in a place that is not their homeland. Gueruth thus carries the idea of a temporary refuge, a place where one stops without staying permanently.
H1628.emploi: Gueruth is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 41:17. This passage recounts that Jeremiah and a group of Judeans stopped at Gueruth, the Inn, after leaving Jerusalem before heading to Egypt. It is a place of passage and rest, strategically located on the road of exile.

sens: To cut, to slice
To be pushed away, set aside
To lose one's place, one's access
H1629.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a physical action: to cut or slice something. It is the image of a brutal separation, a rupture.
2. In the biblical text, this verb is used in the passive voice to describe the state of one who is cut off, separated, pushed away. The psalmist says "I am chased away from your sight": he feels excluded from the presence of God, distanced, as if he were cut off from what supports him (Psalms 31:23).
3. The underlying idea is that of loss of access, of exclusion. One who is thus cut off finds themselves deprived of contact, relationship, and divine protection.
H1629.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally expresses the action of cutting or separating. The image is that of a blade that slices, that divides. The verb can be active (to cut) or passive (to be cut, to be separated), which enriches its use: one can experience being pushed away, set aside, like an object sliced from a whole.
H1629.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved biblical uses, in Psalms 31:23. The psalmist uses it to express his feeling of abandonment or exclusion before God: he believes he is chased away from the divine gaze. It is a word of distress, uttered in haste and emotional turmoil. However, the context shows that this impression is corrected: the psalmist continues by reminding that God has heard his supplication. The word thus illustrates the human consciousness of rupture, even when it is involuntary or psychological rather than real.
H1629.portee: This word connects with the deep spiritual experience of the believer: that of feeling distance from God, the impression of being cut off from His presence. For the Bible reader, it reminds that these feelings of abandonment are authentic and that God takes them seriously. But the psalm also teaches that this subjective impression does not correspond to reality: God does not abandon those who cry out to Him.

sens: Mountain in northern Israel, in the territory of Ephraim, near Shechem
Place where blessings were proclaimed to Israel after crossing the Jordan
Site of the Samaritan temple built after the exile
H1630.detail: Garizim is a mountain located in northern Israel, in Ephraim, not far from the city of Shechem. Its name literally means "cuttings" or "portions," an image that perhaps evokes the rocky slopes of the mountain. According to the Law given to Moses, Garizim had a particular ceremonial role: after the Israelites crossed the Jordan to enter Canaan, six tribes were to stand on Mount Garizim to proclaim blessings, while six others stood on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses (Deuteronomy 11:29; Deuteronomy 27:12). This solemn liturgy indeed took place: Joshua 8:33 reports that all the people, their elders and judges stood on either side, some on the side of Garizim, others on the side of Ebal, to hear the blessing and the curse according to Moses' order. Later, after the exile, the Samaritans erected a temple on this mountain, making it central to their religious practice and distinguishing it from Jerusalem for the Jews.
H1630.origine: The name Garizim comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to cut" or "to divide" (gâraz), hence the meaning of "cuttings" or "portions." This descriptive name applies to a geographical formation, the mountain itself. The word belongs to the group of geographical proper names in the region of Shechem, which often bear names evocative of their natural features. The neighboring twin mountain, Ebal, formed with Garizim a complementary liturgical and geographical set: one for blessings, the other for curses.
H1630.emploi: Garizim appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the context of the Law and the conquest of Canaan. Deuteronomy 11:29 and 27:12 constitute the initial prescriptions: Moses commands that blessings be proclaimed from Garizim upon entering Canaan. Joshua 8:33 reports its actual fulfillment during the Jordan ceremony, where the two mountains serve as the backdrop for the simultaneous proclamation of blessing and curse. Finally, Judges 9:7 mentions Jotham who climbs to the top of Garizim to cry out against the inhabitants of Shechem a prophetic sentence, showing that the mountain remained a place of public speech and spiritual authority. The context is always that of blessing, curse, judgment, or solemn word.
H1630.portee: Garizim embodies for the reader the solemnity with which God establishes His covenant and its conditions: blessing for obedience, curse for disobedience. This mountain reminds us that the entry into Canaan was not silent, but through a public and official word, where all Israel was concerned. For the Christian, Garizim symbolizes the moment when God seals His covenant with His people and clearly proclaims its spiritual consequences.

sens: Cutting tool consisting of a metal blade attached to a wooden handle, used for cutting wood or stone
Figuratively: instrument of destruction or divine judgment
H1631.detail:
1. The axe is the classic tool of the lumberjack and carpenter. It consists of a metal blade fixed to the end of a wooden handle, which is wielded to strike. In Deuteronomy 19:5, a man goes to fell a tree in the forest with his axe in hand: the iron slips from the handle and accidentally kills his companion. In 1 Kings 6:7, during the construction of the temple, neither hammer nor axe resounds, which underscores the miraculous nature of this edifice built in silence.
2. Figuratively, the axe becomes the image of a power that executes or destroys. In Isaiah 10:15, the prophet says that the axe must not boast against the one who wields it: it is merely an instrument in the hand of the Lord, just like the saw or the rod. This image shows that every instrument of destruction remains subject to God's will.
H1631.origine: The Hebrew word garzen comes from a root that expresses the idea of cutting or chopping. It is a simple and concrete term, formed to directly designate this very common tool in the agricultural and architectural life of the ancient Near East. The iron axe was a precious possession, a symbol of labor and technical progress.
H1631.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. Deuteronomy 19:5 and 20:19 mention it in a legal and military context: it is the tool of the lumberjack, but also the instrument of destruction forbidden during a siege (one must not destroy fruit trees). In 1 Kings 6:7, it contrasts with the silence of the temple under construction. In Isaiah 10:15, it becomes a prophetic image of any instrument of judgment, reminding us that only God truly masters the destructive power.
H1631.portee: The axe speaks to us of useful and honest human labor, but also of the danger of instruments of power when pride is involved. It teaches us that no instrument, no talent, no authority can act without God's permission. It invites wisdom: to recognize that our power is never truly ours, but always in the hands of the Lord.

sens: To set aside, reserve for later
Not to consume or use immediately
To preserve, keep intact
H1633A.detail:
1. The word describes the action of putting something aside, intentionally reserving it for future use. It conveys the idea of holding back, not spending or using everything at once. In the text of Zephaniah, the judges are compared to wolves who do not "keep" anything for the morning: instead of leaving leftovers for the next day, they devour everything they find in their path.
2. The meaning also nuances towards the idea of preserving something without destroying or consuming it, leaving it intact. It is to hold something back through discipline or foresight, rather than wasting everything immediately.
3. In context, the verb evokes a form of wisdom or moderation: the one who "keeps" shows restraint, while the one who keeps nothing shows limitless greed.
H1633A.origine: The Hebrew root גרם (ga.ram) evokes the idea of cutting, separating, from which the meaning of "to set apart, reserve" naturally derives. The verb expresses the action of creating a separation between what is used now and what is reserved for later. It is a concrete image: one cuts the portion, sets it aside.
H1633A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zephaniah 3:3. It describes the lack of restraint of the judges of Jerusalem: they keep nothing, reserve nothing, show no moderation in their greed. This is a characteristic trait of their moral corruption — the total absence of restraint or foresight. The context highlights the contrast between one who knows how to hold back and one who devours without limit.
H1633A.portee: This word challenges believers on the virtue of restraint. The Bible values the one who knows how to "keep" — in the sense of mastering their appetites, not consuming everything at once, showing moderation. In contrast, the one who "keeps nothing" reveals a heart dominated by desire and injustice. For the Christian, it is an invitation to cultivate temperance and reject unrestrained covetousness.

sens: To break something into fragments, to reduce to pieces
Figuratively: to destroy, annihilate the strength or resistance of someone
H1633B.detail:
1. The word describes the action of breaking, materially: one breaks bones, one breaks an object into a thousand pieces. In Numbers 24:8, God "breaks the bones" of those who rise against His people — the image is that of a force that crushes, that reduces the power of an adversary to nothing.
