2. Figuratively, to break means to destroy, to overthrow, to render powerless. In Ezekiel 23:34, broken glass becomes the symbol of judgment that destroys, that ends the prosperity and security of the one who receives it. It is total destruction, annihilation.
H1633B.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּרַם (garam) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to reduce to pieces" or "to break." Its primary image is that of a bone being broken, gnawed — a violent and definitive action. The word belongs to the family of verbs of violent action, like other Hebrew verbs that describe destruction.
H1633B.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Numbers 24:8, it is used in the prophetic vision of Balaam: God, having brought Israel out of Egypt, breaks the bones of His enemies — it is an image of total victory and invincible power. In Ezekiel 23:34, the prophet uses it figuratively: the cup of divine judgment will be broken, poured out, and the one who drinks it will be broken himself, reduced to nothing. In both cases, the idea is one of complete and decisive destruction.
H1633B.portee: This word reminds us that God possesses absolute power and truly breaks the resistance of His enemies. For the believer, it also evokes the inevitable divine judgment against those who stand against Him. It is a call not to rebel against God, whose strength is insurmountable.

sens: Hard part of the skeleton that supports the body
Physical strength, vigor
Essence, deep nature of a person or thing
H1634.detail:
1. The bone is the hard element of the skeleton: it is the bony structure of the body. Job 40:13 describes the bones of the Leviathan as "tubes of bronze," an image of extreme solidity. The word literally refers to these bones that bear and support the entire body.
2. The bone represents strength and robustness. In Genesis 49:14, Issachar is called a "strong" donkey (literally "of strong bones"), meaning powerful and vigorous. It conveys the idea of physical solidity.
3. The bone symbolizes the very essence of a person, their intimate life. In Proverbs 17:22, "a joyful heart" "revives the bones," meaning it restores the person from within. Similarly, in Proverbs 25:15, "a gentle tongue can break bones": it reaches the very heart, the deep nature.
H1634.origine: The word in Hebrew comes from a root that expresses the idea of solidity and durability. For the Hebrews, the bone was the symbol of what lasts, of what is solid and vital. The cognate Aramaic (gerēm) has the same meaning. The bone, because it survives for a long time and structures the entire body, naturally becomes a poetic image of strength and deep being.
H1634.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the provided passages. It first refers to the bones of the animal or human body (Job 40:13 with the Leviathan). But biblical Hebrew also uses it metaphorically: physical strength (Genesis 49:14), and especially intimate life, the essence of a person. Proverbs use it to speak of what touches the soul and deep heart. That is why "drying up the bones" means destroying joy and vital energy, while joy "revives the bones" — it restores the whole person.
H1634.portee: For the Christian reader, the bone teaches that true strength is not only physical but also spiritual and emotional. The joy of the heart "revives" — it restores our whole being to its vitality. Conversely, depression and lack of hope "dry us up" and take away our strength. This invites us to seek from God the joy and peace that restore our soul.

sens: Hard part of the skeleton that supports the body
The most solid part, the essence of a thing
H1635.detail:
1. The bone is the hard and white part that forms the skeleton and supports the body of animals and humans. In Daniel 6:24, the lions "broke all their bones," which shows that bones are the most solid part of the body, and breaking them means complete destruction.
2. Figuratively, the word can refer to what is most essential or substantial in something — as one might say "the bone" of a matter to refer to its core — but this figurative use does not appear in the preserved Aramaic texts.
H1635.origine: This Aramaic word גְּרַם (gerem) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word גֶּרֶם (gerem, H1634), which also means "bone." Hebrew and Aramaic share this root. Both terms refer to the hard and mineral structure of the skeleton, and have no obvious metaphorical image at the root.
H1635.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Daniel 6:24, in the account where the king orders the accusers of Daniel to be delivered to the lions. The text describes how the beasts "broke all their bones" — a detail that underscores the violence of the sentence and the total annihilation of the bodies. The use is concrete and literal: there is no figurative nuance.
H1635.portee: This verse reminds us that God protects His faithful servants and that those who unjustly accuse believers face a fearsome judgment. The breaking of bones symbolizes the complete destruction of those who stand against the Lord and His people.

sens: member of a clan of Judah whose ancestor was named Garam
H1636.detail: 1. The Garmien is a descendant of Garam, a man of Judah. This clan or family is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the genealogical census of the children of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:19, where Kehila is referred to as a "Garmien." Like many clan names in the Old Testament, this term indicates the family origin or the group to which a person belongs.
H1636.origine: The Hebrew word גַּרְמִי (Garmien) likely derives from an ancestor named Garam, according to the classic model of Hebrew patronymics: the suffix -י (-i) means "descendant of" or "belonging to." The name Garam may evoke the idea of solidity or hardness (the Hebrew garem means "bone"), giving the name a connotation of strength. This type of designation was common in Israel to identify different families and their genealogies.
H1636.emploi: The Garmien appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:19. He is cited as the qualifier of Kehila, son of the wife of Hodijah. This passage is part of the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah, where the biblical author lists the descendants of various families. The context shows that this clan was an established branch of Judah, recognizable by this patronymic name.

sens: Open area where one threshes grain to separate the grain from the chaff
Open space, public or cleared place
Place dedicated or intended for a specific use
H1637.detail:
1. The threshing floor is the place where harvesters spread the ears of grain to trample them or to use a flail, in order to release the grains. It is an open, hard, and level space, usually at the edge of fields or villages. In *Deuteronomy 16:13*, the feast is celebrated by gathering "the produce of [one's] threshing floor" — indicating how central this harvest was to life.
2. By extension, the word refers to any open space or place: this is why one can speak of the "place" in front of the gate of Samaria where the kings stand (*1 Kings 22:10*), or the place where people gather.
3. The threshing floor takes on a religious dimension when it becomes a meeting place with God. Ornan's threshing floor becomes the site of the future temple, the holiest of places (*1 Chronicles 21:22* and *2 Chronicles 3:1*) — the place where the people offer their sacrifices.
H1637.origine: The Hebrew word *goren* comes from a root that evokes an open and flattened space. It specifically refers to the compacted ground where grain is threshed, distinct from the still-planted field or closed granaries. This image of the threshing floor — a place of transformation from raw grain to useful food — has naturally extended to the figurative sense of any open space or place of passage.
H1637.emploi: The word appears 36 times, mostly in historical narratives and laws. In agricultural contexts, the threshing floor is the place where the harvest takes place (*Ruth 3:2-14*, *1 Samuel 23:1*). It is subject to the tithe: the firstfruits of the grain are taken from it (*Numbers 15:20*, *18:27*). It can also be a refuge (*2 Samuel 24:16-24*) or a witness to miraculous signs (*Judges 6:37*). Ornan's threshing floor is of paramount importance: David purchases land there to build an altar to the Lord, which leads to the construction of the temple. Jeremiah uses the image of the trampled threshing floor to describe the invasion of Babylon (*Jeremiah 51:33*) — the threshing floor becomes a metaphor for destruction.
H1637.portee: The threshing floor reminds us that God transforms labor and toil into food and provision. It also symbolizes the places where the people meet God and where His will is fulfilled, even to the site of the temple itself. For the Christian, it speaks of the necessary stripping away (the chaff removed) so that the useful grain remains.

sens: To be crushed, reduced to crumbs
To experience an inner breaking, a deep distress
H1638.detail:
1. The word literally describes the action of breaking something into fragments — to be crushed, torn apart. This is the sense of a stone that breaks teeth: a violence that physically destroys. In Lamentations 3:16, the suffering poet says, "He has broken my teeth with gravel," an image of brutal and humiliating destruction.
2. The word also applies to the soul, to the inner person. In Psalms 119:20, "My soul is crushed by desire": here, "to break" means to consume, to morally and spiritually disintegrate. The soul is as if crushed under the weight of the intense desire to know God and His laws. It is a breaking of the heart, a deep distress rather than physical destruction.
H1638.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּרַס comes from a root that paints the image of something collapsing, being reduced to crumbs under overwhelming pressure. The "Qal" (passive) form describes the state of one who is broken; the "Hiphil" (active) form is that of one who breaks. The word belongs to the vocabulary of violence and destruction, frequent in passages describing physical or spiritual suffering.
H1638.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 119:20, the psalmist speaks of his soul being "broken" by the desire to know God's commandments — it is a confession of a consumed heart, filled with intense spiritual hunger. In Lamentations 3:16, he describes the broken teeth of the captive, an image of God's judgment and the extreme humiliation of the people in exile. These two uses show the word sliding from the concrete sense (broken teeth) to the figurative sense (the soul ravaged by emotion or suffering).
H1638.portee: This word invites the reader to take seriously the real violence of suffering — physical as in the captive of Lamentations, inner and spiritual as in the psalmist. It also shows that the hunger for God itself can be experienced as a "breaking" of the soul, a force that disintegrates the one who feels it, not by evil but by the good they passionately desire. For the believer, it is an invitation to welcome this breaking of the heart before God as legitimate and holy.

sens: To decrease the quantity or portion of something
To remove, take away a part of something
To deprive someone of what is due to them
To reduce, moderate, or restrict
H1639.detail:
1. The verb first evokes the action of decreasing a quantity: in Exodus 5:8, the Egyptians order that the bricks the Israelites were to produce not be cut off — in other words, not to reduce the task despite their fatigue. It is a matter of quotas and diminished measures.

2. It also means to remove, take away a part: when the Lord states in Ecclesiastes 3:14 that there is nothing to add or cut off from His works, it means that one cannot remove pieces, as they are perfect and complete.

3. The verb can express deprivation, depriving someone of a right or property: in Exodus 21:10, if a man takes a second wife, he must not cut off from the first her food or her marital rights — he cannot deprive her of what is due to her.

4. In a more abstract or figurative sense, to cut off can mean to restrict, limit, or even completely remove: in Numbers 27:4, the daughters of Zelophehad fear that their father's name will be cut off from his family — that is, forgotten, erased, completely removed.
H1639.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּרַע (gara') is probably related to the idea of cutting or slicing. It belongs to a family of words that express the action of removing, decreasing, or reducing. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this verb is often rendered by forms meaning "to remove" or "to take away." The root evokes the concrete image of cutting off a part, from which comes the figurative sense of decreasing or depriving.
H1639.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the wisdom books (Job, Ecclesiastes). In Exodus 5 and 21, it describes concrete acts: reducing a task or depriving of marital rights. In Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32, it applies to divine Law: nothing should be cut off from God's commandments. In the poetic and prophetic books (Job, Ezekiel, Jeremiah), it takes on more varied meanings, from the concrete (cutting hair in Isaiah 15:2) to the figurative (reducing or annihilating). The context determines whether the verb speaks of a material decrease, a deprivation of rights, or a total removal.
H1639.portee: This word reminds the reader of the importance of completeness and integrity: not to cut off anything from God's commandments is to receive them in their entirety, without weakening them through our unbelief or disobedience. It also emphasizes justice: one should not cut off from anyone what is due to them. For the Christian, this verb invites respect for the fullness of God's Word and not to mutilate it according to our preferences.

sens: To sweep away with force
To draw into an irresistible movement
H1640.detail:
1. The word paints the image of water that sweeps away everything in its path with irresistible power. It is the torrent that flows rapidly and carries along whatever it encounters: in the Song of Deborah, the torrent of Kishon "carries away" the defeated enemies in its waters (Judges 5:21).
2. More broadly, it means to be swept away by a superior, inevitable force — a movement that seizes you and propels you far from your position. The image is one of flight or defeat where the enemy cannot resist.
H1640.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of sweeping away, making disappear by pushing ahead. The primary image is mechanical and physical: something that flows, that leaks, that runs off while carrying away what is in its path. This root belongs to the concrete vocabulary of nature and the movement of waters.
H1640.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 5:21, at the heart of the Song of Deborah. This victory poem celebrates the defeat of the Canaanites and describes how the torrent of Kishon, swollen by the rains, sweeps away and carries off the chariots and enemy warriors who cannot resist it. It is a decisive moment: nature itself becomes the instrument of Israel's deliverance.
H1640.portee: This passage teaches that God has control over all elements — even the waters — to accomplish His victory. It reminds us that the power of the Lord infinitely surpasses that of men and their weapons, and that He can turn the appearance of defeat into miraculous triumph. For the reader, it is an invitation to trust in the one who masters the forces of nature.

sens: To drag something, to pull it forcefully towards oneself or elsewhere
To ruminate (for an animal)
To saw, to cut with a saw
To carry away, to remove with violence
To rush, to dash
H1641.detail:
1. To drag something means to pull it strongly in a direction, often despite resistance. This is the primary meaning of the word in Hebrew. It expresses the idea of a brutal or insistent action: one drags despite everything, leaving no choice. In Habakkuk 1:15, the fisherman "draws" the fish into his net by dragging them with the hook: the image is one of a force that captures and ensnares.
2. To ruminate means to chew over what has been swallowed: ruminating animals chew their food again. In Leviticus 11:7, a clean animal is recognized by the fact that it "ruminates" — this word describes the characteristic physiological process of ruminants.
3. To saw means to cut with a saw: the back-and-forth motion of the saw that grinds while cutting stone or wood. In 1 Kings 7:9, the stones of the temple are "sawed" with precision to fit perfectly.
4. To carry away and to rush express irresistible violence: a force that drags everything in its path. In Proverbs 21:7, the violence of the wicked "carries them away" against their will towards their ruin. In Jeremiah 30:23, the divine storm "rushes" upon the wicked in a destructive tempest.
H1641.origine: The verb garar expresses the idea of violent and continuous movement. The root evokes grinding, rubbing, dragging: this is why it covers both dragging, sawing (a repeated motion that rubs), and ruminating (the grinding motion of the jaw). The basic image is one of traction or friction that does not cease, that insists.
H1641.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, in very varied contexts. In Leviticus 11, it describes the rumination of clean animals. In 1 Kings 7, it refers to the sawing of the temple stones. In Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk, it expresses the violent movement of a force that drags: the violence that carries away the wicked, the storm that rushes, the net that draws in prey. The Segond translates the same word with very different verbs depending on the context, as what matters is the common idea of continuous and forced movement.
H1641.portee: This word reminds us that God controls the forces that sweep us away, even the most violent ones. When Jeremiah speaks of the divine storm rushing upon the wicked, it is the assurance that God's judgment is inexorable. Conversely, when Habakkuk mentions the net that draws in the fish, it is the image of capture: God does not let anyone escape. For the believer, it is an exhortation not to be swept away by violence or injustice.

sens: Philistine city in southern Palestine
Residence of Abraham and Isaac
Border region between Canaanite and Philistine lands
H1642.detail: Gerar is a Philistine city located in southern Palestine, near Gaza. It is where Abraham settles during his migration southward (Genesis 20:1), and it is in Gerar that King Abimelech, the lord of the area, takes Sarah into his harem before being warned by God. Later, Isaac also comes there during a famine and establishes his wells in the valley of Gerar (Genesis 26:6, 26:17), where he comes into conflict with the Philistine shepherds over access to water. The city marks the southern boundary of Canaanite territory (Genesis 10:19).
H1642.origine: The name literally means "a place of dwelling" or "lodging," from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of staying or residing somewhere. It is a real city in southwestern Palestine, inhabited by the Philistines, a people established on this coast before the arrival of Israel. The name reflects its role in biblical narratives: it is a place where the patriarchs pass through and stay.
H1642.emploi: Gerar appears ten times in the Bible, mainly in the narratives of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 20 and 26). It is cited as a boundary of Canaanite territory (Genesis 10:19). King Abimelech is its ruler during the visits of Abraham and Isaac. The city is also mentioned in the context of King Asa's wars against the Ethiopians (2 Chronicles 14:12-13), where it seems to be a strategic point in the region.
H1642.portee: The narratives of Abraham and Isaac in Gerar show how God protects His servants even in foreign lands and how He accompanies the patriarchs in their migrations. These episodes reveal that even non-believing kings like Abimelech recognize the divine presence and the holiness of God's people.

sens: crushed or ground grain
newly roasted and crushed ears of grain
the grain offering prepared in this way
H1643.detail:
1. The word first designates grain that has been crushed or ground: wheat, barley, or another cereal reduced to fragments or powder by friction. It is the image of something hard that has been broken, shattered, ground.
2. In the worship of Israel, it specifically refers to newly harvested ears of grain that have been first roasted over fire and then crushed: this is what the Levitical worship prescribed as a firstfruits offering (Leviticus 2:14). This crushed grain retained its granular texture, unlike fine powder.
3. By extension, the word designates the offering itself, that of crushed grain mixed with oil and incense, which the priest burned as a memorial before the Lord (Leviticus 2:16).
H1643.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to crush," "to grind," "to break." It describes the action of reducing something solid into fragments. This same type of action appears in other biblical contexts where it speaks of crushing enemies or grinding grain for food.
H1643.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Leviticus, in verses 14 and 16 of chapter 2. These two verses deal with the same firstfruits offering: the first time, the text describes how to prepare the offering (crushed grain after being roasted over fire), the second time, it explains what the priest does with it (he burns a portion of the crushed grain with oil and incense as a memorial). The meaning remains the same in both usages: it always refers to the grain prepared in this specific manner.
H1643.portee: This offering of crushed grain reminds us that the worship of the Lord involved the fruits of labor: the firstfruits of the new wheat, worked and presented to God with care. It taught Israel that even the most ordinary harvests should be sanctified and offered to God with respect, acknowledging His blessing on the work of their hands.

sens: Expel someone from a place with force
Repel the enemy in battle
Dismiss, send someone away
Agitate, disturb
Set aside, evict
H1644G.detail:
1. Expel with force: the primary meaning is to force someone out of a place against their will, physically. God expels Adam from the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3:24), and the people of Israel are hurriedly expelled from Egypt, without even allowing time to properly prepare for their departure (Exodus 12:39).

2. Repel the enemy: in a military context, the verb means to defeat and drive away adversaries. God promises Moses to drive out the Canaanite nations before Israel (Exodus 34:11) and to send terror to drive them away (Exodus 23:28).

3. Dismiss: the word also expresses the idea of sending someone away from their role or presence. The scoffer must be expelled from the assembly so that quarrels and insults may cease (Proverbs 22:10).

4. Agitate, disturb: in some poetic contexts, the verb describes agitation, instability. The troubled sea cannot calm down (Isaiah 57:20).

5. Set aside: the word can also refer to the action of evicting someone from their position. The prophet Samuel was set aside after his death (1 Kings 2:27).
H1644G.origine: The verb גָּרַשׁ (garash) comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of pushing away, setting aside. It is related to the physical image of repelling something or someone. In Hebrew, the root appears in several forms: in the Qal (simple form), it means "to be pushed out"; in the Piel (intensive form), it reinforces the idea of active expulsion. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of combat, judgment, and banishment.
H1644G.emploi: The verb appears 36 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical and legislative narratives. It first describes the expulsion of Adam from paradise (Genesis 3:24) and the hasty flight from Egypt (Exodus 12:39). Very often, it designates the action of God driving out the nations of Canaan before Israel, thus fulfilling the promise made to the patriarchs: this is the great theme of conquest (Joshua 24:12, Psalms 78:55). The word is also used for cases of personal dismissal or banishment (Proverbs 22:10), and even in contexts of natural disturbance or agitation (Isaiah 57:20, Amos 8:8). Its meaning sharpens according to the context: it can be an act of divine justice, military victory, or simply social rejection.
H1644G.portee: This word reveals that God is sovereign over empires and nations: it is He who chases, who repels enemies, and who fulfills His promises. For the believer, "to chase" also reminds us that obstacles and adversities must be firmly set aside from our lives and communities. The rejection of the scoffer (Proverbs 22:10) shows that maintaining peace in the community sometimes requires separating from those who threaten it.

sens: Chase someone, force them to leave a place or community
Send away a wife, divorce her, remove her from her home
Expel, eject with force
Set aside, reject definitively
H1644H.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to chase someone, to force them to leave. Sarah says to Abraham: "Cast out this servant and her son" (Genesis 21:10) — she wants to expel them from the house and distance them. It is an act of force or authority.
2. In the realm of marriage, the verb takes on the meaning of repudiating, that is, legally sending away one's wife. A woman "repudiated" by her husband (Leviticus 21:7) has been officially removed from the marriage and must leave the home; she changes social status. Numbers 30:10 shows that a repudiated woman is a recognized civil status.
3. The verb can also express exclusion in social relations. In Judges 11:2, Jephthah's brothers "cast him out" — they reject him from the family inheritance, treating him as a stranger in his own family.
4. More broadly, the word evokes any definitive rejection, the act of setting aside with authority.
H1644H.origine: The Hebrew root גרש (garash) expresses the idea of violent or forced movement, of propulsion outward. It is used throughout biblical life: to chase a servant, send away a wife, or exclude someone from a community. The word has retained this sense of authoritative and definitive separation throughout the Old Testament.
H1644H.emploi: This verb appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible. It is concentrated mainly in the Law (Leviticus, Numbers) to describe the status of the repudiated woman, which creates specific rights and prohibitions (a repudiated woman cannot, for example, remarry a priest). It is also used for physical expulsions (Genesis 21:10, Judges 11:2). Ezekiel, Hosea, and Micah use it to speak of God's judgment: He casts out His people, He rejects them. The context changes, but the idea remains one of forced and official rupture.
H1644H.portee: This word reminds us that repudiation is not a trivial act in the Bible: it has serious legal, social, and spiritual consequences. Jesus revisits this topic in Matthew 19, reminding that divorce was not God's plan from the beginning. Understanding the weight of the word "repudiate" in the Old Testament helps to grasp why Jesus insists on the permanence of marriage and the hardness of human hearts that leads to divorce.

sens: what comes from the earth or nature
harvest
fruit of the soil
what is produced or generated
H1645.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what naturally grows from the earth: fruits, plants, everything that is born from the soil and can be gathered. It is the result of nature's growth and fertility.
2. It also evokes the result of an action or force: what is brought to light, what comes out or springs forth from something. The basic meaning, "what is pushed out," explains it: the products come from the earth or their source.
3. In its unique biblical usage (Deuteronomy 33:14), it refers to the best fruits of the sun month by month: the blessing of Joseph includes a land so fertile that it continually offers its best products, its best harvests, throughout the year.
H1645.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of pushing, being put outside, being rejected or expelled. The word "gerash" retains this image: what comes out, what springs forth — hence the meaning of "product" or "harvest." It is a noun formed from a verb that describes the movement of what moves away or unfolds.
H1645.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:14, in the blessing that Moses pronounces over the tribe of Joseph. There he describes the excellent products that the sun brings each month — an image of the agricultural wealth promised to this tribe. Its rare and poetic usage ties it to the theme of divine fertility and the abundance of the Promised Land.
H1645.portee: This word reminds us that fertile and generous land is a blessing from God. By speaking of the "best products of each month," it invites the reader to recognize divine Providence in every harvest, every season, and to give thanks for the food that comes from the soil. It is an invitation to see in every product of the earth a mark of God's love and faithfulness.

sens: Action de prendre par force ou injustement ce qui appartient à autrui
Pillage ou rapine commis par un chef, un gouvernant
Spoliation systématique du peuple par ses dirigeants
H1646.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of seizing something by force or injustice — it is aggravated theft, often accompanied by violence. In Ezekiel 45:9, the princes of Israel are accused of practicing "violence and extortion," meaning they take people's possessions without right or mercy.
2. It particularly describes abuses of power: a leader who exploits his people by stripping them of their lands, income, or rights. It is a state crime, an organized injustice coming from above.
3. The prophetic context shows that this extortion violates the justice that God demands. God commands the princes to cease this practice and to "deliver" the people — that is, to rescue them from these spoliations.
H1646.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to expel" or "to drive away": extortion is a violent tearing away, a dispossession. It denotes the act of taking away from someone what belongs to them, as one drives someone out of their home. The same root evokes the idea of brute force and injustice.
H1646.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 45:9, in a prophecy addressed to the princes and rulers of Israel. God calls them to cease the "violence" and "extortions" against the people, and to practice instead justice and equity. It is a prophetic denunciation of abuses of power: the leaders were illegally enriching themselves at the expense of the weak. The message is clear: God defends the dispossessed and condemns those who abuse their authority to plunder.
H1646.portee: This word reminds us that God stands with the weak and the dispossessed, and that He judges harshly those who abuse power to steal. It calls Christians to exercise authority with justice and honesty, without exploiting others, and to empathize with those who suffer oppression.

sens: Fils aîné de Moïse et de Séphora
Chef de la lignée lévitique fondée par Moïse
Ancêtre d'une ligne sacerdotale
H1647G.detail:
1. Guerschom is the first son of Moses and his wife Zipporah, born during Moses' exile in the land of Midian. His name literally means "foreigner" or "one who dwells as a foreigner," since Moses declares at his birth: "I have been a stranger in a foreign land" (Exodus 2:22). This name reminds us that Moses himself was an exile, living far from his family and people.
2. Guerschom is the head of the Levitical house that bears his name. After the Exodus, his descendants are organized into a priestly family within the tribe of Levi. In 1 Chronicles 23:15-16, he is named first among the sons of Moses, and his sons are listed: Shebuel is the chief of his house.
3. Subsequently, descendants of Guerschom hold important positions: Jonathan, his grandson according to Judges 18:30, becomes a priest for the tribe of Dan, and Shebuel, his son, becomes the overseer of the treasures of the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 26:24), showing how this lineage remains committed to the service of God and worship.
Guerschom thus represents a direct link between Moses and future generations, a living reminder that even the exiled Moses founded a lineage called to serve the people of God.
H1647G.origine: The name Guerschom comes from Hebrew and means "foreigner" or "one who dwells as a foreigner." This meaning directly reflects Moses' situation at the time of his son's birth: he was living in exile in Midian, far from Egypt and Israel. The name carries a sense of humility and recognition of this precarious condition.
H1647G.emploi: Guerschom appears six times in the Bible, notably in Exodus 2:22 and 18:3 where he is presented as the newborn son of Moses in Midian. His descendants later occupy positions of spiritual responsibility: Jonathan, presented as his descendant in Judges 18:30, becomes a priest for Dan, and Shebuel, his son, oversees the treasures of the sanctuary according to 1 Chronicles 26:24. The genealogical lists in 1 Chronicles 23:15-16 and 26:24 show that Guerschom's family remains central in the Levitical and priestly organization, particularly associated with the guarding and administration of the temple's wealth.
H1647G.portee: Guerschom reminds us that Moses, before becoming the liberator of Israel, first experienced exile and strangeness. The name of his son perpetuates this human experience of isolation, showing that men of God are not exempt from trials. However, his lineage prospers and dedicates itself to sacred service, illustrating how God transforms even trials into lasting blessings for future generations.

sens: Fils de la famille sacerdotale de Phinées qui revint de l'exil avec Esdras
Signifie « étranger »
H1647I.detail:
1. Guerschom is a priest from the family of Phinehas who returned from exile with Ezra. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:2, among the leaders of the priestly families who left Babylon for Jerusalem after the captivity. His name appears alongside his colleagues from various Levitical families, showing his importance in the religious renewal of Israel.
2. His name means "foreigner" in Hebrew, which evokes the experience of exile — the Israelites had been foreigners in a foreign land in Babylon. This name carries the memory of distance and return, central themes in the book of Ezra.
H1647I.origine: The name Guerschom comes from a Hebrew root meaning "foreigner" or "temporary resident." This same name is borne by several important figures in the Old Testament: the first son of Moses and Zipporah, and also a son of Levi. These namesakes share the same symbolic meaning: the name reminds of the condition of being a stranger or traveler, which perfectly suits one who returns from exile and reintegrates his land.
H1647I.emploi: Guerschom is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:2. He is cited as a representative of the sons of Phinehas during the return from Babylonian exile with the scribe Ezra, around 458 BCE. His name appears in the list of the leaders of the priestly families who led the return and committed to uphold the Torah. Although not detailed, his role was that of a religious leader in the restoration of worship and the Jewish community.
H1647I.portee: The name Guerschom reminds readers that the return from exile was not merely a geographical return, but a return to the identity and religious vocation of Israel. His belonging to the family of Phinehas, guardians of zeal for the Lord, emphasizes that this renewal involved men dedicated to divine service and faithful to the Law.

sens: son of Levi and founder of the Levitical tribe of the Gershonites
ancestor of the priestly branch responsible for transporting the tabernacle
H1648.detail: Gershon is the firstborn son of Levi, born before Jacob's family descended into Egypt. His name means "exile" in Hebrew, which recalls the condition of a foreign people. In Israel's priestly system, Gershon is the head of one of the three major Levitical families: the Gershonites who descended from him. They are responsible for transporting and maintaining certain parts of the tabernacle, including the tent, the covering, and the curtains (Numbers 3:25). His two sons, Libni and Shimei, themselves fathered distinct priestly families (Numbers 3:21). Throughout the wilderness journey and the settlement in Canaan, the Gershonites are regularly listed alongside their brothers Kohath and Merari in the censuses and organization of worship (Numbers 3:17, 4:41, 26:57).
H1648.origine: The name Gershon comes from Hebrew and literally means "exile" or "banishment," a prophetic allusion to Israel's condition in Egypt. It is a patriarchal family name that founded one of the three branches of the tribe of Levi, alongside Kohath and Merari. In some later passages (1 Chronicles), it is also spelled "Gershom," a variant of the same name.
H1648.emploi: Gershon appears eighteen times in the Bible, mostly in the books of Numbers and 1 Chronicles. He is first mentioned during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:11), then in the census lists of the Levites in the wilderness (Numbers 3, 4, 26). The Gershonites, his descendants, receive cities and pastures in Canaan (Joshua 21:6, 27), demonstrating their established role in Israel's religious life. They accompany the Ark of the Covenant during its transport (1 Chronicles 15:7), confirming their central place in worship. The text of 1 Chronicles also refers to him as "Gershom," with both variants being equivalent.
H1648.portee: Gershon embodies the order and structure that God establishes for His people. His name, which means "exile," reminds us that even in adversity and separation, God organizes a faithful priestly service. By entrusting the Gershonites with a specific part of the tabernacle, God shows that each member of the people has a place and a function in communal worship. It is a lesson in shared responsibility and integrity of worship.

sens: Descendant of Gershon, son of Levi
Member of the Levitical tribe responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple
H1649.detail:
1. A Gershonite is a member of the family descended from Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi mentioned as early as Genesis 46:11. Gershon had two sons, Libni and Shimei, from whom all the Gershonites are descended.
2. In the organization of Israelite worship, the Gershonites formed a division of the Levitical tribe with a specific function: they were responsible for the curtains, veils, and cords of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:24-28). They were distinguished from the Kohathites and Merarites by this particular responsibility. Like all Levites, they served under the authority of the priests and received their sustenance from tithes and the cities assigned to them (Joshua 21:33).
H1649.origine: Gershonite is derived from the name Gershon (גֵּרְשׁוֹן), whose original meaning may evoke exile or separation (from the verb גרש, to expel). Gershon was the firstborn son of Levi and founded a major branch of the Levites. The family name continues through generations and becomes a collective term for all his descendants engaged in the service of the sanctuary.
H1649.emploi: The term Gershonite (and its variant Gershonites) appears twelve times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Book of Numbers during the census of the Levites and the organization of their functions (Numbers 3:21-24, 4:24-28, 26:57). It is also found in Chronicles, particularly when David organizes the temple service (1 Chronicles 23:7, 26:21, 29:8). These references show that the Gershonites maintain their identity and specific role throughout Israel's history, from the wilderness to the time of the permanent temple in Jerusalem.
H1649.portee: The status of Gershonite reminds the reader that worship rendered to God is not a matter of chance: it is based on an established order, families passing on their responsibilities, and everyone knowing their place in the common service. It is an invitation to recognize that God organizes His people according to precise wisdom, and that each believer has a specific function to fulfill in the Body of Christ.

sens: Kingdom in the northern Transjordan, east of the Jordan
Region where the influence of a people and its kings extends
H1650.detail:
1. Geshur is a land located in the northeastern territories of the Jordan, in the region of Transjordan. It is a geographically distinct territory, with its own kings (such as Talmai), and significant enough to be mentioned alongside the territories of Israel (Joshua 13:13).
2. The name designates both the territory and its people: the Geshurites inhabit and govern this region. The king of Geshur is powerful enough to maintain diplomatic alliances with Israel, notably through the marriage of his daughter Maacah to King David (2 Samuel 3:3).
H1650.origine: The name Geshur literally means "proud observer" or "one who looks with pride." It designates a distinct people and land, with its own identity in the ancient Near East. The Geshurites form an independent kingdom for a significant part of the period of the kings of Israel.
H1650.emploi: Geshur appears 8 times in the Bible, primarily in the story of Prince Absalom. When Absalom kills his brother Amnon, he flees to Geshur to his maternal grandfather Talmai, king of that land (2 Samuel 13:37-38). He remains there in exile for three years, showing that Geshur is a safe refuge, a place where Absalom can find protection and political asylum. Later, Joab brings him back to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:23). Absalom himself refers to his stay in Geshur as a period of stability: "Why have I returned from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there" (2 Samuel 14:32). This shows that Geshur is not a humiliating place of captivity, but rather a friendly kingdom where he found refuge. The mentions of Geshur anchor Absalom's story in a real geography of the ancient Near East.
H1650.portee: Geshur reminds the reader that ancient Syria-Palestine is fragmented into several kingdoms and peoples. These dynastic alliances through marriage (Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur, marries David) illustrate how the kings of Israel fit into a regional political network. It is also a place of exile and refuge: it symbolizes both the distance from the promised land and the divine providence that allows a fleeing prince to find safety and survival away from his people.

sens: Inhabitants of the kingdom of Geshur, region east of the Jordan
People distinct from the Israelites, neighbors of the Maacathites
Tribe or ethnic group in southern Palestine, at the borders of Philistine territory
H1651.detail:
1. The Geshurites are the inhabitants of the kingdom of Geshur, located east of the Jordan, in the mountainous region between Hermon and Bashan. Their territory extended to Salcah and formed a transitional zone between the lands conquered by Israel and the neighboring regions (Joshua 13:11).

2. This people lived on the fringes of Israel's territory and was never completely conquered or assimilated: Joshua 13:13 reports that the Israelites "did not drive out the Geshurites and the Maacathites, who lived among Israel." They coexisted with the Israelites without being truly subjected.

3. In David's time, the Geshurites inhabited southern Palestine alongside other ancient peoples, from the region of Shur to Egypt. David himself conducted raids against them, alongside his incursions against other local groups (1 Samuel 27:8).
H1651.origine: The name comes from the kingdom of Geshur (גְּשׁוּר), an ancient region well attested in biblical and extra-biblical texts. The adjective "Geshurites" simply designates the inhabitants of this place, formed according to the common Hebrew model to indicate belonging to a people or region.
H1651.emploi: The term appears six times in the Old Testament, always in geographical or military contexts. It first appears in descriptions of the borders of the conquered territory (Deuteronomy 3:14, Joshua 12:5 and 13:11), then in the account of the incomplete conquest of Canaan (Joshua 13:2 and 13:13), and finally in David's expeditions against the peoples of the southwest (1 Samuel 27:8). The Geshurites are always mentioned alongside the Maacathites, their direct neighbors, suggesting a certain political or geographical proximity. They represent an indigenous people that persisted for a long time without being integrated into the kingdom of Israel.

sens: To cause rain to fall from the sky
To send rain, speaking of God
To receive rain, to be watered
H1652.detail: 1. To cause rain to fall from the sky — the primary meaning of the verb, which describes the meteorological phenomenon of rain. It is the sky that rains, or the rain that falls. 2. To send rain, speaking of God — the Bible recognizes that it is God alone who "makes it rain": in Jeremiah 14:22, the prophet asks if the idols of the nations can make it rain, or if only the Lord controls the rain. This rain is a divine gift, a sign of blessing or judgment. 3. To receive rain, to be watered — passive form, when it is said that a field or a crop "is rainy" or receives rain from the sky.
H1652.origine: The Hebrew verb גָּשַׁם comes from a root that evokes the idea of water falling and wetting. The noun גֶּשֶׁם (geshem), "rain," derives directly from it. In the Hebrew Bible, rain is always a divine matter: it depends on God, not on idols or human magic. This is why this verb is frequently used to speak of God's action rather than a simple natural phenomenon.
H1652.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament and the provided text from the Segond, in Jeremiah 14:22. It is a rhetorical question from the prophet Jeremiah, addressed to God during a drought: "Do the idols of the nations make it rain?" The implicit answer is no. Only the Lord, the living God, can send rain and nourish His people. This context shows that "to rain" in the Hebrew prophets is never a neutral act: it is a sign of divine power and His relationship with Israel.
H1652.portee: This word reminds us that rain and the fertility of the earth depend entirely on God. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize his dependence on the Lord for the essentials of life. The prophet Jeremiah's question urges us to distinguish the true powers (God alone) from the false (the idols), and to place our trust in the one who truly controls heaven and earth.

sens: Water that falls from the sky in drops
Rain as a regular or seasonal meteorological phenomenon
Rain as a blessing from God upon the earth
The absence of rain as punishment or sign of drought
Rain as a figure of the divine word that fertilizes
H1653.detail:
1. Rain is the water that descends from the heavens in drops: during the flood, "the rain fell on the earth for forty days and forty nights" (Genesis 7:12). It is the observable and concrete meteorological phenomenon.
2. In natural cycles, rain returns according to the seasons: Israel depended on the autumn and spring rains for harvest. The text speaks of "rain" at the precise moment it manifests, as when Elijah announces to Ahab: "there is a sound of heavy rain" (1 Kings 18:41).
3. Rain symbolizes God's generosity towards His people: it fertilizes the earth, causes plants to sprout, and nourishes men. Isaiah beautifully states: "As the rain and the snow come down from heaven... without watering, fertilizing the earth" (Isaiah 55:10).
4. The absence of rain becomes an instrument of divine judgment: when Elijah shuts up the heavens, the rain ceases and famine ensues (1 Kings 17:7, 17:14). God controls the rains to punish or restore.
5. Rain illustrates God's creative power: it destroys or brings joy according to His will. In prophetic visions, a violent rain accompanies divine anger (Ezekiel 13:13).
H1653.origine: The Hebrew word גֶּ֫שֶׁם comes from a root that expresses the idea of something that descends or trickles. It is a simple and concrete word, very ancient, that designates the observable phenomenon from the sky. It does not depend on another complex root: it is a direct and fundamental term of Hebrew meteorological vocabulary, used throughout the Bible to speak of rain both as a natural event and as a divine sign.
H1653.emploi: The word "rain" appears about 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical books (Kings, Chronicles), wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes), and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It occurs in very varied contexts: the flood (Genesis 7:12), the end of the drought caused by Elijah (1 Kings 18), normal agricultural cycles (Leviticus 26:4), and divine judgments or restorations (Ezekiel 34:26, Joel 2:23). Sometimes rain is lacking and it is a calamity; sometimes it abounds and it is a blessing. The prophets also use it as an image: Isaiah compares the word of God to the rain that fertilizes (Isaiah 55:10). The basic meaning remains always concrete, but the theological significance varies according to the context.
H1653.portee: For the Christian, rain reminds us that God governs all nature and that no event escapes His sovereignty. It also teaches that material blessings come from God alone: it is a lesson in humility and trust. Finally, the image of rain fertilizing the earth illustrates how the word of God always accomplishes its purpose, without returning empty, and invites the believer to see in natural phenomena the signs of the power and wisdom of the Creator.

sens: Arabian enemy of the governor Nehemiah during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem
H1654.detail: Geshom is an Arab chief who, along with Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite, strongly opposes Nehemiah's efforts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. As soon as he learns of the project, he mocks and despises Nehemiah and his people (Nehemiah 2:19). Later, when the wall is nearly finished, Geshom participates in a plot to lure Nehemiah out of Jerusalem to harm him, pretending to want a peaceful meeting in the valley of Ono (Nehemiah 6:2).
H1654.origine: The name Geshom literally means "rain" in Hebrew, but here it refers to a man, probably an Arab chief or governor of the region. Historians consider him a well-known historical figure, also mentioned in the form Gashmu in some ancient documents.
H1654.emploi: Geshom appears four times in the book of Nehemiah, only during the events of the wall reconstruction (around 444 B.C.). In each mention, he is alongside Nehemiah's other adversaries: Sanballat and Tobiah. His role is exclusively hostile — he mocks the project (2:19), learns of the filled breach (6:1), participates in sabotage attempts (6:2), and appears in the context of letters intended to intimidate Nehemiah (6:6). He represents the external pagan opposition to the restoration of God's people.
H1654.portee: Geshom symbolizes the forces of the world that oppose God's plans and faith. His story shows that Nehemiah, trusting in God, was not deterred by threats and mockery, thus accomplishing his mission despite hostility. It encourages the reader to persevere in their commitment to God in the face of external obstacles.

sens: Physical entirety of a person, in its fleshly materiality
Physical envelope subjected to trials or transformations
Carcass or remains of a creature
H1655.detail:
1. The body is the physical entirety that constitutes a living person. In Daniel 3:27, the fire had no power over the "body" of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: it refers to the tangible, fleshly reality of these men that the flames did not consume.
2. The body is also the material envelope that can undergo humiliation, degradation, or strange transformations. When Nebuchadnezzar "delivered their bodies" rather than serve another god (Daniel 3:28), it means they accepted to risk their entire lives. Similarly, in Daniel 4:33 and 5:21, the king's "body" was "drenched with the dew of heaven": it is the physical and visible experience of his madness and humiliation.
3. The body can also refer to a dead or destroyed creature. In Daniel 7:11, the "body" of the slain animal "was given to the fire to be burned": it refers to the remains, the corpse.
H1655.origine: This Hebrew word גְּשֵׁם (geshem) is very ancient and simply refers to the physical, corporeal, and material reality of a living being. The word evokes the fleshly, substantial envelope that can be touched and seen. It appears mainly in the Aramaic texts of Daniel, indicating it is a language close to the context of the Babylonian captivity.
H1655.emploi: This word appears five times in the Bible, all in Daniel (3:27, 3:28, 4:33, 5:21, 7:11). It always describes something very concrete and physical: either the intact body despite danger (the young Hebrews in the furnace), or the body subjected to trial and transformation (the mad king eating grass), or the destroyed body (the prophetic animal annihilated). Each time, the word emphasizes what is visible, tangible, materially affected.
H1655.portee: This word reminds us that faith does not deny the reality of the body and matter. The three young Hebrews deserved not only spiritual protection: God also preserved their physical bodies in the face of the flames. This shows that our incarnation, our fleshly reality, matters to God. Similarly, when Nebuchadnezzar saw his body humiliated and transformed, he learned that God reigns over matter and flesh.

sens: water that falls from the sky
the act of raining, precipitation
divine blessing, heavenly favor
H1656.detail:
1. Rain is the water that naturally falls from the sky in the form of drops. It is the well-known meteorological phenomenon, essential for the life of plants and animals. In Ezekiel 22:24, the prophet reproaches Jerusalem for not having been "watered with rain on the day of wrath": the rain is here what is lacking, what should have come from heaven to nourish the earth.
2. The word also refers to the event of raining, the action of rain that descends and waters. It is the living process by which the sky gives water to the earth.
3. In biblical language, rain becomes an image of divine blessing. When God sends rain, it is a sign of His favor and care for His people; when He withholds it, it is judgment. In Ezekiel, the absence of rain "on the day of wrath" symbolizes the withdrawal of God's blessing from Jerusalem.
H1656.origine: The Hebrew word gōshem comes from a root that evokes water that falls and waters. It is from the same family as the verb meaning "to water" or "to rain." In Hebrew, this word usually refers to ordinary rain, the kind that comes in its season, rather than torrents or floods. It is a common word in the Old Testament to speak of the fundamental gift from heaven.
H1656.emploi: The word rain appears rarely in the transmitted passages; here it appears only once, in Ezekiel 22:24, in a judgment oracle. Jerusalem is described as a land "that is not purified, that is not watered with rain on the day of wrath." The context is one of punishment: the rain, normally a sign of blessing and fertility, is withheld from the guilty city. This refusal of rain symbolizes divine abandonment and the severe judgment of the Lord on Jerusalem for its sins. Rain represents here the normal flow of grace and life that was once granted to the city.
H1656.portee: Rain reminds us that life depends solely on God. It is not an indifferent natural mechanism, but a gift that God grants or withholds according to His wisdom and justice. For the believer, every rain can be an occasion for gratitude towards God who provides for our needs, and the absence of rain in the Bible invites us to reflect on our relationship with Him.

sens: region in northeastern Egypt, fertile and well-watered
territory granted to the Israelites and their flocks
distinct area where Israel remained separate from the Egyptians
H1657G.detail:
1. Gosen is a region located in the Nile delta, in northeastern Egypt, particularly fertile and favorable for raising livestock (Genesis 47:4). It is where Joseph established his family from Canaan during the famine.

2. Pharaoh granted this land to the Israelites so they could live there with their families and their livestock, recognizing that they were a people of shepherds (Genesis 46:34). Joseph first met his father in Gosen before presenting him to the king (Genesis 46:29).

3. Gosen became a separate space in Egypt: the plagues that struck the land did not affect it (Exodus 8:18, 9:26), already marking the distinction between Israel and Egypt, between the people of God and other nations.
H1657G.origine: The name means "approaching" or "drawing near," perhaps evoking the proximity or accessibility of this region. In Hebrew, Gosen (גֹּשֶׁן) specifically refers to this border territory of the Nile delta where the first Israelite community settled in Egypt, before slavery and the Exodus.
H1657G.emploi: Gosen is mentioned eleven times in Scripture, primarily in the account of Jacob and his family's settlement in Egypt (Genesis 45-47) and in the account of the plagues (Exodus 8-9). It is initially a haven of peace: Joseph settles his father and brothers there, where they find pastures and safety (Genesis 45:10, 46:29). Gradually, Gosen becomes a symbol of divine protection: while Egypt suffers from the plagues, Gosen is spared (Exodus 8:18, 9:26), revealing that God watches over His people even in a foreign land. It is the place of promise before affliction, and already a sign of divine intervention.
H1657G.portee: Gosen tells the story of a people who find refuge and prosperity in a distant land due to the faithfulness and wisdom of a man — Joseph — who has not forgotten God. It is also the place where God begins to manifest His power, protecting His own from the plagues that strike others. For the Christian reader, Gosen reminds us that God leads His people even in exile, and that His protection is not limited to the borders of the promised land.

sens: region in southern Palestine
territory conquered by Joshua
H1657H.detail:
1. Gosen is a region located in southern Palestine, between Gaza and Gibeon. It is mentioned during Joshua's military campaigns against the Canaanite kings: Joshua "struck all the land of Gosen up to Gibeon" (Joshua 10:41), showing that it extends over a well-defined geographical area in southern Palestine.
2. Gosen also appears as a territory that Joshua conquers during his possession of the promised land: "Joshua took all this land... all the land of Gosen" (Joshua 11:16). It is one of the many cities or regions in the south that the Israelites took from the Canaanites.
H1657H.origine: The name "Gosen" literally means "approach" or "that which draws near." Its etymology suggests an accessible or nearby region, perhaps named for its proximity to other important territories or its easy access.
H1657H.emploi: Gosen appears three times in the book of Joshua, always in connection with the territorial conquests in southern Canaan. It is first mentioned in the account of Joshua's victory over the kings of the south (Joshua 10:41), then in the general summary of the conquest (Joshua 11:16), and finally in the allotment of land for the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:51), where it is listed among the eleven cities. These references indicate that Gosen was an important territory or city in southern Palestine occupied by the tribe of Judah.

sens: Chief of the Nethinim at the time of the return from exile
H1658.detail: Guischpa is an officer who led the Nethinim, those temple servants dedicated to the work of worship. He appears only in Nehemiah 11:21, where he is mentioned as one of the two leaders of this group during the return of the exiles to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. Along with Tsicha, he directed the Nethinim established on the hill of Jerusalem.
H1658.origine: The name Guischpa means "caress" in Hebrew. It carries the idea of tenderness or kindness. It is a rare name, attested only once in the Bible, belonging to the period when the Jewish people were reestablishing themselves in their land after the exile.
H1658.emploi: Guischpa is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 11:21. He appears in a list of those who settled in Jerusalem during the return from captivity. His role was to administer the Nethinim, a group of non-Israelites or descendants of war captives dedicated to the service of the Lord's sanctuaries. This mention shows the organization of the restored worship after the exile.

sens: To advance with hands outstretched to feel and find one's way in darkness or uncertainty
To search by groping, without clearly seeing what one is looking for
Figuratively, to be in uncertainty and moral or spiritual confusion
H1659.detail:
1. The word describes the gesture of one who advances with hands before them to feel, touch, and orient themselves when they cannot see — like a blind person along a wall. It is to search by groping, by palpating. In Isaiah 59:10, the prophet describes the exiles who "grope like the blind along a wall": they are lost, disoriented, without light to guide their steps.
2. The meaning extends to any uncertain search, where one tries directions without knowing which is the right one. One moves blindly, without reference points.
3. Spiritually, to grope means to be in moral confusion: to ignore the way of God, to walk without His commandments as a source of light. It is the state of one who has lost direction, who no longer knows where they are going.
H1659.origine: The Hebrew verb gâshash comes from a root that expresses the action of feeling, of touching to sense. The initial image is very physical: the hand groping to find. It naturally applies to one who seeks in darkness, deprived of the sight that provides clarity and assurance of the way.
H1659.emploi: The word appears twice in Isaiah 59:10, in a poetic description of the people in exile, far from God. The prophet paints a picture of walking blindly: the people grope like the blind, staggering at noon as if it were night. This is not a physical incapacity, but a spiritual confusion. Without the light of God and His Word, one can only grope in moral darkness.
H1659.portee: This word reminds the reader that without God and His guidance — His Word, His light — one can only wander blindly, uncertain and disoriented. It emphasizes the vital importance of walking in the light of God to have assurance and certainty in life. To grope is to refuse or lose that light.

sens: Fixed installation where grapes are crushed to extract juice
Device or vat where grape must accumulates
Image of divine judgment crushing its enemies
H1660.detail:
1. The winepress is primarily a rural installation made of stone or wood where harvesters would tread grapes by foot to extract the juice: Joel 3:13 speaks of a winepress "full" of grapes ready to be crushed. It is a building or a hollow dug into the ground, often located near vineyards.
2. The word also refers to the container or vat where the must that flows from the crushed grapes accumulates: in Isaiah 63:2, the prophet asks, "Why are your garments like the one who treads in the vat?", evoking the grape juice that stains clothes red.
3. By powerful imagery, the winepress becomes a symbol of judgment: in Lamentations 1:15, the Lord "has trodden the virgin, daughter of Judah, in the winepress," expressing the complete crushing of the people under divine wrath, like grapes underfoot.
H1660.origine: The Hebrew word gat comes from the root "to tread, to trample." It designates both the physical place where one treads and the action of crushing. The winepress was a daily agricultural tool in the Promised Land, rich in vineyards, and its image of crushing naturally imposed itself to speak of divine judgment that crushes the wicked.
H1660.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in agricultural or prophetic contexts. In Judges 6:11 and Nehemiah 13:15, it is a rural installation where work is done, even on the Sabbath — a context of ordinary life. In Isaiah 63:2 and Lamentations 1:15, the winepress becomes an image of judgment: God "treads" his enemies as the vintner treads the grapes. Joel 3:13 unites the two: a final judgment where the winepress is "full" and the vats "overflow," an image of divine wrath that spills over onto guilty nations.
H1660.portee: The winepress reveals how the Bible draws its images of judgment from daily life and agriculture: what crushes the grapes to extract juice becomes a symbol of divine justice that breaks wickedness. This violent image reminds us that God's judgment is real, total, and inevitable — it is not abstract, but concrete like the crushing of fruit underfoot.

sens: Powerful and fortified Philistine city
Birthplace of the giant Goliath
Center of Philistine presence in Canaan
City where David found refuge fleeing Saul
H1661.detail:
1. Gath was one of the five major cities of the Philistines, a people who occupied the coast of Canaan. Its name means "winepress" in Hebrew, evoking viticultural activity. It represented the military and political power of the Philistines over the promised land (Joshua 11:22).

2. Goliath, the famous giant defeated by David, was from Gath: "the Philistine of Gath, named Goliath" (1 Samuel 17:23). Other giants from the same family were also found in Gath, making it a center of the race of the Rapha (2 Samuel 21:20).

3. David sought refuge in Gath with King Achish to escape the pursuit of King Saul (1 Samuel 27:3). He established his family and men there for a time, seeking protection among the Philistine enemy.

4. The city changed hands throughout history: sometimes under Philistine control, sometimes conquered by the kings of Israel like David (1 Chronicles 18:1) or threatened by foreign kingdoms like Syria (2 Kings 12:17).
H1661.origine: The Hebrew name גַּת (Gath) means "winepress" or "wine vat," from the verb gatat which evokes the action of pressing grapes. This descriptive name reveals that the city was an important viticultural center in the coastal region. The proper name reflects the common practice of naming places by their main economic or geographical characteristic.
H1661.emploi: Gath appears 31 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles. It first appears as one of the five major cities of the Philistines along with Gaza and Ashdod (Joshua 11:22; 1 Samuel 6:17). The city is inextricably linked to Goliath and the giants of Rapha who inhabited it (1 Samuel 17:23; 2 Samuel 21:20). David found refuge there fleeing Saul, an episode detailed in 1 Samuel 27. In the times of the kings, Gath became the focus of wars between Israel and its neighbors: David conquered it (1 Chronicles 18:1), while Hazael of Syria seized it during the reign of Joash (2 Kings 12:17).
H1661.portee: Gath symbolizes in the biblical narrative the pagan power against which the people of God must fight or sometimes submit. The story of Goliath, the giant of Gath defeated by young David with his sling, shows that true strength does not lie in military armament but in faith in God. David's refuge in Gath also illustrates the compromises believers may be forced to make: although an enemy of the Philistines, David must live among them to escape persecution, before finally being established as king.

sens: Small town of the tribe of Zebulun in northern Israel
Border location between Zebulun and other territories
Birthplace of the prophet Jonah
H1662.detail:
1. Gath-Hepher is a small locality located in the lands of the tribe of Zebulun, in northern Israel. Its name literally means "the winepress of the digging" or "the dug winepress," indicating that it was situated in a viticultural region. It is mentioned in the delineation of the borders of Zebulun (Joshua 19:13).

2. The town marks a border point: Joshua 19:13 shows that it served as a geographical landmark for tracing the territorial boundaries of the tribe, confirming its strategic importance at the edge of the allocated lands.

3. Gath-Hepher is most famous as the birthplace of the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai (2 Kings 14:25). It is from there that the prophet who preached repentance to the Ninevites came, and who was swallowed by a great fish in the waters.
H1662.origine: The Hebrew name גַּת הַחֵפֶר (gat-ha-chepher) literally means "the winepress of the digging." Gat comes from the word for "winepress" or "vat," particularly one used to tread grapes to extract juice. Chepher means "to dig" or "to excavate." The name thus reflects the characteristic agricultural viticulture of this region. It was a modest village but known for being the home of the great prophet Jonah.
H1662.emploi: Gath-Hepher appears twice in the Bible. First in Joshua 19:13, where it is listed among the localities that mark the borders of the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the Promised Land after the conquest. It is then mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25, in the historical context of the reign of Jeroboam II, where it is identified as the birthplace of the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai. This second usage connects the geographical site to one of the greatest prophets of the Old Testament, the one who initially refused his mission before being brought back to obedience by a famous miracle.
H1662.portee: Gath-Hepher reminds us that God's prophets were not abstract figures, but men rooted in concrete places, with families and origins. It also emphasizes that God calls witnesses from the smallest village as well as from the grandest palace. The humble village becomes memorable because it gave birth to the one who delivered the message of repentance to a great nation.

sens: Inhabitant of Gath, a Philistine city
Person from Gath
H1663.detail: 1. The term refers to an inhabitant or native of Gath, one of the five main cities of the Philistines (Joshua 13:3). Gath was an important fortress for God's people against the Philistines. Ittai the Gittite (2 Samuel 15:19) is the most famous example: this foreign warrior chose to remain by King David's side even during his flight, showing remarkable loyalty despite his Philistine origin.
H1663.origine: The word comes from גַּת (Gath), the name of the city. Gath literally means "winepress" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a form or function of the city. The adjective gittite simply indicates belonging to this place, similar to how one might say a Parisian or a Lyonnais.
H1663.emploi: This term appears about ten times in the Bible, mainly in the books of Samuel and Chronicles. It refers either to the city itself or its inhabitants. In 2 Samuel 15:18 and 15:19, we see the "Gittites" numbering six hundred men following King David into exile, and Ittai of Gath who refuses the king's order to return to Gath, so deep is his commitment to David. The city is also mentioned in connection with the Ark of the Covenant: it rests with Obed-Edom of Gath (2 Samuel 6:10-11) where it brings divine blessing for three months.
H1663.portee: The passage of Ittai of Gath shows how God welcomes one who, though a foreigner and Philistine, chooses to serve the king of Israel with unwavering loyalty. His story invites the reader to see beyond borders and origins: true loyalty transcends natural belonging.

sens: City of Judah
Place of refuge for refugees
Locality listed among the cities of Benjamin
H1664.detail: 1. Guitthaïm is a city located in Judah, whose Hebrew name literally means "two winepresses" or "two wine vats," suggesting a viticultural activity in this region. 2. It appears in 2 Samuel 4:3 as a refuge: the inhabitants of Beeroth fled there and established themselves permanently, demonstrating its role as a city of asylum in ancient Judah. 3. In Nehemiah 11:33, it is listed among the cities populated by the Benjaminites after the return from exile, indicating its administrative and demographic importance during the time of reconstruction.
H1664.origine: The Hebrew name Guitthaïm comes from the root gat (גַּת), which means "winepress" or "wine vat," particularly a winepress carved in stone for treading grapes. The plural yim indicates here two winepresses, suggesting that the city was a center of viticultural production in Judah. This type of geographical name reflects a natural or economic characteristic of the place.
H1664.emploi: Guitthaïm appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Samuel 4:3, during the account of David's reign, the Beerothites fled there as a refuge and established a permanent residence. In Nehemiah 11:33, it is mentioned among the cities occupied by the descendants of Benjamin after the Babylonian exile, showing that it remained an important Benjaminite locality during the Persian period. These two occurrences place it in the Benjaminite territory, north of Jerusalem.

sens: Title or musical indication in the psalms
Possible reference to a winepress or the city of Gath
Melody or tune known in connection with the Feast of Tabernacles
H1665.detail: 1. The word Gittith appears in the titles of three psalms (Psalms 8, 81, and 84) as a musical indication, likely indicating to what tune or melody the psalm should be sung or played (Psalms 8:1). 2. The origin of the word suggests a link either to a winepress (gat in Hebrew means winepress) or to Gath, a Philistine city, which could indicate a melody of foreign or popular origin well known (Psalms 81:1). 3. The association of Gittith with the Feast of Tabernacles in certain contexts suggests that it was a recognized festive melody used for songs of celebration and joy (Psalms 84:1).
H1665.origine: The word Gittith likely comes from the Hebrew gat (גַּת), which means "winepress" (winepress), or from the name of the city of Gath in Philistine territory. This possible double etymology — either the image of the winepress or the reference to a place — suggests that Gittith designated either an instrument or a popular melody associated with these origins. In antiquity, musical indications in the psalms often referred to melodies already known to the people.
H1665.emploi: Gittith appears only three times in the Bible, solely in the titles of Psalms 8, 81, and 84. This word falls into the category of musical indications present in the psalm headers, alongside other notations like "On the harp" or "To the chief musician." The three psalms where it appears are psalms of praise and celebration: Psalm 8 praises God's majesty and creation, Psalm 81 recalls the deliverance from Egypt and the obligations of the law, and Psalm 84 celebrates the house of God and the Feast of Tabernacles. This recurrence in contexts of celebration and joy suggests that Gittith was a joyful and festive melody, recognizable by the faithful of the time.
H1665.portee: Discovering these ancient musical indications reminds us that biblical worship was a living and embodied act, where music held a central place in the worship of God. The use of the same well-known melody for several psalms showed how the assembly of Israel prayed together, using recognized songs. This invites us to value music and singing as authentic means of praising God and building community.

sens: Son of Aram, one of the ancient Syrian patriarchs
H1666.detail: Gueter is one of the four sons of Aram mentioned in the biblical genealogies (Genesis 10:23 and 1 Chronicles 1:17). He appears alongside his brothers Uz, Hul, and Mash, whose descendants likely formed peoples or regions of the ancient Levant. His name means "fear" in Hebrew. Although few biographical details are given, his mention in these two genealogical lists underscores the importance of his lineage in the history of pre-flood and post-flood peoples according to the biblical narrative.
H1666.origine: The name Guéter (גֶּתֶר) literally means "fear" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses fear or dread. This name belongs to the Aramean patriarchal tradition and is borne by a direct descendant of Shem, the father of the Semitic peoples. Like his brothers, Guéter represents a branch of the genealogy of Aram, ancestor of the Aramean peoples.
H1666.emploi: Guéter appears only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:23, where he is listed as the third son of Aram after the flood, and in 1 Chronicles 1:17, which repeats this same genealogy. These two parallel mentions highlight the stability of this genealogical tradition throughout the Old Testament. His omission from narrative accounts suggests that he is primarily an eponymous ancestor of a community or region rather than a historical figure who left a personal mark in the biblical text.

sens: City of the tribe of Dan, in the land of Philistia
Place of residence assigned to the Levites
H1667G.detail: Gath-Rimmon is a city that belonged to the tribe of Dan, located in the Philistine plain not far from Joppa. It appears in the list of cities allocated to the tribe of Dan during the division of the territory after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 19:45). Later, this city was given to the Levites as one of their cities of refuge, along with its surrounding lands, according to the provisions regarding Levitical cities (Joshua 21:24; 1 Chronicles 6:69). It thus represents a place where the descendants of Levi could dwell and serve the Lord, even though they did not possess their own territory.
H1667G.origine: The name literally means "press (or winepress) of the pomegranate." It combines two roots: "gat" (gath) which refers to a press — a common image in the Levant for crushing grapes or extracting oil — and "rimmon" which means pomegranate, a well-known Mediterranean fruit. The name likely evokes a characteristic of the terrain or a locally known agricultural resource.
H1667G.emploi: Gath-Rimmon appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in passages that enumerate the cities assigned to the different tribes and to the Levites after the conquest. It is first mentioned among the cities of Dan (Joshua 19:45), then twice in the lists of Levitical cities: once in the book of Joshua (21:24) and once in the parallel account of 1 Chronicles (6:69). It is each time associated with its surrounding lands (its suburbs), indicating that it was an urban center of some importance, capable of sustaining a Levitical community.
H1667G.portee: Gath-Rimmon illustrates how God provided for the needs of the Levitical people by granting them cities and lands throughout the territory of Israel. It reminds us that even without their own territorial inheritance, the Levites received a stable place and resources to dedicate themselves to the service of the Lord and the teaching of His law. It is a testimony to the provision and divine organization of the chosen people.

sens: Levitical city of Manasseh, in the West Bank
H1667H.detail: Gath-Rimmon is a city assigned to the Levites, taken from the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh that occupied the West Bank (Joshua 21:25). Its name literally means "press of the pomegranate," combining two images: the press (a facility for extracting juice) and the fruit of the pomegranate, symbols of fertility and abundance. It was one of the forty-eight cities that the twelve tribes offered to the descendants of Levi so that they would have a place to live and cultivate fields, as the tribe of Levi did not receive a territory of its own as an inheritance.
H1667H.origine: The Hebrew name combines "gat" (גַּת), the wine or oil press, and "rimmon" (רִמּוֹן), the pomegranate. These two words evoke agricultural facilities or products, suggesting a fertile region. According to some sources, Gath-Rimmon is another name for the city of Ibleam (יִבְלְעָם), indicating that places sometimes had multiple names according to ancient sources.
H1667H.emploi: Gath-Rimmon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 21:25, in the list of cities assigned to the Levites.
