It is mentioned alongside Thaanach, another city that also belonged to the Levites of the same territory. Its single biblical mention places it among the forty-eight cities of refuge and Levitical residence, essential to the religious and territorial organization of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: this (to indicate something close or present)
the other, another (to distinguish or oppose)
each, all (to enumerate or generalize)
H1668.detail:
1. The word marks what is present before the eyes or mind: "Is this not Babylon the great" (Daniel 4:30) — the king points to the city where he stands, as if to designate it with his finger.
2. It serves to distinguish two things from one another: "four great beasts came up from the sea, different from one another" (Daniel 7:3) — each beast is differentiated from the others. This is also the sense of "the knee against the other" (Daniel 5:6): the king's knees are knocking together, one striking the other.
3. It expresses the idea of distribution or succession: "another little horn came up" (Daniel 7:8) — a new horn, distinct from those that existed before.
H1668.origine: This is an Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Judeans in exile in Babylon). It comes from the same root as the Hebrew "geh" (גֵּה), which means "this" or "that." It is a demonstrative word, belonging to the family of words that point and designate: like a finger that shows something. In the Aramaic of Daniel's visions, it is equivalent to the Hebrew "zeh" (זֶה).
H1668.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, all in Aramaic, in chapters 4, 5, and 7 of the Book of Daniel. It is a very simple term, common in Aramaic for showing or distinguishing. In Daniel 4:30, it designates the present city. In Daniel 5:6 and 7:3, it marks opposition or distinction: "one and the other." In Daniel 7:8, it introduces something new: "another horn." Its meaning thus varies from simple pointing to comparative distinction.
H1668.portee: This word reminds us that the Book of Daniel speaks in Aramaic — the language of the exiles — to reveal to the Judeans deported to Babylon visions that concern them directly. It is a humble demonstrative that anchors the visions in the concrete and the visible: the beasts, the horns, the city are shown as real and close.

sens: To become weak, exhausted, in reference to the body or soul
To suffer, to be in pain and distress
To waste away, to lack what revives (food, comfort, hope)
H1669.detail:
1. To consume literally means "to wear out, to weaken gradually." It is the image of a lamp that gradually goes out, or of a person whose vitality is being exhausted. In Psalm 88:10, the one who prays says: "My eyes waste away from grief," meaning that his gaze is weakening, that his life is flowing away in tears and torment.
2. To consume also expresses moral suffering, the grief that gnaws at the soul. It is not an instantaneous physical pain, but a distress that settles in and persists. It is the symptom of a wounded soul, lacking comfort.
3. To consume also means "to languish," that is, to be deprived of what gives joy and life — love, divine presence, hope. In Jeremiah 31:25, the Lord promises to satisfy "every languishing soul," the one that is wasting away far from Him.
H1669.origine: This Hebrew root expresses the idea of gradual weakness and wasting away. It is related to the weakening of vitality, as when one dies slowly from exhaustion or grief. The underlying image is that of water flowing away, of strength extinguishing, of what is consumed by burning.
H1669.emploi: The verb "to consume" appears three times in the Bible. In Psalm 88:10, a afflicted psalmist describes how suffering consumes him: his eyes weaken under the weight of distress and he calls upon the Lord in his anguish. In Jeremiah 31:12 and 31:25, in a context of consolation, the word describes the soul that suffers from being far from the Lord — but the divine promise is that this state of languishing will come to an end: God will refresh the thirsty soul and will no longer allow anyone to consume with grief.
H1669.portee: This word reminds us that prolonged suffering weakens not only the body but also the mind and faith. It invites the reader to recognize their exhaustion, their silent distress — and to turn to God, who alone can restore and satisfy them. It is a word of healing for those who feel consumed from within.

sens: Sudden and intense fear
State of mental weakness or discouragement
Lack of energy in the face of danger
H1670.detail:
1. Terror is a fear that seizes suddenly, a violent fright. In the passage from Job where Leviathan (that terrifying aquatic monster) is described, terror leaps before him: it is the dread that rushes to meet one who confronts it (Job 41:13).
2. The word can also express a collapse, a failure of the soul — when courage crumbles and willpower falters in the face of peril. It is less an emotion than a paralysis: one no longer has the strength to react.
3. More broadly, it is the absence of energy that should allow us to stand firm: a kind of inner capitulation before what threatens us.
H1670.origine: The Hebrew word דְּאָבָה (de.a.vah) expresses the idea of "becoming weak" or "losing courage." It paints a picture of failure: that of the body collapsing, that of the soul crumbling. It is a rare term in biblical Hebrew, capturing a moment: when fear is no longer a simple emotion, but a true dissolution of self.
H1670.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 41:13. It describes the terror that precedes the monstrous creature of Leviathan — this giant of the waters that inspires terror even before being confronted. The unique mention of the word underscores its intensity: it is a terror so powerful that it deserves its own term. Job places it in a poem intended to show the overwhelming greatness of divine creation.
H1670.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that authentic fear in the face of powers that surpass man is a natural reaction — but that God remains master of all that terrifies. Terror can paralyze us; only faith in God restores strength and peace.

sens: State of physical or moral weakness and dejection
Dull gaze, lifeless eyes
Deep sadness or distress of the soul
H1671.detail:
1. The word first designates the state of one who weakens gradually, who withers: it is the effect of prolonged suffering that exhausts body and mind. In Deuteronomy 28:65, God warns Israel that if they disobey Him, they will experience this state of exhaustion — the heart agitated, energy gnawed by anxiety.
2. The word also describes the expression on the face of one who suffers: "fainting" eyes, lacking brightness, revealing an interior ravaged by sorrow. It is the visible sign of fatigue and grief.
3. Finally, it is the deep suffering of the soul, a kind of moral consumption where the whole being withers under the weight of misfortune or guilt.
H1671.origine: The Hebrew word is related to a root that evokes the idea of weakening, of gradual decline. The basic image is that of a life that fades, like a plant deprived of water. It is a term that paints the condition of one who is slowly extinguishing, emptied of strength and momentum.
H1671.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:65. It is part of the series of curses that God pronounces against Israel if they transgress His covenant. It describes the psychological and physical effects of divine disfavor: a state of perpetual malaise, anxiety gnawing at the heart, which is reflected in the gaze. The context shows that it is a suffering related to insecurity, lack of peace, and the feeling of being abandoned.
H1671.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin has real consequences, affecting the whole being: the body weakens, the soul is distressed, and even the gaze testifies to this. But it also invites one to seek restoration and peace by returning to God, for He alone can heal this faintness and restore strength and joy.

sens: To experience fear, to dread something or someone
To be worried, to care, to be concerned about a situation
To be vigilant, to take care about something
To have respect or reverence for someone
H1672.detail:
1. To experience fear, to dread something or someone: it is to feel a real or imagined threat and to dread it. Jeremiah says to King Zedekiah: "I fear the Jews who have defected to the Chaldeans" (Jeremiah 38:19) — he fears being delivered into their hands and mistreated.
2. To be worried, to care, to be concerned about a situation: it is to be gnawed by a concern that weighs on the mind. Saul's father no longer thinks about the lost donkeys, but he is "worried about you" (1 Samuel 10:2) — he is anxious about not having news of his son.
3. To be vigilant, to take care about something: it is to be attentive to danger or to what could go wrong. In a drought, the tree "does not fear" (Jeremiah 17:8) — it is not worried about the lack of rain because its roots draw the water it needs.
4. To have respect or reverence for someone: it is to recognize the authority or power of a person and to be aware of it. It is less panic fear than respect mixed with dread, as seen in the relationship of the people to God.
H1672.origine: The verb דָּאַג (da'ag) comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of mental trouble and worry. It is related to Hebrew words meaning agitation and anxiety. The basic image is that of an inner disturbance, a troubled soul. The word is notably found in the Psalms and the prophets, where it often describes man's reaction to danger, guilt, or the absence of God.
H1672.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used in very varied contexts: first to express familial and domestic worry (Saul and his father are concerned for each other: 1 Samuel 9:5 and 10:2), then in the Psalms to describe the fear related to moral guilt (Psalm 38:19), and finally among the prophets to denote fear in the face of political or military threats (Jeremiah 38:19), or conversely the absence of fear in one who trusts in God (Jeremiah 17:8). The word thus nuances between daily worry, spiritual guilt, and reverence or trust in God.
H1672.portee: This word invites the believer to examine the source of their fears. The Bible does not condemn prudence, but it highlights that true security comes from trust in God, not from the absence of fear. The tree that "does not fear" in drought is not so because it ignores danger, but because its roots are nourished. Similarly, the Christian can go through trials without anxiety when their trust in God is deep and well-rooted.

sens: Man of Edom, chief of the king Saul's shepherds
H1673.detail: Doeg is an Edomite (that is, a man from the kingdom of Edom, a neighbor and rival of Israel) who holds an important position with King Saul as chief of his shepherds (1 Samuel 21:7). This character becomes infamous for his role in the persecution of David: he reports to Saul that David has taken refuge with the priest Ahimelech at Nob (1 Samuel 22:9), which triggers a tragic cascade of events. By the king's order, Doeg himself kills eighty-five priests of the Lord, bearers of the linen ephod, thus nearly annihilating the sanctuary of Nob (1 Samuel 22:18). David, later learning that his flight inadvertently caused this slaughter, takes moral responsibility before Abiathar, the last surviving priest (1 Samuel 22:22). Psalm 52 is composed on the occasion of Doeg's betrayal, highlighting the malice of the informer and the injustice of his actions.
H1673.origine: The name Doeg (Hebrew דֹּאֵג) literally means "one who fears" or "one who is afraid" — a certain irony for a man who commits a massacre without scruple. The etymology suggests a root expressing fear or anxiety. His Edomite origin is explicitly mentioned at every occurrence, emphasizing that he is a foreigner to the people of Israel, and perhaps a subordinate servant who became an executor of royal vengeance.
H1673.emploi: Doeg appears five times in the Old Testament: four times in 1 Samuel 21-22 (during the historical events themselves) and once in the title of Psalm 52 (a later poetic composition about these same events). First introduced simply as a servant locked "before the Lord" at Nob (1 Samuel 21:7), he gradually becomes the pivot of a tragedy: an eyewitness of David at the priest's, he betrays David to Saul, then executes royal vengeance against the priests, committing an atrocity that the Church recognizes as an act of unjust cruelty. Psalm 52 designates him as the archetype of the wicked who "loves evil" and rejoices "in the ruin of others" — transforming a political event into a universal spiritual lesson.
H1673.portee: The story of Doeg reminds us that betrayal is a weapon of destruction, and that those who commit it bear a moral responsibility even if they obey the orders of a king. It also shows how personal ambition (the desire to please Saul) can lead to unnecessary crimes. For the Christian reader, this account illustrates the fragility of human justice in the face of human cruelty, and why David felt forever indebted to the slaughtered priests — a guilt that runs through the psalm and teaches us to fear the mechanism of evil triggered by a single word.

sens: Feeling of fear and worry in the face of danger or uncertainty
Inner agitation, persistent discomfort of the heart
Physical and moral distress associated with lack or famine
H1674.detail:
1. Anguish is primarily a feeling of intense fear and concern: it arises when one fears that something bad may happen, or that a threat looms over us. The Israelites of the Jordan feared that their sons would be separated from Israel, hence their anguish about this (Joshua 22:24).
2. It is also a deep trouble of the heart that overwhelms a person from within: the worry lodged in the heart brings one down and depresses them (Proverbs 12:25). It acts like a storm that disturbs the soul, a troubled sea that cannot calm down (Jeremiah 49:23).
3. Finally, the word designates the concrete and visceral distress of the body in the grip of famine, hunger, or deprivation: Jerusalem will eat its bread with anguish and drink its water with fear, for the land will be stripped bare (Ezekiel 12:18-19).
H1674.origine: The Hebrew word דְּאָגָה comes from a root that expresses trouble, the concern that seizes someone. It designates this mental and emotional agitation that rises from the heart when security collapses. The root evokes the idea of being preoccupied or troubled by an imminent threat.
H1674.emploi: This word appears six times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophetic books (Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Joshua, and Proverbs). It describes sometimes a moral and psychological worry (Joshua 22:24: relational fear; Proverbs 12:25: heart trouble), and sometimes an anguish related to concrete and visible disasters (Jeremiah 49:23: confusion in the face of bad news; Ezekiel 4:16, 12:18-19: distress from famine and siege). In all cases, anguish puts a person in a state of agitation, both physical and mental, in the face of a real or feared threat.
H1674.portee: Anguish is presented in the Bible not as a shameful weakness, but as a deep human reaction to the loss of security and the rupture of covenant or well-being. The text teaches us that the anguish of the heart brings us down (Proverbs 12:25), but also that the good word of the Lord can rejoice us and deliver us from it. In the face of crises and threats, recognizing our anguish is the first step toward trusting in God, who alone can give us peace.

sens: To move quickly through the air by flapping wings or gliding
To swoop down on someone with the speed and force of a bird of prey
To soar, to remain suspended in the air
H1675.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to move quickly through the air by flapping wings. Psalms 18:11 describes the Lord who "flew" on a cherub, gliding on the wings of the wind — an image of divine power and majesty.
2. The word also describes the rapid attack of a predator swooping down on its prey. Jeremiah 48:40 and 49:22 compare the advance of an enemy to that of an eagle that "flies" and "spreads its wings" over its target — an image of relentless threat and domination.
3. "Soaring" or "remaining suspended" is an aspect of flight: staying in the air without apparent effort. Deuteronomy 28:49 speaks of a nation that will "fly" upon Israel like an eagle, emphasizing the swift and inevitable descent.
H1675.origine: The verb דָּאָה (da'ah) comes from a root expressing rapid and light movement in the air. It evokes the concrete image of a bird with outstretched wings cleaving the sky. The word belongs to the poetic and biblical vocabulary of spectacular natural phenomena — storm, lightning, eagle's flight — where speed and power unite.
H1675.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of great dramatic intensity. In Psalms 18:11, it designates the majestic flight of the Lord; in Deuteronomy 28:49, it describes the sudden attack of a formidable enemy; in Jeremiah 48:40 and 49:22, it announces divine judgment through warrior imagery where the eagle's flight symbolizes the inevitability of punishment. In each case, the verb emphasizes not only speed but also the power and invincibility of the one who flies.
H1675.portee: This word reminds us that the speed and strength of God surpass all human resistance. When the Lord "flies," it is to accomplish His will with majesty; when an enemy "flies" like an eagle, it is to carry out the judgment that God allows. The word invites the believer to respect divine power and to understand that no one can escape God's plan.

sens: Bird of prey with swift flight
Impure creature according to the Mosaic Law
H1676.detail:
1. The kite is a bird of prey characterized by its swift flight and agile movements. It hunts by diving on its prey with great speed. In Leviticus 11:14, it is listed among the unclean birds that the Israelites were not to eat.
2. In the context of the Law, the kite represents one of the creatures that God declared impure for the people of Israel. This classification was part of the dietary system in Leviticus that distinguished clean animals from unclean animals, guiding daily life and obedience to God.
H1676.origine: The Hebrew word דָּאָה (da'ah) designates a bird of prey known for its speed in flight. The term may be related to roots expressing speed or agility. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, renders this word with a term meaning 'kite,' confirming that it is a specific raptor recognizable in the Mediterranean region.
H1676.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 11:14. In this passage, Moses lists the unclean birds according to the Law given to Israel. The kite is mentioned alongside other raptors like the falcon. This classification is part of the dietary code that framed the religious and practical life of God's people in the Old Testament.
H1676.portee: This word reminds us that God gave Israel specific laws for food and ritual purity, which symbolized the separation of God's people and their obedience to His word. Although the Christian believer is not bound by these dietary prohibitions (see Mark 7:19), this teaching reveals the importance God places on our discernment and daily choices in order to live in communion with Him.

sens: Large wild animal with powerful limbs, covered in thick fur, carnivorous and formidable
Brute force and deadly violence
Relentless threat that preys on the weak
Divine fury against sin
H1677.detail:
1. The bear is a wild animal known for its strength and danger. David recounts that he fought a bear that attacked his flock (1 Samuel 17:34): the bear here represents a fierce predator that a shepherd must confront to protect his sheep.
2. The bear symbolizes brutal and deadly violence. Two bears came out of the forest and mauled forty-two children who mocked the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 2:24): it is a blind and destructive force.
3. The figurative bear represents a tyrant or a merciless oppressor. A wicked person who dominates a poor people is compared to 'a roaring lion and a hungry bear' (Proverbs 28:15): he is hungry for power and devours the weak.
4. The bear can also symbolize divine anger. The Lord tells Hosea that He will attack Israel 'like a bear robbed of her cubs' (Hosea 13:8): this is the justified fury of a God betrayed by His people, formidable and merciless toward sin.
H1677.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּב (dov) simply designates the bear, this animal with massive limbs. It belongs to the very ancient vocabulary of wild creatures that the Hebrews were well acquainted with in the East and the Mediterranean. The Hebrew word also has an Aramaic equivalent of the same form (דֹּב). The dov is never presented in the Bible as a mere animal: its strength, ferocity, and hunger immediately make it a natural image of violence.
H1677.emploi: The word bear appears about twelve times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and wisdom literature. David mentions it as a predator he had to overcome (1 Samuel 17:34-37), thus establishing his legitimacy to confront Goliath. In prophetic warnings, the bear embodies the threat: either a creature sent by God to punish disrespect (2 Kings 2:24), or an image of tyranny (Proverbs 28:15 and 17:12). The prophets Isaiah and Hosea use it to describe divine fury toward unfaithful Israel (Isaiah 59:11; Hosea 13:8). The context determines whether the bear is a real danger or a supernatural power.
H1677.portee: The bear reminds the reader that God protects His faithful in the face of deadly perils. David defeats the bear by faith in the Lord (1 Samuel 17:37), which encourages the believer to trust in adversity. But the bear also symbolizes divine judgment: the formidable threat that sin brings upon the rebel. Seeing God act 'like a bear' toward Israel is a call to repentance and respect for the covenant.

sens: ferocious animal with fur, carnivorous quadruped
creature symbolizing a warrior power or an empire
H1678.detail:
1. The bear is a wild and powerful animal, known for its brute strength and voracious appetite. In Daniel's vision, this bear stands 'on one side' and is commanded to 'devour much flesh,' an image that shows a hungry and unrestrained predator.
2. In apocalyptic visions, the bear represents a ruthless political or military power. Here, it symbolizes an empire — according to commentators, the Medo-Persian Empire — characterized by its greed and destructive violence.
H1678.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew דֹּב (dov), which properly designates the bear. This entry concerns the Aramaic form of the same word, used in the Aramaic portion of the book of Daniel (chapters 2 to 7). The bear was known in the ancient Near East as a feared beast, a symbol of brute strength.
H1678.emploi: The word appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament: in Daniel 7:5, where it is among the four monstrous creatures of the prophetic vision. This bear is the second animal, followed by the leopard and the lion. Its role is entirely symbolic: it embodies a regnum, a kingdom marked by oppression and greed. In other biblical and Jewish apocalypses, wild animals regularly serve as representations of earthly empires.
H1678.portee: This vision reminds the reader that the political powers that dominate the world, however formidable they may be, are merely creatures in God's hand. The hungry bear does not represent an ultimate force, but a temporary instrument of the divine plan. For the believer, this invites not to fear the tyrannies of the present time, for they are judged in advance by the Lord.

sens: Physical strength and bodily power
Capacity for endurance and persistence
Moral and spiritual solidity
H1679.detail:
1. Vigor denotes physical strength, the energy of the body capable of acting and persevering. In Deuteronomy 33:25, Moses blesses the tribe of Asher by promising that its vigor will last as long as its days — meaning that God will grant it the strength to endure the trials and labors of life.
2. The word also evokes the ability to maintain oneself over time, to resist without weakening. The promise is not a fleeting strength, but a strength that accompanies each day of existence.
3. This vigor has a spiritual dimension: it is the power that God grants, enabling His people to persevere faithfully in their days, whatever they may be.
H1679.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּ֫בֶא (dova) has an obscure original meaning, but it evokes the idea of stable and lasting strength. The root may be related to terms expressing solidity and permanence. In ancient Hebrew texts, this word appears rarely, making its etymology difficult to establish with certainty, but the context of Deuteronomy 33 reveals that it is a divine power granted to the people.
H1679.emploi: The word appears only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:25, in the blessing that Moses pronounces over the tribes of Israel before his death. This unique occurrence is found in a solemn passage where Moses confers a specific divine promise to each tribe. For Asher, the blessing concerns the vigor that will last all its days — a promise of persistent strength in the face of challenges. The rarity of the word emphasizes the importance of this particular blessing.
H1679.portee: This promise of constant vigor reminds the believer that God does not grant strength only for a moment, but for each day. It teaches that our ability to persevere in faith is not our own work, but the renewed gift of God. For a life marked by trials, this word brings peace: God promises that His strength will accompany us all along the way.

sens: To move smoothly and without jolts on a surface
To flow fluidly from one place to another
To pass lightly, without stopping
H1680.detail:
1. The verb describes a fluid and graceful movement, without harshness — that of a substance flowing gently or an object sliding quietly across a surface. In the Song of Songs (7:10), the beloved's wine "slides" on the lips of those who sleep: the image evokes a sweetness that penetrates effortlessly, spreading with elegance.
2. The word can also refer to an unobstructed passage, a natural flow from one place to another — like the flow of a poured drink that flows easily.
3. Figuratively, it suggests a discreet action, occurring without jolt or abruptness, leaving a delicate trace.
H1680.origine: The Hebrew root דָּבַב (dav-av) expresses the idea of smooth and continuous movement. It is a rare root in biblical Hebrew, and this verb appears only once in the Old Testament, making it a very particular word. The underlying image is that of a gentle and almost imperceptible progression, like the sliding of a fluid substance.
H1680.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Songs 7:10. It describes the beloved's wine that "flows easily" and "slides" gently on the lips of those who fall asleep. The poetic and romantic context of the Song makes it a word of delicacy and grace. Its uniqueness makes its use all the more striking: the writer chose this rare term to express a fluid and unresisting intimacy.
H1680.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the beauty of what happens gently and effortlessly — a grace that imposes itself quietly. In the language of the Song, it expresses the harmony of two beings meeting without friction or violence, reminding the believer that true love operates through gentleness rather than force.

sens: Evil and false words reported about someone to discredit them
Malicious rumor spread to harm someone's reputation
Damning gossip circulated from one person to another
H1681.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of wicked words reported about someone to harm them. Joseph reports to his father "the bad words" of his brothers (Genesis 37:2) — bad things he has heard and will repeat. It is a form of backbiting, malicious reporting.
2. The word also refers to the act of discrediting someone through words, particularly through lies. The spies sent by Moses "slandered" the Promised Land (Numbers 13:32), meaning they circulated a bad report about it to discourage the people: "it is a land that devours its inhabitants." This is a form of negative propaganda.
3. More broadly, it encompasses any malicious rumor circulated: "the bad words of many" mentioned in the psalm (Psalms 31:14), things said about you to harm you, often in secret ("they conspire together"). One who "spreads slander" (Proverbs 10:18) acts foolishly: they sow discord.
H1681.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of whispering and rumor — something murmured, reported quietly from one ear to another. This is why slander is often linked to secrecy, to words that spread in hiding. The word is related to the idea of "reporting": one who spreads slander is a reporter, someone who carries bad news from one side to another.
H1681.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and wisdom literature. Its most dramatic use is found in Numbers: the ten spies who "slandered" the Promised Land caused a revolt among the entire people and died struck by a plague, while Joshua and Caleb, who had courage, were spared — slander destroyed an entire generation. In the Psalms and Proverbs, it appears as a weapon of the wicked: it is a grave sin, contrary to the wisdom of God. The word can refer interchangeably to the gossip itself ("words") or the act of spreading it ("slander").
H1681.portee: Slander appears in the Bible as a grave sin that destroys communities: it sows doubt, fear, and discord. It is particularly dangerous because it often spreads in secret, like a whisper. God's judgment on the spies who slandered the Promised Land shows that God does not accept defamation. For the Christian, this word invites one to keep their words pure and not to spread rumors, even if they seem true: slander destroys others and offends God.

sens: Flying insect that produces honey
Swarm of bees considered a threat
Image of the enemy attacking in numbers
H1682.detail:
1. The bee is an insect known for producing honey: Samson discovers a swarm of bees and honey in the carcass of a lion he had killed (Judges 14:8), an image of a sweet find emerging from something dead.
2. Used as an image of an enemy army that descends upon someone and pursues them: the Amorites who launch an attack on the Israelites are compared to bees that harass them (Deuteronomy 1:44), so massive and coordinated is their assault.
3. Enemies are described as surrounding the psalmist like bees, then disappearing like a fire that goes out (Psalms 118:12) — the image evokes a constant threat but also the possibility of victory over these assailants.
H1682.origine: The Hebrew word דְּבוֹרָה (devorah) comes from a root that evokes buzzing and noise, which reflects the characteristic sound of the bee. The same word in Hebrew is also a feminine proper name (the prophetess Deborah), as the buzzing of the bee was a distinctive and memorable sound for ancient Hebrews.
H1682.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts where the bee symbolizes a threat or aggression in numbers. In Deuteronomy 1:44 and Psalms 118:12, enemies are compared to bees that attack: this image emphasizes both the multitude of assailants and the stinging nature of their attack. In Isaiah 7:18, the Lord "whistles" for the bees of the land of Assyria to come, expanding the symbolism to the divine will to call enemies. The exception is Judges 14:8, where the bee is simply the producer of honey, without a warrior connotation.
H1682.portee: The bee reminds Christians that they may be surrounded by enemies or obstacles in numbers, but like the fire that goes out, these threats are never permanent. It invites one to see divine providence in all things: even what seems threatening can serve God's purposes.

sens: The nurse of Rebekah who accompanied her from Mesopotamia to Canaan
A woman whose death and burial are worthy of remembrance in the history of Israel
H1683G.detail:
1. Deborah was the trusted servant of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau. She traveled with her from the house of Bethuel in Mesopotamia to the land of Canaan, sharing the years of her life and winning her affection. Her name means "bee" in Hebrew, and she symbolizes the faithfulness of those who serve in the patriarchal families.
2. Her death was memorable: she was buried near Bethel, under an oak tree that was named "the oak of weeping" (Genesis 35:8). This funeral honor shows that she was dear to the house of Jacob and that her life of service was recognized and respected by the entire family.
H1683G.origine: The name Deborah comes from the Hebrew dbr which literally means "bee." Bees are hardworking creatures, faithful to their role, which suits a devoted servant. In the Bible, this name also evokes a prophetess who judged Israel during the time of the Judges (Judges 4-5), although this is a different person.
H1683G.emploi: Deborah appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 35:8. She is mentioned at the time of her death, after Jacob and his family returned to Bethel to erect an altar. Her burial under an oak tree, near Bethel, and the name given to this place — the "oak of weeping" — suggest that the inhabitants of the land and Jacob's family honored her. Although she is never mentioned elsewhere, her presence alongside Rebekah during all the years of Rebekah's life makes her a discreet yet precious figure of faithfulness.
H1683G.portee: Deborah reminds the reader that the great biblical narratives rely on the faithfulness of humble and forgotten people. Her story and respect deserve a place in the memory of Israel, even though she was neither a prophetess nor a judge. She embodies the loyal and discreet service that supports the families and generations of God's people.

sens: Prophetess and judge of Israel before the monarchy
A woman endowed with wisdom and spiritual authority
H1683H.detail:
1. Deborah is a prophetess and judge who governs Israel during the period of the Judges, before the establishment of the monarchy (Judges 4:4). She sits under a palm tree and renders justice to the children of Israel who come to consult her (Judges 4:5).
2. She embodies a woman whom God endows with remarkable spiritual power: she guides the general Barak into battle against Sisera and tells him that it is a woman, not he, who will kill the enemy (Judges 4:9, 4:14). She also sings the victory song with Barak (Judges 5:1).
H1683H.origine: The name means "bee" in Hebrew. It evokes a small but active, hardworking, and organized creature. Deborah thus represents a figure of a working and leading woman. There is no etymological link with other major biblical words: it is a unique name chosen for this prophetess.
H1683H.emploi: Deborah appears 9 times in the Bible, primarily in Judges 4—5, the account of her deliverance of Israel against Sisera and the Canaanite army. She is never merely a spectator: she summons the warriors (Judges 4:10), urges Barak to action (Judges 4:14), and she herself descends into battle. After the victory, she composes a song of praise (Judges 5:1, 5:7, 5:12, 5:15). She embodies a rare female prophetic leadership in the Old Testament, recognized and awaited by the people.
H1683H.portee: Deborah teaches that God can raise anyone—man or woman—to accomplish His purposes. She shows that a woman can exercise authority and wisdom with courage: she judges Israel, inspires the warrior, and leads to victory. For the Christian reader, she is an example of faithfulness to the voice of God and service in the time assigned to her, with the assurance that God goes before those who obey Him (Judges 4:14).

sens: To present to God a victim, an animal, or a possession in an act of worship or propitiation
To perform the sacrificial rite at the temple or altar
H1684.detail:
1. To offer a sacrifice is to present to God a victim — animal or precious possession — as a sign of worship, gratitude, or to obtain forgiveness for sins. It is a fundamental religious act in temple worship, where the believer acknowledges God's lordship and his need for reconciliation.
2. The verb also designates the accomplishment of the rite itself: the one who offers a sacrifice places it on the altar, according to the prescribed rules, so that it ascends to God. In Ezra 6:3, the house of God is specifically rebuilt "to be a place where sacrifices are offered," showing that the temple exists primarily for this central religious function.
H1684.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew "zavach" (H2076), which means "to slaughter" or "to ritually kill." The basic image is that of the controlled killing of a victim in honor of God. This family of words expresses the fundamental idea of sacrificial worship: to kill in order to offer, to destroy in order to give.
H1684.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Aramaic, in the decree of King Cyrus reported in Ezra 6:3. This decree authorizes the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem and specifies that the building must serve as a place where sacrifices are offered. The usage shows that sacrifice is the very reason for the temple's existence: the temple is not primarily a building, but a space where the community fulfills its worship toward God.
H1684.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that access to God comes through sacrifice: it is a visible, costly act that engages the body and possessions. Although the New Testament transcends the regime of animal sacrifices by revealing the unique sacrifice of Christ, this word shows the continuity of God's design: throughout all times, God has desired to be worshiped by offerings that cost something to the one making them.

sens: what is offered to God on the altar, an animal or possession slaughtered in homage or to obtain His forgiveness
the act of offering a victim to God
H1685.detail:
1. The sacrifice is an offering presented to God by slaughtering it on the altar — a victim (animal or possession) intended to honor God, to thank Him, or to atone for sin. When King Cyrus's edict orders the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem "to be a place where sacrifices are offered" (Ezra 6:3), it acknowledges that this holy building will serve these important religious acts.
2. The word can also designate the act of offering itself — the cultic gesture by which one presents a victim to God on His altar. This is at the heart of Israel's religious life.
H1685.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew word "mizbeach" (מִזְבֵּחַ), which means "altar." The altar is the place of sacrifice: the word naturally comes from it. The root evokes the idea of slaughtering, striking — the violent act that transforms a living victim into an offering to God. In the Old Testament, sacrifice is at the heart of the worship rendered to the God of Israel.
H1685.emploi: This word appears only once in Aramaic in the Bible, in the edict of King Cyrus (Ezra 6:3). Cyrus orders the exiled Jewish people to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem as "a place where sacrifices are offered." This is a recognition by a pagan king that the Jewish temple had a central religious function: to be the seat of sacrificial worship. Although the term is rare in Aramaic, the concept is fundamental throughout Scripture.
H1685.portee: This passage shows that sacrifice was not a secret or marginal practice: it was the religious institution that even foreign kings recognized as essential to the worship of the true God. It reminds us that God ordained the sacrificial system so that His people could reconcile with Him and serve Him. It also sheds light on the sacrifice of Jesus, the ultimate offering that fulfills the meaning of all previous sacrifices.

sens: pigeon excrement
fertilizer or fuel of little value
H1686.detail:
1. The word literally refers to pigeon droppings, a substance hardly worth mentioning. In 2 Kings 6:25, during the terrible famine in Samaria, the Bible lists exorbitant prices: a donkey's head is worth eighty shekels of silver, and a quarter of a cab (a small measure) of pigeon droppings is worth five. It's absurd, like paying for garbage.
2. By extension, this droppings represents something worthless, a waste. It could be used as fertilizer or fuel (dry material for burning), but it was so abundant and valueless that under normal circumstances it would never have been sold. The crisis in Samaria makes the ridiculous precious: it is the image of hunger that transforms waste into merchandise.
H1686.origine: The Hebrew word divyonim is formed from dov (pigeon, particularly the dove or wild pigeon) and a suffix indicating possession or relation. The root evokes the bird that coos and returns to its nest. In Hebrew, pigeon often appears in a noble sense (pure offerings at the Temple), but here, it is its waste that fascinates: the contrast highlights the extremity of the famine.
H1686.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in 2 Kings 6:25. The context is that of the siege of Samaria by the Aramean army (around 850 B.C.), where the famine becomes so severe that the inhabitants eat unimaginable things and sell worthless items. This unique occurrence reinforces the dramatic effect: the very mention of this miserable product will mark the reader and show the absolute horror of the situation.
H1686.portee: This passage reminds the believer that extreme famine and misery can reduce humanity to total destitution. It also invites gratitude for daily bread and vigilance against pride: fortified and opulent cities can collapse. For the prophet Elisha, who intervenes in this story, it is an opportunity to show that the word of God surpasses visible reality.

sens: The innermost and most sacred chamber of the temple or tabernacle
The place where the ark of the covenant rests
The heart of the temple, separated from the rest by a veil
The place where God manifests His presence in a concentrated manner
H1687.detail:
1. The sanctuary is the most intimate room of the temple or tabernacle, where God particularly dwells. It is a rectangular chamber, completely isolated and closed, which can be imagined as the "secret heart" of God's house. In 1 Kings 6:19, Solomon "prepared the sanctuary within the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the Lord": it is in this sanctuary that the most important chest of all Israel rested.
2. This sanctuary was a highly protected space, separated from the rest of the temple by a magnificent veil. In 1 Kings 6:21, it was "overlaid with gold" and "the veil was hung with chains of gold before the sanctuary": every detail was designed to show that one was entering a divine space. Only the high priest entered there once a year, on the Day of Atonement.
3. The sanctuary was also the seat of God's manifestation. In Psalms 28:2, the psalmist prays by lifting his hands "toward the sanctuary", the place where God listens and responds. This is why two enormous cherubim of olive wood, "ten cubits high", were placed inside (1 Kings 6:23): they symbolized the divine presence and the majesty of God.
H1687.origine: The Hebrew word דְּבִיר (devir) comes from a root meaning "to speak" or "to say": it is a place where God speaks. It is also found in the form "oracle" in ancient Greek (the term δάβιρ). This is why the sanctuary is not just an empty room, but the focal point where the word of God becomes audible to His people. The word suggests that this place was the seat of divine communication.
H1687.emploi: The word "sanctuary" appears 16 times in biblical Hebrew, almost always in passages describing Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6-8 and 2 Chronicles 3-5). There is only one exception: Psalms 28:2, where the psalmist directs his prayers toward this earthly sanctuary. The accounts of the construction show how Solomon built it with care: he placed it at the heart of the house (1 Kings 6:19), covered it with pure gold (1 Kings 6:21), put two giant cherubim there (1 Kings 6:23), and separated it from the rest by a veil (1 Kings 6:21). The word always designates this unique and isolated chamber, never the other parts of the temple. It is the place where the ark of the covenant was kept and where the divine presence concentrated.
H1687.portee: For the Christian, the sanctuary of the ancient temple reveals how God desired to be close to His people, but also separated by holiness. This golden chamber, covered with veils and guarded by cherubim, shows that access to God required respect and purification. Jesus transformed this reality: by dying, He tore the veil of the temple (Matthew 27:51), finally opening direct access to God for all. Each believer now becomes a sanctuary where the Spirit of God dwells (1 Corinthians 6:19).

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Judah, west of Hebron, in the mountainous region
Place of refuge and city given to the priests of the tribe of Levi
H1688A.detail:
1. Debir was an important city in the mountainous lands of Judah, located west of Hebron. It was formerly known as Kirjath-Sepher, which means "city of the book" (Joshua 15:15). It was a fortified city with its own king, which Joshua conquered and destroyed during the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 10:38-39).
2. After the conquest, Debir was designated as a city of refuge and given to the priests of the tribe of Levi to dwell in (Joshua 21:15; 1 Chronicles 6:58). It thus served as a religious center and an asylum for those who had committed unintentional homicide.
H1688A.origine: The Hebrew name דְּבִיר (Debir) literally means "sanctuary" or "holy place", which perfectly fits its function as a city of refuge and a priestly city. The word comes from the same root as other Hebrew religious terms designating holy places. This meaning reflects the religious importance that the city acquired after its conquest and its assignment to the Levitical priests.
H1688A.emploi: Debir appears nine times in the Old Testament, mainly in the book of Joshua (six occurrences) which recounts its conquest by Joshua in the years 1400-1380 B.C. It is mentioned as one of the Canaanite royal cities that Joshua defeated and destroyed (Joshua 10:38-39, 12:13). It is then listed among the cities given to the Levitical priests (Joshua 21:15) and is mentioned in the context of the elimination of the Anakim, those giants who inhabited the territory (Joshua 11:21). It is also referred to as Kirjath-Sanna or Kirjath-Sepher in ancient sources (Joshua 15:15, 15:49).
H1688A.portee: Debir reminds the Christian reader that God established cities of refuge in the Old Testament to protect even those guilty of unintentional homicide, showing His mercy. The assignment of this city to the priests emphasizes that certain places were consecrated for divine service and intercession for the people. For the believer, it is an example of how God organized the life of His chosen people around justice and holiness.

sens: Fortified city of Manasseh in Gilead, east of the Jordan
H1688B.detail: Debir is a city located in Gilead, in the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, east of the Jordan. It is mentioned in the account of the distribution of lands among the tribes of Israel, notably as a geographical landmark for delineating the borders of the territory assigned to Manasseh (Joshua 13:26).
H1688B.origine: The name Debir comes from two Hebrew words: לֹא ("no") and דְבָר ("pasture"), which literally means "without pasture" or "no pasture". This designation likely evokes the nature of the terrain or a particular feature of the place at the time of its naming.
H1688B.emploi: Debir appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua (13:26), where it is cited as a reference point in the description of the borders of the territory of Manasseh in Gilead. It is among the cities listed to establish the precise limits of this tribe's land inheritance after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: City of Judah, in the Promised Land
H1688G.detail: 1. Debir is a city mentioned during the description of the borders of the territory of Judah in the Promised Land. It is located in the region between the valley of Achor and Gilgal, on the road that descends from Jerusalem to the Dead Sea. Its name literally means "sanctuary" or "holy place" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a place of worship.
H1688G.origine: The name Debir comes from the Hebrew root "dabar" which means "word" or "oracle," and the term was applied to sacred places or sanctuaries — the dome or the holy of holies of a temple. Several cities bore this name in Israel, suggesting the religious significance of the term. This place was meant to mark important landmarks in the sacred geography of the Promised Land.
H1688G.emploi: Debir appears in the passage that lists the borders of the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah after the conquest. Joshua 15:7 mentions it as a landmark in the delineation of the northeastern boundary of Judah, between the valley of Achor and the region of Gilgal. It served as a territorial marker to delineate the lands assigned to each tribe.

sens: King of Eglon at the time of the conquest of Canaan by Joshua
H1688H.detail: Debir is a Canaanite king who rules over the city of Eglon at the arrival of the Israelites in the Promised Land. He is among the five allied kings who unite against Joshua and the Israelites: Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem, Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debir of Eglon. These kings seek to resist the Israelite conquest, but they will be defeated and killed during Joshua's military campaigns in Canaan.
H1688H.origine: The name Debir literally means "word" or "oracle" in Hebrew, coming from the root דבר ("speak"). It is a common theophoric name in the ancient Near East, borne by several high-ranking figures.
H1688H.emploi: Debir is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Joshua 10:3, where he is listed as one of the five Canaanite kings who unite to fight Joshua. His brief but significant appearance illustrates the resistance that the Canaanite kingdoms opposed to the Israelite invasion and the decisive role of Joshua in the conquest of the promised land.

sens: desert region near Syria
place of desolation in the prophecies of Ezekiel
H1689.detail: 1. Dibla is a region or desert located near the northeastern border of Israel, in the vicinity of Syria. It is a dry and inhospitable place, often associated with desolation. 2. In the prophetic vision of Ezekiel, God threatens to make the land of Israel more solitary and desolate than the desert of Dibla (Ezekiel 6:14): this name thus evokes complete abandonment, total ruin of the promised land.
H1689.origine: The name literally means "place of the cake of figs" in Hebrew (derived from דִּבְלָה, dibla). It is another spelling or variant of the name Riblah (רִבְלָה, rivlah), a well-known region in the Syro-Palestinian territory. The word rests on the image of figs, characteristic fruits of the Levant, but designates a real place marked by its aridity.
H1689.emploi: Dibla appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 6:14, where the prophet announces divine judgment against unfaithful Israelites. God declares that He will make the land more desolate than the desert of Dibla, meaning unprecedented destruction. This name is chosen for its reputation as a sterile and uninhabited region, a symbol of the annihilation that God will inflict on the land of Israel due to the idolatry of its people.
H1689.portee: This name reminds us that the prophetic threats of divine judgment have real and precise geographical consequences. For the believing reader, Dibla symbolizes the spiritual and material aridity that follows abandonment of God. It is a call to repentance: remaining faithful to the Lord is the only protection against total desolation.

sens: Cake or mass of dried figs pressed together
Nutritious and energizing food carried on journeys or campaigns
Remedy or poultice applied to a wound or ulcer
H1690.detail:
1. The word refers to a cake of figs — a compact mass formed by pressing together dried figs. It is a highly concentrated and nourishing food. Abigail brings two hundred to David: she loads them on donkeys with other provisions (1 Samuel 25:18).
2. These masses of dried figs are eaten as travel or campaign food, as they keep for a long time and quickly restore energy. When the Egyptian that David encounters has eaten nothing for three days, he is given a piece of dried fig mass and raisins, and he regains strength (1 Samuel 30:12).
3. In a medical usage, a mass of dried figs becomes a remedy: the prophet Isaiah orders one to be applied to Hezekiah's ulcer, and the king is healed (2 Kings 20:7; Isaiah 38:21). Figs were believed to have healing properties.
H1690.origine: The word comes from the root that means "figs," in Hebrew דְּבַר (debar). A "debela" is literally a cake or block made of pressed figs. This process of drying and compressing was common in the ancient Near East to preserve fruits and facilitate transport.
H1690.emploi: The word appears five times, mostly in the historical accounts of David and during the reign of Hezekiah. In three verses (1 Samuel 25:18; 1 Samuel 30:12; 1 Chronicles 12:40), it refers to a food item that is carried in large quantities to feed an army or supply servants. In two verses (2 Kings 20:7; Isaiah 38:21), the same word changes usage: it becomes a poultice, a direct therapeutic application to a wound.
H1690.portee: This entry shows how the Bible simply speaks of everyday things: food that revives, care that heals. It reminds us that God provides for our needs through the fruits of the earth, and that ancient wisdom recognized in simple foods both nutrition and remedy. It is also a lesson in generosity — Abigail brings her best to divert David from vengeance.

sens: father of Gomer, the wife of the prophet Hosea
H1691.detail: Diblaïm is the father of Gomer, the woman whom the prophet Hosea married. He is a figure from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel, known only through this marriage.
H1691.origine: The name Diblaïm literally means "two cakes" or "two portions of cake" in Hebrew. Nothing is known about the symbolic or personal significance of this name in the story of Hosea.
H1691.emploi: Diblaïm appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 1:3, where he is mentioned as the father of Gomer. The prophet Hosea receives the Lord's command to take a woman named Gomer, daughter of Diblaïm. This mention is purely genealogical and situates Gomer within her family before her marriage to the prophet.

sens: Physically stick to something, remain attached
Follow someone closely, catch up or pursue
Remain faithfully with someone, be loyal to them
Bind closely to someone in a relationship of covenant or love
Adhere to something mentally or morally, hold firmly to it
H1692.detail:
1. Physically stick: the word first evokes the image of two things sticking together, remaining joined. In Job 29:10, the tongue sticks to the roof of the mouth: it remains glued there as if paralyzed. In Job 38:38, the dust sticks together, forming a solid mass.
2. Pursue, catch up: when the word describes people, it means to follow someone closely in order to reach them. In Judges 18:22, the people gather and pursue the sons of Dan. In 2 Samuel 1:6, the chariots and horsemen were close to reaching Saul.
3. Remain faithfully with someone: it is to accompany someone, to stay by their side. In Ruth 1:14, Ruth clings to Naomi and refuses to leave her. In Ruth 2:21 and 2:23, Ruth asks to remain with the servants of Boaz.
4. Bind by love or covenant: the word expresses a deep and lasting bond. In Genesis 2:24, a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife: this is the bond of marriage. In Deuteronomy 13:4 and 30:20, Israel must cling to the Lord, meaning to remain faithful to Him and serve Him with all their heart.
5. Adhere morally, hold firmly: the word can also mean "to follow a conduct" or "to adopt." In 2 Kings 18:6, King Hezekiah clings to the Lord; he embraces His way. In Psalms 101:3, an evil conduct will not cling to one who rejects it.
H1692.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the image of two things sticking together, welding together. The word has a very physical force at the outset: one thinks of glue, of adhesion. In Hebrew, there are related words that also describe the idea of binding or perseverance. This root is also used to express faithfulness and covenant in the relationship with God.
H1692.emploi: The word appears 52 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books and the Psalms. It is used first in a concrete sense: cling physically (the roof of the mouth, the dust). It also describes military or personal pursuit: catching up with someone. But its most important use is spiritual and relational: clinging to God, to His covenant, to His law. Genesis 2:24 marks the marital bond. Deuteronomy and Joshua constantly recap the imperative to cling to the Lord (Deuteronomy 10:20, 30:20; Joshua 23:8). In Ruth, the word describes faithfulness and devotion between people. In the Psalms, it also expresses moral adherence to divine will or rejection of evil.
H1692.portee: This word reveals what the Bible means by faithfulness to God: not a distant or occasional obedience, but a deep and lasting adherence, as one clings to a loved one. Genesis 2:24 shows that marriage is the model of this inseparable attachment. For the Christian, to cling to God means to persevere in the relationship with Him, keep His commandments, and refuse anything that would draw us away. It is a faithfulness that manifests itself through concrete actions.

sens: Remain attached, glued to something or someone
Adhere strongly, without separating
Form a covenant, a lasting bond
H1693.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to be glued, attached to something like iron or clay that mix together. It is the image of material adhesion, of a union by close contact.
2. In a figurative sense, the word designates moral or political union: to form a covenant, a strong bond between peoples or kingdoms. In Daniel 2:43, the kingdoms "will mingle through human alliances" but will not truly be "united" — the word expresses here the bond that one seeks to establish, even if it remains fragile like iron mixed with clay.
H1693.origine: This Aramaic word is the P'al form (the Aramaic equivalent of the simple Hebrew) of davaq, a very ancient Hebrew verb meaning "to cling, stick to." The root evokes the physical idea of sticking, remaining glued. It is also found in the Hebrew name "debek" (the glue). In Aramaic, in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the verb retains this force of adhesion, applied to kingdoms that attempt to bind themselves through marriages.
H1693.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in the dream that King Nebuchadnezzar confides to the prophet Daniel. It describes the statue with feet mixed: the future kingdoms "will mingle" through human alliances, seeking a solid union, but like iron and clay, they will remain separate. The use emphasizes the impossibility of a true political union between different dynasties, despite efforts of marriage and alliance.
H1693.portee: This word invites the reader to see beyond political appearances: human alliances, even carefully forged, do not produce true unity if the foundations are not solid. For the believer, it is also a reminder that only God creates a lasting and deep union — this is fragile when it rests solely on human calculations.

sens: Place where two pieces of armor join, or small gap between them
Junction, welding of two elements
H1694.detail: 1. When speaking of a war armor, it is the place where two metal plates touch or assemble, and where the armor is not continuous. It is a flaw through which a weapon can penetrate. King Ahab of Israel is killed in 1 Kings 22:34 by an arrow that strikes him precisely "at the defect of the breastplate" — between the moving pieces, where no protection exists. 2. More broadly, the word designates the action of joining, welding, or riveting two elements together. In Isaiah 41:7, the workers who make an idol look with satisfaction at the "welding" where two parts of wood or metal join, before fixing it with nails.
H1694.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to stick, adhere, join." It evokes the idea of two things coming close and touching, whether it is pieces of armor that meet or materials that are joined by welding. The family also includes words designating adherence or physical binding.
H1694.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice in 1 Kings 22:34 and 2 Chronicles 18:33 (the same account), it describes the weak point of a warrior's armor, the defect between the plates. Once in Isaiah 41:7, it speaks of the welding in idolatrous manufacturing. In all cases, it is a point of junction, a seam or a stitch, but the context changes: military in the kings, manufacturing in Isaiah.
H1694.portee: This word reminds us that human defenses, even the strongest, have flaws. The king's death by the defect in his breastplate illustrates the biblical image: no earthly protection is total, and we depend solely on God's providence. For the believer, it is an invitation not to rely on one's own strength or plans, but on God's protection and guidance.

sens: To be glued to something, to adhere physically
To be in close contact, to touch
To remain close to someone with affection and loyalty
To stay united to God in obedience and trust
H1695.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to be glued, to adhere to a surface like two objects that are closely touching. In 2 Chronicles 3:12, the wing of one cherub "joined" the wing of the other, meaning they were directly touching.
2. The word also describes close contact between people. In Proverbs 18:24, a friend can be "attached" to someone more strongly than a blood brother: the image is one of proximity and loyalty that binds two beings together.
3. In Deuteronomy 4:4, the verb takes on a spiritual dimension: you have "clung" to the Lord your God. It is the image of remaining firmly attached to God through obedience and trust, without detaching from Him. This bond is what keeps the people alive in their relationship with their God.
H1695.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of sticking, adhering. The word belongs to a family of terms that describe intimate union and closeness. In Hebrew, this root paints the image of a physical bond that has become a powerful metaphor for emotional and spiritual ties: what remains stuck together does not separate.
H1695.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Deuteronomy 4:4, it denotes the attachment of the people of Israel to God after the revelation at Sinai: it is an act of loyalty that guarantees life. In 2 Chronicles 3:12, it is purely descriptive: the elements of the temple physically join together. In Proverbs 18:24, it depicts sincere friendship as a bond stronger than blood ties. The word consistently expresses the idea of a lasting union, whether physical or emotional.
H1695.portee: This word invites the believer to understand attachment to God not as a fleeting feeling, but as a tenacious and concrete adherence. The figure of one who "clings" to the Lord reminds us that faith is not detached: it manifests through obedience and closeness a true bond. It is also a word for Christian friendship: a true friendship is one that "sticks" more than blood ties.

sens: To emit words, articulate meaningful sounds
To communicate with someone, engage in conversation
To convey a message, make something known
To give an order, command
To make a promise, commit by word
To be the subject or content of a discussion
H1696G.detail:
1. To speak is primarily to open the mouth and produce intelligible words. This is the simplest and most common meaning of the verb: when God spoke to Noah (Genesis 8:15), He emitted audible and understandable words.
2. But to speak also means to communicate with another person, to establish an exchange. Moses gives Aaron precise instructions about the sacrifice (Leviticus 10:12): it is not just about pronouncing sounds, but about conveying content to someone else.
3. To speak also means to announce, declare, make a reality known. Jeremiah announces what the Lord has declared about the nations (Jeremiah 25:13): the verb here denotes the proclamation of a prophetic word.
4. To speak can also mean to give an order or command. God speaks to Abraham (Genesis 17:3) not only to communicate but to command him to fulfill His will.
5. In certain contexts, to speak carries the meaning of promising or committing. The Lord speaks to someone by granting a promise or a covenant.
6. Finally, to speak can mean to be the subject of a discussion: "the days will speak" (Job 32:7) means that the years and experience will testify, will take the floor to teach.
H1696G.origine: The Hebrew root דָבַר (dabar) evokes the idea of emitting words, making one's voice heard. The noun derived from it, דָבָר (dabar), means "word" or "thing," because a word is a reality that exists once pronounced. This family of words traces back to the very ancient idea of the creative power of the word: to say is to make exist. The verb appears in nearly all biblical books and remains one of the most frequently used verbs to describe communication, especially the word of God.
H1696G.emploi: This verb is extremely frequent in the Old Testament (over 970 times), far surpassing all other communication verbs. It appears from the book of Genesis and spans all historical, poetic, and prophetic books. Speaking is primarily the act of the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob), then of the prophets who receive and transmit the divine word. The context changes depending on the speaker: when God "speaks," the verb emphasizes His authority and the certainty of His word; when a human "speaks," it often involves a simple conversation, a request (Abraham speaking to God in Genesis 18), or a command (Moses to Aaron). The meaning also shifts according to grammatical construction: "to speak to" someone highlights the exchange, while "to speak of" or "to speak on" emphasizes the content or subject addressed.
H1696G.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reveals the centrality of communication in the relationship between God and humanity. The entire history of salvation rests on the word: God speaks to Abraham, to Moses, to the prophets, and ultimately to mankind. Understanding this verb is to grasp that God is not distant or silent, but constantly addresses His people. It is also to recognize that the word, in biblical Hebrew, is not just a simple sequence of sounds, but a reality endowed with power and effectiveness.

sens: To submit a people, a nation under one's authority
To reduce to nothing, to make disappear
To command, to dominate
H1696H.detail:
1. To subjugate means to submit a people or a nation to one's authority, to place them under one's domination. It is the image of a conqueror making his enemies obedient subjects: in Psalm 47:4, God "subjugates nations" and puts "peoples under our feet."

2. To perish or cause to perish means to reduce to nothing, to completely annihilate. In 2 Chronicles 22:10, Athaliah "caused the entire royal line to perish": she killed those who might contest her throne, making them disappear.

3. The verb can also express broader domination: to command, to have authority over someone. It is to exercise absolute power, as when God "subjugates" His enemies in Psalm 18:48 — He disposes of them according to His will.
H1696H.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of crushing, bringing down, overthrowing. The same family gives the word "davar" (word), because to say a word is also to "subjugate" or impose by the force of authority. The meaning "to subjugate" is more related to verbal forms (Hiphil) where the subject causes the submission or destruction of another.
H1696H.emploi: This verb appears here in its sense of domination or annihilation. The three provided usages show its application in a political or theological context: submitting peoples to one's authority (Psalms 18:48 and 47:4, where God is the subject) or causing a lineage to perish (2 Chronicles 22:10). The Hebrew verb we are studying thus covers both the idea of submission and that of destruction, depending on the context and grammatical formulation used.
H1696H.portee: This word reminds the reader that true authority is never with humans — it is God alone who truly "subjugates" nations. When Athaliah seeks to eliminate the royal line to maintain power, she fails: God protects the one who will survive. For the believer, this is a comfort: no human power can annihilate what God wants to preserve.

sens: To express a word, to state something by speaking
To express a commitment to someone: to promise
To communicate between several people
To give an order, a command
To announce a decision or intention in advance
To be stated, to be said by someone
H1696I.detail:
1. The most basic meaning is to speak, to express words: "The Lord of hosts, who planted you, calls disaster upon you" (Jeremiah 11:17), where the verb means "declares" or "pronounces." 
2. Very often, to say carries the weight of a promise, a solemn commitment to someone: "The Lord has fulfilled the word that He spoke" (2 Chronicles 6:10), meaning the promise He made to David for his son to reign in his place.
3. The verb can also mean to converse, to dialogue between several people, to exchange words together.
4. To say can be a command, an order addressed to the listener: the Lord "commands His sons and His household after Him to keep the way" (Genesis 18:19).
5. The word also carries the meaning of announcing in advance, decreeing a future intention: "Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon, I have given to you, as I said to Moses" (Joshua 1:3), God's declaration engaging its fulfillment.
6. Finally, to say can be passive: to be stated, to be uttered by someone else.
H1696I.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of word and communication. The Hebrew word דָּבָר (dabar) in the singular means "word" or "matter," and the verb is its dynamic core: to speak is to "produce a word." The same root generates words related to communication: the one who speaks, the thing said, the promise stated. It is a fundamental verb in Hebrew, widespread throughout all biblical books.
H1696I.emploi: This verb appears about 78 times in the Hebrew biblical text according to the provided usages, especially in the Torah and historical books, but also abundantly in the prophets. It is massively used to express God's promises: "the Lord had promised" (Deuteronomy 9:28), "what the Lord had promised" (Joshua 21:45, 23:14, 1 Kings 8:56). The verb is also very commonly used to describe the statement of laws and commandments (Leviticus 23:44, Deuteronomy 27:3). In the prophets, it means to pronounce a judgment or a threat (Jeremiah 11:17, 18:7-9). The nuance varies: to say can be a simple statement, but when the subject is God, to say equates to decreeing, and the spoken word will infallibly come to pass.
H1696I.portee: This verb reminds us of the power of the word, especially God's word: when the Lord says, His word does not return void; it accomplishes what He has determined (Isaiah 55:11, not provided here). For the believer, this means that the promises God has spoken will be fulfilled. It also invites us to take our own words seriously: to say is to engage our responsibility and integrity.

sens: A set of sounds and words that a person pronounces
Message, information, or news communicated to someone
Order or command given by someone of higher authority
Matter, subject, or situation being discussed
Promise or commitment made to someone
What is said, what is being talked about
H1697G.detail: 1. The most direct meaning: what comes out of the mouth, the spoken words. In Genesis 11:1, all the men "had one language and the same words," meaning they spoke exactly the same way. 2. A transmitted message, news. In 2 Kings 20:4, "the word of the Lord" comes to Isaiah: God communicates something to him through the prophet's voice. 3. An order or instruction that imposes itself. Ezekiel receives the order to listen to "the word that will come out" of God's mouth (Ezekiel 3:17): it is a command he must execute. 4. A subject, a matter, something being discussed. When Jacob "heard the words of his sons" (Genesis 37:11), he was learning their words, their discourse. 5. A promise or commitment. Judah says "word kept!" in Genesis 44:18, meaning he keeps his promise. 6. What is said in a group, the rumor or what circulates. In Exodus 23:7, "you shall not listen to a false word": one must not spread lies or gossip.
H1697G.origine: The Hebrew word דָּבָר comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to say" or "to speak." It is a fundamental word in Hebrew, present in all periods of biblical language. It first designates what comes out of the mouth — the words — before expanding to encompass everything that "is said," in the sense of the subject or matter being discussed. The basic image is that of the word that emerges and spreads, carrying an intention or authority.
H1697G.emploi: The word דָּבָר is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, used over 1400 times. It appears in all books, from the Pentateuch (the first five books) to the Psalms and the Prophets. Often, it is found in phrases like "the word of the Lord," which designates the direct revelation that God addresses to the prophets (1 Samuel 3:19: "none of his words fell to the ground"). In narratives, it refers to the words of one character to another, the orders of a master, the promises exchanged. In moral exhortations, "word of truth" or "false word" marks the importance of speaking rightly (Psalms 119:43). The word thus encompasses declaration, order, as well as the matter or subject being treated: which allows Jeremiah to say "tell them this word" (Jeremiah 14:17) while introducing a long and serious prophetic message.
H1697G.portee: The believer who hears about "word" in the Bible learns to pay attention to what is said, particularly to what God says. It is a word that unites the power of human speech (capable of doing good or harm) and the absolute effectiveness of divine speech (which creates, which commands, which is fulfilled). Listening to the word of God thus becomes the central act of faith: it means receiving a message, an order, a promise that transforms everything. It also calls us to be mindful of our own words, for they carry weight.

sens: What is said, expressed by the mouth of a person
The action of speaking, the discourse itself
A promise, a commitment made on one's word
An order, an instruction to follow
A matter, a question, a subject being discussed
A fact, a thing that happens or is done
H1697H.detail:
1. The word is primarily what comes out of the mouth: the words we express, the thought conveyed in language. Laban said to Jacob: "Well! Let it be according to your word" (Genesis 30:34), in other words: "Okay, I will do what you ask."
2. The term also refers to the very act of speaking, the ongoing discourse. Samuel saw a man "speaking well" (1 Samuel 16:18), someone who masters the art of speech.
3. A word can be a promise or a personal commitment: when one says "on my word," one is putting oneself at stake, making a promise.
4. Word also means an order or instruction received from a superior. Elizabeth followed "according to the word of Elijah" (1 Kings 17:15), she obeyed what he had told her to do.
5. By extension, the term designates a matter, a question under discussion: Absalom asks Hushai: "Should we do what Ahithophel said, or not?" (2 Samuel 17:6), he is referring to the plan itself.
6. Finally, word can simply mean a fact or a thing: "a vain word," something unimportant that is said.
H1697H.origine: The word דָּבָר (davar) comes from a very ancient Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "putting back," "pushing back," then "saying" (as if the word comes from the depths of the heart that must be brought to light). This same root gives rise to words in the family of "reasoning," "matter," "thing." It is a fundamental word in Hebrew, very rich, encompassing both the action of speaking and its content, the statement and the order, the promise and the fact.
H1697H.emploi: דָּבָר appears 41 times in the provided passages, always in a pivotal position of meaning: it is the word of communication and authority. In historical narratives (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), it primarily designates the order received from a prophet or a king, the instruction to follow (Elisha, David). In dialogue, it represents the reply, what is said to one another, what is asked (Absalom, Esther). Job uses it for the act of speaking itself, the dialogue. Isaiah and Jeremiah use it for the prophetic word, the order of the Lord. Thus, the word naturally glides from the concrete sense (the words) to the strong sense (what must be done, the authority that speaks).
H1697H.portee: The word "word" reveals how seriously the Bible takes what is said: the word is not a vain noise; it engages the one who pronounces it and connects the one who utters it to the one who listens. When a prophet speaks in the name of God, his word is not just information — it is order, promise, power. For the Christian, this shows that the words of Jesus are not to be taken lightly: they create, they save, they engage our obedience.

sens: Statement or utterance formulated by the mouth, what is said
Commandment, order, directive
Subject of conversation, news, information
Matter, situation, particular case
Concrete thing, object
Fact, event, circumstance
H1697I.detail:
1. A word is what comes out of the mouth: a statement, a discourse, a simple phrase. In Genesis 15:1, "the word of the Lord" refers to the message addressed to Abram in the vision. It is the heard word, which carries a weight of reality.
2. A word can also be a commandment or directive to follow. In Exodus 35:1, Moses states "the things that the Lord commands to do," that is, words-commandments that require action. The divine word here obliges to act.
3. By extension, this term designates any subject being discussed: news, an event reported. In 2 Samuel 13:21, "King David learned all these things," meaning the facts that had occurred.
4. The word extends to any matter or situation, any particular case that deserves attention. In Esther 5:14, "this advice" (this word, this counsel) pleases Haman: it is a proposal, a matter to be addressed.
5. Word can also designate a concrete object or possession. In 2 Kings 20:13, "there was nothing that Hezekiah did not show them": here, word means "thing" in the sense of a material object.
6. Finally, word is used for any fact or event: the acts, the actions taken. This is the broadest sense: anything that exists or occurs can be called a word.
H1697I.origine: The Hebrew word דָּבָר (dabar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of speaking, of saying. The family of words includes verbs and nouns revolving around speech and enunciation. The primary image is that of the voice, of the word that comes out of the mouth and creates a reality — a commandment that is obeyed, news that is reported, a fact that is named. This shift in meaning from "spoken word" to "named thing" or "matter" shows how biblical Hebrew sees the word as creative: to name a thing is almost to create or establish it.
H1697I.emploi: The word dabar is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with over 270 occurrences. It appears as early as Genesis and spans all historical books, laws, and narratives.
