In a divine context, dabar designates the word of God: a direct communication, a revelation, a commandment (Genesis 15:1: "the word of the Lord was addressed"). In a legal or administrative context, it refers to matters to be judged, orders to be executed (Exodus 35:1: "the things that the Lord commands"). In a narrative context, it describes events or reported information (2 Samuel 13:21: "all these things"). The word thus covers the complete spectrum: from the most specific (a unique word) to the most general (a matter, a fact, a thing). This versatility reflects the biblical view where the word is never empty: it names, orders, informs, and creates.
H1697I.portee: For the Christian, understanding that dabar primarily applies to the divine word is essential. When the Bible speaks of "the word of the Lord," it designates a serious, performative communication: what is said comes to pass. This is why the word of God creates (Genesis 1) and why God's commandments obligate. But the term also applies to all human words: our words, our promises, our orders carry weight. This vocabulary invites the believer to take seriously what is said and what is done, knowing that every word counts before God.

sens: What is said, expressed by the mouth
Narrative, account, message
Matter, thing, case, concrete situation
Act, action, accomplishment
Promise, commitment of God to His people
H1697J.detail:
1. The word is primarily what comes out of the mouth: an utterance, a discourse. In 2 Samuel 14:13, the woman reports the "words" of the king, his own statements that judge him. In 1 Chronicles 25:5, Heman reveals the "words" of God, meaning His messages.

2. By extension, a word is a narrative or teaching conveyed: in Psalms 105:42, God remembers His "holy word," the covenant He declared to Abraham.

3. The term also refers to a matter, a situation, a case to be addressed. In Deuteronomy 13:14, an investigation is conducted to determine if "the matter" (the accusation) is true; in Deuteronomy 17:4, 17:9, 17:10, judges examine a "word" (a case, a dispute).

4. A word can be an act, an action carried out. In Joshua 21:45 and 1 Kings 8:20, God fulfills His word: He brings it to pass, He turns it into action.

5. Finally, the word becomes a divine promise: it is the commitment that God makes to His people and that He "fulfills" (Jeremiah 33:14). It is the word that binds God to His servants and is realized in history.
H1697J.origine: The Hebrew word "davar" comes from a root that expresses the idea of "saying" or "speaking." It is related to the notion of communication, of putting into words. In ancient Hebrew texts, this word is one of the most common: it encompasses both discourse (what is said) and reality (what is done), for Israel, to say is to act — the word of God never returns void. The Greek word "logos" often translates "davar" in the Greek version of the Old Testament.
H1697J.emploi: The word "davar" appears 24 times in the provided biblical usages, mainly in the historical and prophetic books of the Old Testament. It is especially frequent in legal contexts (Deuteronomy 13:14, 17:4, 17:9, 17:10: examining a matter) and in accounts of the fulfillment of God's promises (Joshua 21:45, 1 Kings 8:20, 2 Chronicles 6:10: God fulfills His word). In the Psalms and among the prophets, "davar" takes on a strong theological significance: it is the word that God has spoken and that He keeps (Psalms 105:42, Jeremiah 33:14). The word oscillates between a concrete sense (legal case, action) and a spiritual sense (divine promise, commitment).
H1697J.portee: For the believer, understanding that God keeps His "word" is a source of assurance and trust. The Bible affirms that God's promises are not empty words: they are realized, they come to pass in history. This invites the Christian to take seriously the commitments of God stated in Scripture and to base his faith on divine faithfulness. It also recognizes that, for God as for man, the word carries a responsibility: it creates a reality, it engages.

sens: What a person has done, what has happened
An event, a memorable fact
The entirety of acts and deeds of a life or reign
A word, what is said
A subject of conversation, a matter
What is written, a story told
H1697K.detail:
1. What a person has done, what has happened: the word primarily designates the concrete result of an action, what is set, accomplished. In 1 Samuel 11:5, when it is reported to Saul "what the men of Jabesh had said," the words and events that occurred are conveyed to him. It is the thing itself, the tangible event.
2. An event, a memorable fact: the emphasis is on what happens and deserves to be remembered. In 1 Kings 16:14, "the actions of Elah" refer to the significant facts of his royal life that were important enough to be recorded.
3. The entirety of acts and deeds of a life or reign: when historians wrote "the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel," they recorded "all the actions" of a king (2 Kings 13:8). This term encompasses the entire lived history of a person.
4. A word, what is said: the word can simply refer to the spoken words, the thing said. This is the simplest and most common usage: what comes out of the mouth.
5. A subject of conversation, a matter: in more general contexts, the word extends to any reality being discussed, to what occupies attention — a question, a case, what is debated (Esther 1:17-18).
6. What is written, a story told: the "Chronicles" (the word itself) are precisely collections of actions recorded in writing, of memory preserved.
H1697K.origine: The Hebrew word דָּבָר comes from a root that evokes the idea of "putting forward, pushing, proposing." It is related to other words meaning "to speak" and "to lead." Its primary meaning is what is set, established, made present — whether by word or by action. This is why it can mean both the spoken word and the accomplished fact: both "set" something real in the world. This word is very common in biblical Hebrew and remains one of the most versatile terms in the holy language.
H1697K.emploi: This word appears 64 times in the provided biblical usages, mostly in the historical books (Kings and Chronicles) and occasionally in the Psalms and Jeremiah. In the accounts of the kings, it constantly recurs in the formula: "The rest of the actions of [such a king]… is it not written in the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel?" (see 1 Kings 14:19, 2 Kings 13:8). This repetition shows that the word has crystallized to designate the memorable facts of a reign. In 1 Samuel 11:5 and 2 Samuel 11:18-19, it refers to the transmission of a word or news. In the Chronicles, the word expands: it can qualify the religious affairs of a king (2 Chronicles 29:29) or his constructions. Its fundamental meaning remains: what exists, what has happened, whether said or done.
H1697K.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the Bible is primarily a narrative of what has truly happened. The "actions" recorded are not inventions or abstract lessons, but historical realities. Moreover, the form of the word — which unites word and deed — invites reflection on the power of the word: a spoken word becomes an action, it establishes a new reality. This is how the word of God works: it never remains an empty word, it accomplishes what it was sent for.

sens: Word spoken, discourse
Thing said, declaration, account
Subject in dispute, case to be judged
Fact, event, matter
Occupation, activity, task
H1697L.detail:
1. The most primitive meaning: the word that comes out of the mouth, the spoken statement. It is language in action, living word (Deuteronomy 16:19: the "words of the righteous" corrupted by gifts).
2. By extension, what is said becomes a thing, a matter that is spoken about. A declaration, an accusation, a narrative that is transmitted (Deuteronomy 22:14: "he imputes criminal things to her").
3. Very often in the Bible, a case refers to a judicial matter, a dispute between two people that the judge must examine and resolve. The judges of Israel dealt with these cases (Exodus 18:16: "they come to me; I pronounce between them").
4. The word broadens further: case becomes fact, event, or any matter — what happens, what exists, anything that can be the object of an action or a word (Deuteronomy 24:1: "something shameful").
5. By metonymy, the case also refers to the occupation, activity, the work of a person — what they are concerned with (Psalms 112:5: the righteous man "conducts his affairs with justice").
H1697L.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that primitively expresses the idea of speaking, saying. It is found in other words of the same family that mean "word," "discourse." The starting image is the word that goes out, that manifests itself. From there, the word has shifted from the meaning of "word" to "what is spoken about," then to "thing" in general and to "judicial matter." This evolution follows the natural movement of thought: the word pertains to something, and that something becomes the "case."
H1697L.emploi: The word appears very frequently in the Torah and the history of Israel, especially in judicial and administrative contexts. It is particularly abundant in chapters 16 to 24 of Deuteronomy, which deal with justice and law. At Sinai, Moses explains to Jethro (Exodus 18) how he judges the people's cases. In these legal contexts, the case is always a matter between two parties, a dispute that the judge examines in light of the Law. The word is also used for accusations (Deuteronomy 22:14) and for grounds for divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1). Outside the judicial framework, it simply means thing, fact, or occupation (Psalms 112:5, Ecclesiastes 8:3).
H1697L.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God Himself is a just judge who examines cases and defends the oppressed. The Law of Moses emphasizes impartial and transparent judgment: each case must be handled according to truth, not appearance or gift. Understanding how Israel conceived of a "case" helps to better grasp the biblical meaning of justice and responsibility before God. It is also a reminder that in the Kingdom of God, every word and act will be examined at their true value.

sens: Word, spoken or written statement
Thing, matter, subject being discussed
Reason, motive for which something happens
Occasion, circumstance that gives rise to an event
Act, action, work
H1697M.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the spoken or written word, what is stated: it is the most concrete and original image of the Hebrew word.
2. By extension, it designates the thing being spoken about, the matter, the subject: in Joshua 5:4, "the reason" for which Joshua circumcised refers to the situation or the matter itself.
3. It also means the cause, the hidden or declared motive of an event: "because of you" in Deuteronomy 4:21 explains why the Lord was angry with Moses.
4. It can designate the concrete occasion, the moment or circumstance that provokes something: in Nehemiah 8:4, Ezra is placed on a platform "on this occasion," meaning for this specific event.
5. Finally, it encompasses the act, the action, or the work: what is done, accomplished, or happens.
H1697M.origine: The Hebrew word דָּבָר (davar) comes from a root that means "to say" or "to speak." Its primary image is therefore the word, what comes out of the mouth. From there, it naturally extends to everything that can be said — a subject, a matter, an event — then to anything that is spoken about or that occurs. It is a very frequent word in the Old Testament, fundamental for understanding how ancient Hebrew connects word to reality.
H1697M.emploi: This word appears 33 times in the provided usages, mostly in the sense of "cause" or "reason" introducing an explanation. In Genesis 12:17 and Genesis 20:18, it explains why the Lord intervenes ("concerning Sarai"). In Deuteronomy 4:21 and Deuteronomy 15:10, it indicates the reason for a divine action ("because of"). In Joshua 5:4 and 1 Kings 11:27, it means rather "reason" or "occasion," the circumstance of an act. In Nehemiah 8:4, it designates the occasion, the particular event. The word is often used after prepositions ("because of," "concerning") to mark the causal or circumstantial link.
H1697M.portee: This word sheds light on how the Bible understands the causes of events: nothing happens by chance, but for a reason that is often visible (a fault, a decision) or hidden (the purpose of God). Understanding the "causes" mentioned in Scripture helps the reader to see divine wisdom and justice at work, and to grasp that our actions have consequences.

sens: A part, a determined quantity allocated to someone
What is received regularly, each day or each time
An allocation, a ration of food or salary
H1697N.detail:
1. A portion is a part, a measured and distributed quantity. In Exodus 16:4, the people must gather "each day the necessary amount" of bread from heaven: a determined portion for one day. It is a measure, a defined share.

2. The word also designates what is received regularly at fixed intervals. In 2 Chronicles 9:24, "each year" presents are brought: an annual portion. It is the same pattern that repeats.

3. A portion can be an allocation, a maintenance provided regularly. In 2 Kings 25:30, the king "constantly provided for his daily maintenance": he paid each day the necessary portion to live. Similarly, in Nehemiah 11:23, a "fixed salary" was granted daily to the singers: a daily portion of remuneration.
H1697N.origine: The Hebrew word dāḇār comes from a root that primarily means "word, thing said." The meaning of "portion" is an extension of this: what is said, prescribed, or fixed becomes what is allocated, assigned. In Hebrew, the same word can designate both the "word" (what is stated) and "the matter, the thing, the portion" (what practically results from it). This is why it appears in lists of varied translations: the context determines whether the emphasis is on the stated content or on the practical reality that results from it.
H1697N.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the provided usages, almost always in a context of regular allocation or distribution. In Exodus 16:4 and Leviticus 23:37, it designates the prescribed quantity: that which must be gathered or offered. In 2 Kings 25:30, Nehemiah 11:23, and Jeremiah 52:34 (according to the references), it refers to a food allocation or a daily salary paid regularly. The word often conveys the idea of "each day," "each time," or "fixed quantity" — which shows that "portion" emphasizes less on absolute size than on the determined and repeated nature of what is provided.
H1697N.portee: Understanding that God distributes with regularity and just measures inspires confidence. The daily portion of heavenly bread in Exodus 16 teaches that it is enough to receive what God grants each day, without hoarding or fearing tomorrow. For the Christian, it is a call to depend on divine providence and to accept with gratitude what is due, rather than to covet or hoard.

sens: Sound statement, what is said or spoken
Thing, fact, concrete or abstract reality
Action, act, exploit
Story, event worthy of remembrance
Matter, subject of conversation or reflection
H1697O.detail:
1. The word is primarily what comes out of the mouth: an utterance, a discourse. This is the most direct and common meaning of the word in Hebrew. All verbal communication falls within this domain.

2. However, the word quickly extends to encompass any reality, anything that exists or occurs, which can be pointed to or recounted. Genesis 44:7 illustrates this flexibility: "how would we say such a thing?" — not words, but an accusation, a serious fact.

3. Human action, an exploit, or a significant gesture is also referred to as "word": 1 Samuel 17:27 reports that "the people repeated the same things" when speaking of David's exploits. The action carries the weight and presence of a word.

4. When reading "the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel" (1 Kings 15:31 and elsewhere), it is a record of acts and events deemed worthy of remembrance — the gestures that make history, which human words transmit and preserve.

5. By extension, it is the very matter of discourse, the object being discussed: in Genesis 18:25, "this manner of acting" literally translates to "this word," meaning the question, the subject of which Abraham contests the relevance.
H1697O.origine: The word דָּבָר comes from a root that fundamentally means "to speak." In ancient Hebrew, the word is never a simple empty expression: it is an act, it produces reality — hence its shift towards "thing," "fact," "matter." The same root appears in other forms: דִּבֵּר (to speak), דִּבְרָה (word), and even in proper names ending in -dbar. This word also appears in biblical Aramaic (דָּבַר) and in other neighboring Semitic languages with identical meanings.
H1697O.emploi: The word appears 56 times in the provided biblical usages, almost always in narrative or historiographical prose (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah). The meaning varies according to the context: it is primarily a "word" or an "affair" in dialogue narratives (Genesis 18, 32, 39, 44), then very often "action" or "chronicle" in the history of the kings (the formula "the rest of his actions" recurs regularly). The word can also designate an ordinance or a decree (Deuteronomy 4:32, Isaiah 8:20). In all cases, it is a unit of meaning and reality, a block of life that deserves to be named and remembered.
H1697O.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the word is not insignificant: to speak is to create, to establish reality. The Hebrew Bible sees in the word an active force — this is why God speaks and things come to be (Genesis 1). Learning what a "word" is in Hebrew means understanding that our words and actions are never separate: they together form the fabric of our testimony.

sens: Deadly disease that strikes humans
Disease that affects livestock
Epidemic sent by God as punishment
Scourge that ravages an entire people
H1698.detail:
1. The plague is primarily a contagious and deadly disease that rapidly decimates the population: it "walks in darkness" and strikes indiscriminately the rich and the poor (Psalms 91:6), sowing terror and death among the inhabitants of a land.

2. The word also refers to diseases of livestock — the mortality of the herd, cattle disease — which destroy the wealth and economy of peoples, as seen in the plagues of Egypt where God strikes Pharaoh's herds (Exodus 9:3, 9:15).

3. In biblical theology, the plague is regularly presented as a divine judgment, one of the three forms of punishment that God inflicts on His rebellious people, alongside famine and the sword: "you will die by the sword, by famine, or by the plague" (Jeremiah 42:22).

4. It is a collective scourge that strikes an entire nation or city, an instrument of divine wrath capable of exterminating men, women, children, and animals simultaneously (Ezekiel 14:19, 14:21), worse than any natural calamity.
H1698.origine: The Hebrew word דֶּ֫בֶר comes from a root evoking speech, but also destruction: it is related to the verb דָּבַר ("to speak") and the noun דָּבָר ("thing, word"). This ancient connection suggests that the plague descends "like a word" from God that is realized irresistibly. In Greek, it is rendered as λοιμός (loimós), which specifically denotes plague, deadly contagion.
H1698.emploi: The word appears 48 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in historical narratives and prophecies. It is very frequent in the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 5, 9), in the blessings and curses of the covenant (Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28), and especially in the prophetic books, notably Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The Bible often lists the plague alongside famine and the sword as the three major forms of divine judgment (2 Samuel 24:13, Jeremiah 21:6-7). Sometimes it is also associated with other scourges: locusts, rust, mildew, diseases (1 Kings 8:37, 2 Chronicles 6:28). The word consistently retains its meaning of divine calamity, never of a simple ordinary disease.
H1698.portee: The plague reminds us that God's judgment is real and terrifies nations that reject His commandments. It also teaches the importance of turning to God in repentance to avert His anger: when the people pray and plead, God can stop the plague (2 Chronicles 20:9). For the believer, this word invites us to see beyond natural scourges the hand of God that governs history and reminds us of the serious consequences of collective sin.

sens: Grassland where herds graze
Place of food and rest for animals
Image of a gathered people entrusted to care
H1699A.detail: 1. The pasture is the grassy land where sheep and lambs go to graze and find their food — what Segond directly translates as the French word "pâturage." In Isaiah 5:17, after the judgment on the rebellious vines, sheep graze "as in their pasture," an image of land returned to its wild state. 2. By extension, it is the peaceful living place of the herds: Micah 2:12 speaks of the gathering of the remnant of Israel, compared to sheep "in its pasture," united and protected like a flock in its nourishing enclosure. 3. In biblical figurative language, the pasture becomes an image of the rest, protection, and abundance that God offers to His people, who is their shepherd.
H1699A.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּבֶר (dober) comes from the root דבר (dabbar), which expresses the idea of word or spoken thing. But here, the word has specialized to designate the place where the livestock is spoken to, or rather the grazing place where the flock "gathers": it is a concrete, pastoral space, linked to the life of the shepherd. In Hebrew, it is a rural word, infrequently used, that remains alive among the pastoral peoples of the ancient Near East.
H1699A.emploi: The word דֹּבֶר (dober) appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the prophetic context of divine judgment and restoration. In Isaiah 5:17, after the judgment on Israel's injustices, the pasture ironically becomes the place of reversal: sheep graze where the vines of the rich have been destroyed. In Micah 2:12, the same word becomes a promise of comfort: God will gather the remnant of Israel and lead them like a shepherd his flock to pasture, an image of restoration and peace. It is a word that carries both judgment and hope.
H1699A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word evokes the image of the shepherd and the flock that Jesus takes up in saying "I am the good shepherd" (John 10). The pasture is not primarily a place, but a relationship: that of a people entrusted to the care of a benevolent leader who nourishes and protects them. It is a word of comfort: even after judgment, God does not abandon His own; He gathers them and brings them back to calm and abundance.

sens: Statement, remark made by someone
Prophetic or divine message
Thing said, matter or subject being discussed
H1699B.detail: 1. In the most concrete sense, a word is anything that comes out of a person's mouth — a statement, a remark. In Jeremiah 5:13, the expression "no one speaks in them" literally means "no word in them": the false prophets produce only wind, with no true discourse to convey. 2. Often, this word specifically refers to a word from God, a divine or prophetic message: it is the word of the Lord that comes to the prophets and that they must proclaim. 3. By extension, a word can also refer to the thing being discussed, the matter or subject: the word thus becomes what occupies the heart and the mouth, what is being dealt with.
H1699B.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to speak" or "to say." It is a noun derived from the verb: it thus designates the act of speaking concretized in a statement. The same root produces other forms that all express verbal communication, whether human or divine. This word is the primary expression of relationship and authority: when God speaks, His word creates and orders.
H1699B.emploi: This word appears only once in this specific usage. In Jeremiah 5:13, it is used to denounce the false prophets: while true prophets are filled with the word of the Lord and proclaim it with authority, these impostors carry only an empty word, wind without substance. It is a polemical usage that highlights the emptiness of one who speaks without divine mission.
H1699B.portee: This verse reminds the reader of the strength and seriousness of true word. The word of God is never hollow or superficial; it carries weight and reality. Distinguishing the true word from the false requires discernment, and this text invites the believer to evaluate what they hear: is there a divine substance behind it, or just wind?

sens: Eldest son of Levi, ancestor of a branch of the Levites
Lineage of Levites responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple
H1647H.detail:
1. Gershom is the eldest son of Levi, the patriarch from whom all the Levites descended (1 Chronicles 6:16). He is the brother of Kohath and Merari, and he himself has sons, notably Libni and Shimei (1 Chronicles 6:17), whose names appear in the Levitical genealogies.
2. The descendants of Gershom form an important branch of the Levites of the Temple. They receive thirteen cities for their habitation and service (1 Chronicles 6:62, 6:71), including Golan in Bashan and Ashtaroth. This distribution of cities shows their recognized role in the religious organization of Israel.
H1647H.origine: The name Gershom means "stranger" or "expulsion." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of exile or separation. It is the name given to Levi's firstborn, who will become the head of one of the three major families of Levites, alongside Kohath and Merari.
H1647H.emploi: Gershom appears six times in the Bible, solely in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6, where the descendants of Levi's three sons are listed. These passages describe his lineage (son of Levi), his own sons, and the genealogy of his descendants up to the time of the Temple. The texts also mention the cities assigned to his descendants for their cultic service, highlighting the institutional importance of this Levitical branch in the religious life of Israel. Gershom rarely appears with narrative details: it is mainly through these genealogical lists that he is known.
